OpenTelemetry — Complete OTCA Guide

From Zero to OpenTelemetry Certified Associate

A comprehensive guide covering observability fundamentals, OpenTelemetry architecture, instrumentation, the Collector, metrics, traces, logs, and OTCA certification preparation — using anihpj/jobpost Django project deployed on Docker & Kubernetes with full OTel instrumentation.

🔭 OpenTelemetry CNCF Observability Traces Metrics Logs OTLP Collector 🐳 Docker ☸️ Kubernetes 🟢 Beginner-Friendly

🔭 Welcome to the OpenTelemetry Complete Learning Guide!
Aligned with the official OTCA (OpenTelemetry Certified Associate) syllabus from the Linux Foundation. From observability basics to production-grade telemetry pipelines — using anihpj/jobpost on 🐳 Docker & ☸️ Kubernetes.

🗺️ Master Summary & Roadmap

Your Journey to OTCA Certification

This guide maps directly to the OTCA syllabus from the Linux Foundation. Every chapter, diagram, and practice question builds your understanding systematically — from observability fundamentals to managing production telemetry pipelines. We use anihpj/jobpost throughout as our hands-on demo, deployed on 🐳 Docker (local dev) and ☸️ Kubernetes (production). See Appendix D for the complete setup.

🔄 The Evolution: Monitoring → Observability

How Real Companies Evolved Their Observability
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              THE EVOLUTION — HOW THE INDUSTRY CHANGED                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  📟 2000s: Nagios/Zabbix       📊 2010s: Graphite/Grafana                │
  │  "Is the server up?"           "What's the CPU curve?"                   │
  │  • Ping + disk check           • Time-series metrics                     │
  │  • Alert if CPU > 90%          • Beautiful dashboards                    │
  │  • Monolith: 1 server          • Still: known unknowns only              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🔍 2018: Jaeger/Zipkin        🧠 2022+: OTel + AI                       │
  │  "Where is the bottleneck?"    "Why is it broken?"                       │
  │  • Distributed tracing          • Correlated signals                     │
  │  • Microservices visibility     • SLO-based alerting                     │
  │  • Still: separate tools        • AI anomaly detection                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🏢 REAL EXAMPLE: Shopify (2,000+ services)                               │
  │  2020: 15+ monitoring tools, no standards, debug=45min                   │
  │  2023: 100% OTel, 1T spans/day, debug=3min, 35% cost reduction           │
  │  Key: Unified on OTLP protocol → one pipeline for all telemetry           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔄 Telemetry Data Lifecycle — From Code to Dashboard

A Real Span's Journey — Step by Step
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              ONE SPAN'S JOURNEY THROUGH THE PIPELINE                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  1. YOUR CODE (Django view)        2. OTel SDK (in-process)               │
  │  ┌────────────────────────┐       ┌────────────────────────┐            │
  │  │ with tracer.start_as_  │       │ Span created in memory │            │
  │  │   current_span(        │──────▶│ trace_id: a1b2c3...    │            │
  │  │     "jobpost.create"): │       │ span_id: 00f067aa...   │            │
  │  │   span.set_attribute(  │       │ start_time: now        │            │
  │  │     "user.id", 42)     │       │ attributes populated   │            │
  │  │   JobPost.objects      │       │ span.end() called      │            │
  │  │     .create(...)       │       │ → BatchSpanProcessor   │            │
  │  └────────────────────────┘       └───────────┬────────────┘            │
  │                                               │                          │
  │  3. BATCHING (200ms or 512 spans)             │                          │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐   │                          │
  │  │ Spans queued until timeout or batch full│◀──┘                          │
  │  │ Protobuf-encoded for efficiency         │                              │
  │  │ gRPC stream → Collector:4317            │                              │
  │  └────────────────────┬───────────────────┘                              │
  │                       │                                                  │
  │  4. COLLECTOR (receive→process→export)   5. BACKEND (Jaeger/Tempo)       │
  │  ┌────────────────────────┐             ┌────────────────────────┐       │
  │  │ Memory limiter checks  │             │ Span stored in DB      │       │
  │  │ Batch re-groups        │────────────▶│ Indexed by: trace_id,  │       │
  │  │ Attributes enriched    │             │   service, operation   │       │
  │  │ Filter drops /health    │             │ Available in Jaeger UI│       │
  │  │ Exporter sends OTLP     │             │ Waterfall view ready  │       │
  │  └────────────────────────┘             └────────────────────────┘       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⏱️ TOTAL LATENCY: ~200ms batch wait + ~5ms network + ~10ms processing   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📈 Your 5-Part Learning Journey

1
Part 1: Fundamentals (Ch 1-4) 🟢 18%

What is observability? The 3 pillars. OTel architecture. Context propagation & sampling. Real skill: Explain observability to your team.

2
Part 2: API & SDK (Ch 5-11) 🟡 46%

Manual & auto instrumentation. Traces deep dive. Jaeger. Real skill: Instrument any Python app with OTel.

3
Part 3: Metrics & Collector (Ch 12-14) 🟡 26%

6 instrument types. RED/USE/Business metrics. Prometheus + Grafana. Real skill: Build production dashboards.

4
Part 4: Pipelines & Backends (Ch 15-18) 🔴 10%

Logs bridge. Collector deep dive. Exporters. Vendor backends. Real skill: Deploy production Collector + switch backends.

5
Part 5: Exam Prep (Ch 19-22) 🔴

Strategy, 10 labs, 3 practice exams, quick-ref cards. Real skill: Pass the OTCA with confidence.

🛠️ SRE / Platform Engineer — Practical OTel Ops

This is the operations-focused companion to the OTCA study guide. While the main chapters teach you concepts for the exam, this section covers what you'll actually DO day-to-day as an SRE or Platform Engineer running OTel in production.

Daily SRE Workflow with OpenTelemetry
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              SRE DAILY OPS — HOW OTEL FITS YOUR WORKFLOW                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ☀️ MORNING (Dashboard Review):                                          │
  │  1. Open Grafana → anihpj RED dashboard                                  │
  │  2. Check: Error rate < 1%? P95 latency < 500ms?                        │
  │  3. Check: Any alerts fired overnight?                                   │
  │  4. Check: Error budget remaining > 50%?                                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🔥 INCIDENT RESPONSE (When Something Breaks):                           │
  │  1. Grafana alert fires: "POST /api/jobs/ error rate > 5%"              │
  │  2. Click exemplar on latency spike → opens exact trace in Jaeger        │
  │  3. Trace shows: "INSERT jobpost" span = 2.1s (normally 180ms!)         │
  │  4. Copy trace_id → paste in Loki: {trace_id="..."}                      │
  │  5. Log shows: "DB connection pool exhausted (20/20), waiting 2s"       │
  │  6. Root cause: Connection pool too small after deploy                   │
  │  7. Fix: Increase pool from 20→50, restart                              │
  │  8. Verify: Error rate drops to 0%, latency back to 180ms               │
  │  ⏱️ Total time to root cause: ~3 minutes (vs 30+ without OTel)          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🌙 EVENING (Capacity Planning):                                         │
  │  1. Check: Job creation rate trend (last 30 days)                        │
  │  2. Check: P99 latency trend (degrading?)                                │
  │  3. Check: DB pool utilization at peak                                   │
  │  4. Plan: Scale replicas from 3→5 before Black Friday                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔧 Common SRE Tasks with OTel

Deploy new service: Add OTel SDK, set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, point to Collector — done.
Debug latency: Find slowest span in Jaeger waterfall → fix bottleneck.
Set SLO: Define error budget in Prometheus → Grafana alert when budget burns.
Cost control: Enable tail sampling → keep only errors + 10% normal traces.

📊 Key Metrics Every SRE Needs

Golden Signals (RED): Rate, Errors, Duration per endpoint
Resource (USE): CPU, Memory, DB pool, Cache hit ratio
SLO Tracking: Error budget remaining %, burn rate
Business: Jobs created, applications submitted, users registered

⚠️ SRE Anti-Patterns to Avoid

  • "I'll add OTel later": Instrument on Day 1. Retrofitting is 10x harder.
  • "100% sampling in production": At 1000 req/s that's 260M spans/month = 1TB storage.
  • "I'll just grep the logs": With trace_id injection, Loki queries are instant. grep is not.
  • "One dashboard for everything": RED for services, USE for infra, Business for stakeholders.
  • "Alert on everything": Alert on SLO burn rate, not individual metric thresholds.

📚 OTCA Exam Amplification Pack

Consolidated study reference — every must-know fact, diagram, and pattern from all 22 chapters in one place.

🔑 Top 10 Must-Know Facts

1. OTel is NOT a backend — it generates/collects telemetry
2. OTLP: gRPC:4317, HTTP:4318
3. 6 metric instruments (Counter through ObservableGauge)
4. RED for services, USE for infrastructure
5. Collector is optional but recommended
6. Batch + Memory Limiter ALWAYS in production
7. Sampling is for TRACES only (not metrics/logs)
8. Logs Bridge API — bridge, don't replace
9. traceparent: 00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-{flags}
10. Instrument once, export anywhere — no vendor lock-in

📐 Key Diagrams to Remember

• Trace waterfall (parent→child spans)
• OTel Architecture (API→SDK→Collector→OTLP→Backend)
• Metrics pipeline (Instrument→Meter→Reader→Exporter)
• Collector pipeline (Receiver→Processor→Exporter)
• Context propagation (traceparent header flow)
• LGTM Stack (Loki+Grafana+Tempo+Mimir)
• Three-signal correlation (trace_id links all)

📋 Part 1 Summary — Fundamentals of Observability

🗺️ What Part 1 Covers (OTCA Domain 1 — 18%)

Part 1 builds your foundation in observability. You'll understand why monitoring evolved into observability, what the three pillars are, how OpenTelemetry fits into the CNCF ecosystem, and where context propagation and sampling fit into distributed tracing. Every concept is tied back to our simple anihpj/jobpost Django demo app.

  • Ch 1: What is Observability? — Logs, Metrics, Traces, and the evolution from Nagios to OTel
  • Ch 2: Intro to OpenTelemetry — The CNCF standard, vendor neutrality, project structure
  • Ch 3: Architecture Deep Dive — API, SDK, Collector, and OTLP protocol
  • Ch 4: Context Propagation & Sampling — W3C Trace-Context, Baggage, Head/Tail sampling

🚀 How to Implement — Your First Observability Pipeline

Here's the complete setup you'll build through Part 1. Start with this Docker Compose file to run all the observability components alongside anihpj:

Docker Compose — anihpj + OTel + Jaeger (Development Stack)
version: '3.8'
services:
  # Your Django application (the thing we're observing)
  anihpj:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      - OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=anihpj-api
      - OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4317
      - OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio
      - OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.25
      - OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=deployment.environment=development
    depends_on:
      - otel-collector

  # OpenTelemetry Collector — receives, processes, exports telemetry
  otel-collector:
    image: otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:latest
    command: ["--config=/etc/otelcol/config.yaml"]
    volumes:
      - ./otelcol-config.yaml:/etc/otelcol/config.yaml
    ports:
      - "4317:4317"   # OTLP gRPC
      - "4318:4318"   # OTLP HTTP

  # Jaeger — trace storage and visualization backend
  jaeger:
    image: jaegertracing/all-in-one:latest
    ports:
      - "16686:16686"  # Jaeger UI
      - "4317"         # OTLP (internal)

  # Optional: Prometheus for metrics
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:latest
    ports:
      - "9090:9090"

  # Optional: Grafana for unified dashboards
  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:latest
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
1
docker compose up

Start the full stack in one command

2
curl localhost:8000

Hit anihpj endpoints to generate traces

3
localhost:16686

Open Jaeger UI — see your first traces!

4
localhost:9090

Open Prometheus — see metrics accumulating

5
localhost:3000

Open Grafana — build dashboards

💡 What Just Happened?

When you ran docker compose up, you launched a complete observability pipeline: Your Django app (anihpj) sends traces and metrics to the OTel Collector via OTLP on port 4317. The Collector batches and forwards them to Jaeger (for traces) and Prometheus (for metrics). Grafana queries both to show unified dashboards. This is the exact architecture you'll understand deeply by the end of Part 1.

📋 OpenTelemetry — Master Implementation Summary

This is your one-page roadmap to implementing OpenTelemetry from zero to production. It summarizes the complete journey covered across all 22 chapters — refer back to this page whenever you need the big picture.

🎯 What is OpenTelemetry? — One Sentence Definition
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                          │
  │   OpenTelemetry is a CNCF standard that lets you instrument your code    │
  │   ONCE (using a vendor-neutral SDK) and export telemetry (traces,        │
  │   metrics, logs) to ANY backend (Jaeger, Prometheus, Datadog, etc.)      │
  │   by changing ONLY configuration — ZERO code changes.                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │   OTel = GENERATE + COLLECT + EXPORT.  NOT store.  NOT visualize.       │
  │                                                                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🚀 The Complete Implementation Flow — 5 Steps from Zero to Production
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          HOW TO IMPLEMENT OPENTELEMETRY — THE COMPLETE JOURNEY            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1: INSTRUMENT (Ch 5-7) — Add OTel to your code                     │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ pip install opentelemetry-distro                                   │  │
  │  │ opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install  ← Auto-discover instrumentations│  │
  │  │ export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=anihpj-api  ← REQUIRED!                   │  │
  │  │ opentelemetry-instrument python manage.py runserver                │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Result: Your app now generates spans, metrics, and correlated logs │  │
  │  │          with ZERO code changes (auto-instrumentation)!            │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STEP 2: COLLECT (Ch 16) — Deploy the OTel Collector                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ docker run otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib \                  │  │
  │  │   -v ./otelcol-config.yaml:/etc/otelcol/config.yaml               │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ config.yaml:                                                       │  │
  │  │   receivers: [otlp]  ← Accept data from your app                  │  │
  │  │   processors: [batch, memory_limiter]  ← ALWAYS include these!    │  │
  │  │   exporters: [otlp/jaeger, prometheus, logging]  ← Route to backs │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Result: Central pipeline for batching, filtering, and routing      │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │

  │  │ docker run jaegertracing/all-in-one  ← Traces on :16686           │  │
  │  │ docker run prom/prometheus           ← Metrics on :9090           │  │
  │  │ docker run grafana/grafana           ← Dashboards on :3000        │  │

  │  │ Grafana: RED dashboard (Rate, Errors, Duration) → SLO tracking    │  │

  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ • Sampling: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio, ARG=0.1 │  │

🔍 TRACES

Question: "Where in the journey?"
A trace = tree of spans showing one request's path through all services. trace_id (32 hex) connects them all.

auto-instrumentation → free!

📊 METRICS

Question: "How much? How fast?"
6 instrument types: Counter(↑), UpDown(↕), Histogram(dist), ObsGauge, ObsUD, ObsCounter.

RED = Rate + Errors + Duration

📝 LOGS

Question: "What happened?"
Bridge existing logger → OTel injects trace_id automatically → correlate with traces.

LoggingInstrumentor().instrument()

🛠️ Quick-Start — Copy-Paste to Get OTel Running

🐍 Python (anihpj) — 5 Commands to Instrument
# 1. Install OTel distro + bootstrap all instrumentations
pip install opentelemetry-distro
opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install

# 2. Configure OTel
export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=anihpj-api
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4317

# 3. Run with automatic instrumentation
opentelemetry-instrument python manage.py runserver
🐳 Docker — Collector + Jaeger Backend
# Jaeger all-in-one (traces backend + UI on :16686)
docker run -d --name jaeger \
  -p 16686:16686 -p 4317:4317 \
  jaegertracing/all-in-one

# OpenTelemetry Collector (receives & exports telemetry)
docker run -d --name otel-collector \
  -p 4317:4317 -v ./otelcol-config.yaml:/etc/otel/config.yaml \
  otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib

⚠️ Top 5 OTCA Exam Traps to Avoid

#Trap StatementCorrect Answer
1"OTel replaces Prometheus/Jaeger"NO — OTel COMPLEMENTS them. Generates telemetry; they store it.
2"OTel is an observability backend"NO — OTel generates & collects. Backends store & visualize.
3"The Collector is required"NO — Optional but recommended. SDK can export directly.
4"span.set_attribute() propagates downstream"NO — Attributes are LOCAL. Use baggage for cross-service data.
5"Sampling applies to metrics too"NO — Sampling is for TRACES only. Metrics are aggregated.

Chapter 1: What is Observability? — The Big Picture 🟢 Beginner

Chapter 1: What is Observability? — Understanding the Fundamentals

Before diving into OpenTelemetry code and collectors, let's understand why observability exists, what problems it solves, and how it fundamentally differs from traditional monitoring. We'll use our anihpj/jobpost Django app to make every concept concrete and actionable.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📖 Concepts 🎯 Foundation
🎓 OTCA Relevance
Domain 1: Fundamentals ~18% Foundation

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — Observability in Plain English

If you're completely new to observability, here's the simplest way to understand it:

1. Think of your application as a car. Traditional monitoring is like your dashboard — it tells you speed, fuel level, engine temperature. If the "check engine" light comes on, you know something is wrong. But you don't know what — a loose gas cap? A failing catalytic converter? You need a mechanic with diagnostic tools.

2. Observability is those diagnostic tools. It lets you ask: "Why did the engine misfire at 2,500 RPM specifically when the outside temperature was below 40°F?" You can investigate problems you never anticipated when building the dashboard.

3. The "Three Pillars" are your diagnostic data: Logs = the car's event history ("At 14:30, fuel pressure dropped to 20 PSI"). Metrics = the gauges (RPM, temperature, fuel consumption rate over time). Traces = following one specific drive from ignition to parking — seeing exactly where delays happened.

4. For anihpj: When a user says "Job posting failed," traditional monitoring might show "CPU at 45%, memory at 60% — everything looks fine!" But with observability, you can trace that exact failed request and see: "The auth service responded in 25ms ✅, the validation passed ✅, but the PostgreSQL INSERT took 30 seconds and timed out ❌ — there's a table lock!"

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ How monitoring evolved into observability — and why the shift matters for modern systems
  • ✅ The Three Pillars: Logs ("what happened"), Metrics ("how much"), and Traces ("where in the journey")
  • ✅ Why traditional monitoring tools fail in microservices architectures
  • ✅ The key differences between monitoring and observability — it's not just semantics
  • ✅ How the anihpj/jobpost Django application generates all three signal types
  • ✅ Hands-on: See the three pillars in action on a real Django application
Why "Observability vs Monitoring" Matters on the OTCA Exam

The OTCA exam tests your understanding of observability as a property of the system, not just a set of tools. Key concepts to internalize:

  • Observability is a system property — Can you answer NEW questions about your system without writing new code? If yes, your system is observable.
  • Monitoring tells you WHAT; observability tells you WHY. The exam will test this distinction with scenario-based questions.
  • The Three Pillars work TOGETHER. Logs alone aren't observability. Metrics alone aren't observability. You need all three, correlated.
  • OpenTelemetry is the enabler — It generates the rich telemetry data that makes a system observable.

1.1 The Evolution: Monitoring → Observability

The Evolution of System Understanding — Four Eras
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  FROM MONITORING TO OBSERVABILITY                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  │  │  📟 2000s    │   │  📊 2010s     │   │  🔍 2018+     │   │  🧠 2022+     │
  │  │  MONITORING  │──▶│  METRICS+VIS │──▶│  DISTRIBUTED  │──▶│  OBSERVABILITY│
  │  │              │   │              │   │  TRACING      │   │              │
  │  ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤

  │  │ Zabbix       │   │ Grafana      │   │ Zipkin       │   │ + LGTM Stack │
  │  │              │   │ Prometheus   │   │              │   │              │
  │  ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤
  │  │ Question:    │   │ Question:    │   │ Question:    │   │ Question:    │
  │  │ "Is it up?"  │   │ "What curve?"│   │ "Where slow?"│   │ "WHY broken?"│
  │  ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤
  │  │ Data:        │   │ Data:        │   │ Data:        │   │ Data:        │
  │  │ Binary       │   │ Time-series  │   │ Spans+Traces │   │ Logs+Metrics │
  │  │ up/down      │   │ metrics      │   │              │   │ +Traces+Context│
  │  ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤   ├──────────────┤

  │  └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Traditional monitoring emerged in the era of monolithic applications. You had one server, one database, one log file. If something went wrong, you checked: Is the server up? Is the CPU under 90%? Is disk space OK? These were known unknowns — you knew what could go wrong and set up alerts for those specific scenarios.

But modern systems are different. An anihpj microservices deployment might have: Django API pods, PostgreSQL, Redis cache, Celery workers, Nginx ingress, and an authentication sidecar. A single user request touches 5+ services. When something breaks, the question isn't "Is the CPU high?" — it's "Which of these 5 services caused the checkout latency spike, and why?"

This shift — from known unknowns to unknown unknowns — is what drove the evolution from monitoring to observability. Observability isn't about having more dashboards; it's about having rich enough telemetry data that you can ask questions you never anticipated when you built the system.

📖 Key Term: Observability (O11y)

Observability is a measure of how well you can understand the internal state of a system from its external outputs. A system is "observable" if you can answer new, unanticipated questions about its behavior without deploying new code or instrumentation. The term originates from control theory (Rudolf E. Kálmán, 1960) — a system is observable if you can determine its complete internal state by observing its outputs.

🚢 The Shipping Port Analogy — How OpenTelemetry Observability Works

Think of observability like a global shipping operation. Your application is a shipping port — thousands of containers (requests) moving through cranes (spans), conveyor belts (context propagation), and shipping lanes (OTLP).

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              🚢 THE SHIPPING PORT — OPENTELEMETRY OBSERVABILITY           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  📦 CONTAINERS (Requests) arrive at the port                              │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  Each HTTP request is a "shipping container" — it has a unique     │  │
  │  │  tracking number (trace_id), a manifest (attributes), and travels  │  │
  │  │  through multiple stops (spans) before reaching its destination.   │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  🏗️ CONTAINER CRANES (Spans) process each container                       │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐          │  │
  │  │  │ Crane A  │  │ Crane B  │  │ Crane C  │  │ Crane D  │  ...     │  │
  │  │  │ (nginx)  │  │ (Django) │  │  (DB)    │  │ (Redis)  │          │  │
  │  │  │ 10ms     │  │ 230ms    │  │ 180ms    │  │ 12ms     │          │  │
  │  │  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘          │  │
  │  │  Each crane (span) processes the container and adds its timestamp  │  │
  │  │  and metadata to the tracking log.                                 │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  🔗 CONVEYOR BELTS (Context Propagation) connect cranes                   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  traceparent header = "tracking number" passed between cranes      │  │
  │  │  Every crane writes to the SAME tracking log → one unified trace!  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  🚢 SHIPPING LANES (OTLP Protocol) carry data to warehouses               │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  OTLP (gRPC:4317 / HTTP:4318) = standardized shipping lanes        │  │
  │  │  All containers travel on the SAME lanes regardless of destination  │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐                     │  │
  │  │  │ Jaeger   │    │Prometheus│    │  Loki    │                     │  │
  │  │  │Warehouse │    │Warehouse │    │Warehouse │                     │  │
  │  │  │(Traces)  │    │(Metrics) │    │ (Logs)  │                     │  │
  │  │  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘                     │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🎯 KEY INSIGHT: OTel is the PORT INFRASTRUCTURE — cranes, conveyor      │
  │     belts, and shipping lanes. The warehouses (Jaeger, Prometheus,       │
  │     Loki) STORE the goods but don't move them. OTel MOVES the data.      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧑‍🏫 Novice's Takeaway: OpenTelemetry doesn't store your data — it's the transportation infrastructure that moves telemetry from your application (the port) to observability backends (the warehouses). Instrument your code once (build the port), and your telemetry flows to any backend you choose (any warehouse). This is why OTel is called "vendor-neutral" — the shipping lanes (OTLP) work with ALL warehouses.

1.2 The Three Pillars: Logs, Metrics, and Traces

Observability rests on three fundamental types of telemetry data. Each answers a different question about your system, and together they provide a complete picture. Think of them as three lenses through which you view your application.

📝 Pillar 1: Logs — "What Happened?"

Logs are timestamped, immutable records of discrete events that occurred in your application. They are the oldest and most familiar form of telemetry — and still one of the most valuable when done right.

Log Line Anatomy — Structured JSON with Trace Correlation
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     STRUCTURED LOG RECORD (anihpj)                       │
  │                                                                         │
  │  {                                                                      │
  │    "timestamp":     "2026-06-07T14:30:00.123Z",  ← When                 │
  │    "severity":      "ERROR",                      ← How bad             │
  │    "message":       "Failed to save JobPost #99", ← What happened       │
  │    "trace_id":      "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",  ← Links to    │
  │    "span_id":       "00f067aa0ba902b7",                  ← trace!       │
  │    "service.name":  "anihpj-api",                  ← Which service      │
  │    "user.id":       42,                            ← Business context   │
  │    "job.id":        99,                            ←                    │
  │    "db.operation":  "INSERT",                      ← Technical context  │
  │    "error.type":    "IntegrityError"               ←                    │
  │  }                                                                      │
  │                                                                         │
  │  🔑 KEY: Structured JSON logs are SEARCHABLE, not just readable.        │
  │  In Loki/Elasticsearch: {service.name="anihpj-api", severity="ERROR"}  │
  │  instantly finds all errors from the API service.                       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Structured vs Unstructured Logging:

❌ Unstructured (Old Way)

"User 42 created job 99 titled Software Engineer at 14:30"

  • ❌ Requires regex parsing
  • ❌ Breaks when message format changes
  • ❌ Cannot query: "Show all logs where user_id=42"
✅ Structured (New Way)

{"user_id":42, "job_id":99, "action":"create", "title":"Software Engineer"}

  • ✅ Machine-parseable JSON
  • ✅ Queryable: {user_id=42}
  • ✅ Aggregatable: Count by action type

📊 Pillar 2: Metrics — "How Much?"

Metrics are numeric measurements collected and aggregated over time intervals. Unlike logs (discrete events), metrics give you the big picture — trends, rates, and distributions.

📈
Counter

Only increases (monotonic). Total requests: 13,247. Total jobs created: 847. Like a car's odometer — never goes down.

📊
Gauge

Goes up AND down. Active connections: 47. Queue depth: 156. Memory usage: 62%. Like a car's fuel gauge.

📉
Histogram

Distribution into buckets. Request latency: [0-10ms]: 5, [10-50ms]: 23, [50-100ms]: 12. Gives you p50, p95, p99.

🧭
Summary

Pre-calculated quantiles. p50=3.2ms, p95=45ms, p99=580ms. Computed client-side (less flexible than histogram).

🔍 Pillar 3: Traces — "Where in the Journey?"

A trace is a tree of spans that shows the complete path of a request through a distributed system. Each span represents a single unit of work — a database query, an HTTP call, a cache lookup.

Trace Waterfall — POST /api/jobs/ on anihpj (Total: 245ms)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TRACE ID: 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736                             │
  │                                                                         │
  │  TIME (ms)  0          50         100        150        200        245  │
  │  ────────── ───────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬────────────── │
  │                        │          │          │          │               │
  │  SPAN A ██████████████████████████████████████████████████  anihpj-api   │
  │  (root)   POST /api/jobs/ [SERVER]  245ms               ███████████████ │
  │           │              │          │          │          │               │
  │           ├─ SPAN B ██                                    anihpj-auth    │
  │           │  auth.validate_token [CLIENT]  8ms            ██              │
  │           │                                               │               │
  │           ├─ SPAN C ████████████████████                  PostgreSQL      │
  │           │  INSERT INTO jobpost [CLIENT]  180ms          ███████████████ │
  │           │  ⚠️ BOTTLENECK! (73% of total time)           │               │
  │           │                                               │               │
  │           └─ SPAN D ██                                    Redis           │
  │              SET cache:job:99 [CLIENT]  12ms              ██              │
  │                                                                         │
  │  KEY INSIGHT: The DB INSERT takes 73% of total time. Without traces,    │
  │  you'd just see "POST /api/jobs/ is slow (245ms)" with no visibility    │
  │  into WHY. With traces, the bottleneck is immediately identifiable.    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

1.3 Why Traditional Monitoring Falls Short in Microservices

🏢 MONOLITH (anihpj v1)

1 process, 1 log file, easy to debug

  • Single codebase — grep finds everything
  • One database — queries are local
  • Debug time: ~5 minutes
  • Monitoring: "CPU > 90%? Alert!"
  • Dashboard: 1 server = 1 dashboard
🌐 MICROSERVICES (anihpj v2)

5+ services, 5+ log streams, complex interactions

  • Request bounces across: Nginx → Django → Auth → PostgreSQL → Redis
  • "Where did this request fail?" — impossible with metrics alone
  • "Which service caused the latency spike?" — guesswork without traces
  • Debug time: 2+ hours (WITHOUT OTel)
  • Cardinality explosion: 100 services × 50 endpoints × 10 status codes = 50K combinations
⚠️ The Cardinality Problem That Kills Traditional Monitoring

In a monolith, you might have 50 metrics. In a microservices environment with 20 services, each exposing 10 endpoints, with 5 HTTP methods and 10 status codes, the combinations explode: 20 × 10 × 5 × 10 = 10,000 unique time series. Traditional monitoring dashboards were never designed for this. You can't pre-build a dashboard for 10,000 metrics — you need to be able to query and explore ad-hoc. This is the heart of observability.

☸️ The Kubernetes Factor — Why OTel is Essential in K8s

Kubernetes amplifies the observability challenge. In a typical K8s deployment, anihpj would run as multiple Pods spread across nodes. A single user request might hit any replica, and Pods are ephemeral — they start, die, and restart constantly. Traditional monitoring that relies on fixed IP addresses and hostnames breaks down completely in K8s.

In this K8s deployment, OTel solves three critical problems: (1) Pod ephemerality — the OTel Agent (DaemonSet) on each node collects telemetry regardless of which Pods come and go, (2) Service discovery — OTel automatically tags spans with k8s.pod.name, k8s.namespace.name, making traces searchable by K8s metadata, and (3) Centralized pipeline — the Gateway Collector handles batching, filtering, and routing without burdening application Pods.

1.4 Observability vs Monitoring — Key Differences

Aspect🔔 Monitoring🔭 Observability
Core Question"Is it working?""WHY isn't it working?"
Data CollectedPre-defined metrics (CPU, RAM, disk)Rich telemetry: logs + metrics + traces + context
ApproachKnown unknowns (you know what to watch)Unknown unknowns (discover what you didn't anticipate)
DashboardsFixed, pre-built, hard-coded queriesDynamic, ad-hoc queries — explore any dimension
AlertingThreshold-based: CPU > 90% → ALERTSLO-based + anomaly detection + pattern analysis
Tool ExamplesNagios, Zabbix, Datadog (classic)OpenTelemetry + Jaeger + Grafana LGTM
OTel's RoleGenerates the raw dataEnables the exploration — data is rich enough to query any way
Best ForSimple systems, known failure modesComplex distributed systems, emergent behaviors
📖 The Best Analogy: Security Camera vs Building Blueprint

Monitoring is like a security camera — it shows you pre-defined views of specific areas. If something happens in a camera's blind spot, you never know. Observability is like having the complete building blueprint plus the ability to rewind time — you can explore ANY room, ANY angle, and trace the exact path someone took through the building. You're not limited to where you pre-installed cameras.

🐍
anihpj — The Django Project

A job posting platform (like LinkedIn Jobs, simplified). Django project with one app: jobpost. Models: Skills, User, Author, Location, JobPost. Real HTTP endpoints, real database queries, real caching — perfect for learning observability. Deployed on Kubernetes as a simple 2-replica Deployment.

📋
jobpost — The Django App

Handles job posting CRUD operations. Users create jobs with skills, location, and author info. Every create/read/update/delete operation generates telemetry we'll observe, trace, and analyze throughout this guide.

☸️ anihpj on Kubernetes — A Simple K8s Deployment

Throughout this guide, we'll deploy anihpj as a Kubernetes Deployment with 2 replicas, a PostgreSQL StatefulSet, and Redis for caching. This mirrors real production setups. Here's the K8s manifest that deploys anihpj with OTel auto-instrumentation:

YAML — anihpj K8s Deployment with OTel Sidecar
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: observability-demo
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: anihpj/api:v2.4.1
        env:
        - name: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME
          value: "anihpj-api"
        - name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
          value: "http://localhost:4317"
        - name: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER
          value: "parentbased_traceidratio"
        - name: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG
          value: "0.25"
        - name: OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES
          value: "deployment.environment=production"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
      # OTel Collector Agent as sidecar (local batching)
      - name: otel-agent
        image: otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:latest
        args: ["--config=/etc/otelcol/config.yaml"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: otel-config
          mountPath: /etc/otelcol
      volumes:
      - name: otel-config
        configMap:
          name: otel-agent-config

This is a real production pattern: the OTel Collector runs as a sidecar container in the same Pod as Django. The app sends telemetry to localhost:4317 — the sidecar handles batching and forwarding to the central Gateway Collector. Zero network latency for the first hop, automatic retry, and the sidecar can be configured independently of the app.

1.6 Hands-On: See the Three Pillars in Action on anihpj

1
Start anihpj

Django runserver, no OTel yet

2
Hit Endpoint

curl POST /api/jobs/ — observe: no visibility

3
Install OTel

pip install opentelemetry-api + sdk

4
Add 10 Lines

Manual instrumentation — see console output

5
Observe

Counter, span, log with trace_id

6
Realization

"I did ONE endpoint. I have 50 more..." → auto-instrumentation!

Terminal — Before vs After OTel
# BEFORE OTel — Blind to system behavior
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/jobs/ -d '{"title":"SWE"}'
{"id": 99, "title": "SWE", "status": "created"}   # ← That's all you see!

# AFTER OTel — Rich telemetry on console
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/jobs/ -d '{"title":"SWE"}'
{
  "name": "POST /api/jobs/",
  "context": {
    "trace_id": "0x4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
    "span_id": "0x00f067aa0ba902b7"
  },
  "attributes": {
    "http.method": "POST",
    "http.url": "/api/jobs/",
    "http.status_code": 201,
    "user.id": 42
  },
  "status": "OK",
  "duration_ms": 245
}
# Also: counter jobs_created_total incremented by 1
# Also: log line emitted with same trace_id for correlation
💡 The "Aha!" Moment

After instrumenting just ONE endpoint, you see: request count, latency, success/failure status, who made the request, and a trace ID you can use to find related logs. This is powerful — but you have 50 endpoints. Manually instrumenting all of them is tedious. This is why auto-instrumentation exists (Chapter 6). But first, understanding manual instrumentation (Chapter 5) gives you the foundation to know what auto-instrumentation is doing under the hood.

1.7 The Unified Debugging Workflow — How the Three Pillars Correlate

The real power of observability isn't in having three separate pillars — it's in how they work together to tell a complete story. Each pillar is a different lens, and when you look through all three at once, system behavior becomes crystal clear.

🔗 The Three Pillar Correlation — A Real anihpj Debugging Scenario
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            UNIFIED OBSERVABILITY — DEBUGGING "JOB CREATION FAILED"         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1: 📊 METRICS — The ALERT                                          │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Grafana Dashboard:                                                 │  │
  │  │   POST /api/jobs/  Error Rate:  ████████░░ 8.2%  (normally <1%)  │  │
  │  │   P99 Latency:      ██████████ 4.2s  (normally 250ms)            │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Alert fires: "jobpost_create_error_rate > 5% for 5 minutes"       │  │
  │  │ Question answered: "IS there a problem?" → YES, error rate spiked │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STEP 2: 🔍 TRACES — The INVESTIGATION                                   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Click exemplar in Grafana → opens Jaeger trace:                    │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Trace ID: 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736  Duration: 30.2s       │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ █████ anihpj-api    POST /api/jobs/          30,200ms   ⚠️ ERROR  │  │
  │  │  ├─██ auth.validate_token                     8ms       ✅ OK     │  │
  │  │  ├─██ validate_job_data                       3ms       ✅ OK     │  │
  │  │  ├─████████████████████████████████  INSERT   30,000ms  ❌ TIMEOUT │  │
  │  │  └─██ SET cache:job:99                       12ms       ✅ OK     │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Question answered: "WHERE is the problem?" → DB INSERT times out  │  │
  │  │ Insight: 99.9% of time is in the DB call (30s of 30.2s total)     │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STEP 3: 📝 LOGS — The ROOT CAUSE                                        │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Copy trace_id → query Loki:                                        │  │
  │  │   {trace_id="4bf92f...e4736"}                                      │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Results (chronological):                                           │  │
  │  │  14:30:00.100 INFO  "Acquiring DB connection from pool"            │  │
  │  │  14:30:00.105 INFO  "Connection pool: 0/20 available (all in use)" │  │
  │  │  14:30:30.150 ERROR "INSERT jobpost TIMEOUT after 30000ms"         │  │
  │  │  14:30:30.151 ERROR "All connections held by: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE│
  │  │                      (started 14:28:45, duration 105s)"            │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Question answered: "WHY did it happen?" → Table lock held by       │  │
  │  │ another query for 105s, exhausted connection pool                  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🎯 THE FULL PICTURE — 30 minutes → 3 minutes                            │
  │  Without OTel: "Job creation is failing" → grep logs for "error" →       │
  │  find nothing obvious → check DB manually → 30+ minutes of guesswork     │
  │  With OTel: Metrics detect → Traces locate → Logs explain → 3 minutes    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 METRICS Role

Detection & Alerting
Answer: "IS there a problem?"
Best for: SLOs, dashboards, trends, capacity planning
Weakness: Can't explain WHY (only THAT)

🔍 TRACES Role

Localization
Answer: "WHERE is the bottleneck?"
Best for: Request-level debugging, service dependency analysis
Weakness: Individual traces don't show aggregate patterns

📝 LOGS Role

Root Cause
Answer: "WHY did this happen?"
Best for: Detailed event context, error stack traces
Weakness: Volume — too many to browse without trace_id

🧠 The Mental Model for the OTCA Exam

The exam will present scenarios and ask "Which signal would you use?" Here's the decision tree:

  • "Alert me when error rate exceeds 5%" → Metrics (aggregation over time)
  • "Why did this specific user's request fail?" → Traces (follow the request path)
  • "What was the exact SQL query that timed out?" → Logs (detailed event records)
  • "Show me all errors across all services in the last hour" → Logs (filtered, aggregated)
  • "Is our system getting slower week over week?" → Metrics (trends over time)

🎯 SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets — Why Metrics Matter

TermDefinitionOTel Connection
SLI (Service Level Indicator)A metric that measures service quality: latency, error rate, throughputOTel generates SLIs via metric instruments (Counter for errors, Histogram for latency)
SLO (Service Level Objective)A target for an SLI: "99.9% of requests complete in <250ms over 30 days"OTel provides the raw data; Grafana/Prometheus calculate SLO compliance
Error BudgetThe allowed deviation from SLO: 0.1% error budget = 43 minutes of allowed downtime/monthWhen error budget is exhausted, teams stop shipping features and fix reliability
💡 OTCA Exam Connection

The OTCA exam expects you to understand that OTel is the instrumentation layer that generates SLIs. It does NOT define SLOs (that's an SRE/operator task), but without OTel's rich metrics, you can't calculate meaningful SLOs. This is a common exam trap: "Does OpenTelemetry define SLOs?" → NO. OTel generates the raw telemetry that SLOs are computed from.

1.9 The Telemetry Signal Lifecycle — From Code to Dashboard

Understanding the complete journey of a telemetry signal — from the moment it's created in your application code to when it appears on a dashboard — is fundamental to passing the OTCA. Let's trace the full lifecycle:

🔄 Complete Telemetry Lifecycle — 6 Stages
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                TELEMETRY SIGNAL LIFECYCLE — FROM CODE TO DASHBOARD         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STAGE 1: 📝 GENERATION (in your code)                                   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ anihpj/jobpost/views.py:                                           │  │
  │  │   span = tracer.start_span("create_job")                           │  │
  │  │   span.set_attribute("job.title", "Software Engineer")             │  │
  │  │   counter.add(1, {"status": "created"})                            │  │
  │  │   logger.info("Job created", extra={"job_id": 99})                 │  │
  │  │                                                                    │  │
  │  │ At this point: Raw telemetry exists ONLY in process memory         │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STAGE 2: 📦 BATCHING & BUFFERING (in SDK)                               │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ SpanProcessor / MetricReader:                                       │  │
  │  │   • Spans queued in BatchSpanProcessor (default: 512 spans/batch)   │  │
  │  │   • Metrics collected by PeriodicExportingMetricReader (every 30s)  │  │
  │  │   • Logs batched by BatchLogRecordProcessor                         │  │
  │  │                                                                    │  │
  │  │ KEY: SDK batches data BEFORE sending — reduces network overhead     │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STAGE 3: 🚀 EXPORT (OTLP over gRPC/HTTP)                                │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ OTLP Exporter serializes to Protobuf → sends to Collector           │  │
  │  │   endpoint: http://collector:4317  (gRPC)                           │  │
  │  │   protocol: grpc                                                    │  │
  │  │   compression: gzip                                                 │  │
  │  │                                                                    │  │
  │  │ All three signals travel on the SAME protocol (OTLP)                │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STAGE 4: ⚙️ PROCESSING (Collector Pipeline)                             │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ receivers: otlp → processors: [batch, memory_limiter, attributes]  │  │
  │  │   → exporters: [otlp/jaeger, prometheus, logging]                  │  │
  │  │                                                                    │  │
  │  │ Collector can: filter spans, enrich with k8s metadata, sample tail,│  │
  │  │ route to multiple backends, transform attributes with OTTL          │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STAGE 5: 💾 STORAGE (Backend Database)                                  │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Traces → Jaeger (Cassandra/Elasticsearch) or Tempo (S3/GCS)       │  │
  │  │ Metrics → Prometheus (TSDB) or Mimir (S3)                          │  │
  │  │ Logs → Loki (S3) or Elasticsearch (SSD)                            │  │
  │  │                                                                    │  │
  │  │ Retention: 15 days (hot storage), configurable for cold storage    │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STAGE 6: 📊 QUERY & VISUALIZATION (Grafana / Jaeger UI)                 │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Grafana queries Prometheus (PromQL), Loki (LogQL), Tempo (TraceQL) │  │
  │  │ Jaeger UI shows waterfall traces                                   │  │
  │  │ Dashboards + Alerts + SLO tracking                                 │  │
  │  │                                                                    │  │
  │  │ The engineer FINALLY sees: "Job creation p99 = 4.2s (SLO: < 250ms)"│  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⏱️ Latency Budget

Stage 1→2: ~0ms (in-memory)
Stage 2→3: ~200ms (batch timeout)
Stage 3→4: ~1-5ms (localhost or local network)
Stage 4→5: ~1-10ms (network)
Stage 5→6: Query-dependent
Total end-to-end: ~200-500ms

🔑 Key OTCA Insight

The SDK does NOT send every span individually — it BATCHES them. This is critical for production performance. If you see a question about "Why is my OTel SDK causing latency?" the answer often involves batching configuration or sampling rate.
