📝 OTCA Practice Questions — Chapter 3

Q1

What are the four main components of the OpenTelemetry architecture?

Show Answer
Answer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          OTEL'S FOUR ARCHITECTURAL COMPONENTS                 │
  │                                                              │
  │  API (Interfaces)      SDK (Implementation)                  │
  │  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────┐      │
  │  │ Tracer       │     │ TracerProvider (sampler,      │      │
  │  │ Meter        │────▶│   exporter, batching)         │      │
  │  │ Logger       │     │ MeterProvider                 │      │
  │  │ Context      │     │ LoggerProvider                │      │
  │  └──────────────┘     └──────────────┬───────────────┘      │
  │                                      │                       │
  │  COLLECTOR (Pipeline)                ▼                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ Receivers → Processors → Exporters → OTLP (Wire)    │   │
  │  │           (batch/filter/        (gRPC:4317,         │   │
  │  │            enrich)              HTTP:4318)          │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

API = contracts (WHAT you can do). SDK = implementation (HOW it's done). Collector = standalone pipeline (RECEIVE → PROCESS → EXPORT). OTLP = how data travels between components (gRPC:4317, HTTP:4318). The OTCA exam will test your ability to distinguish which component is responsible for what.

Q2

Why is the API separated from the SDK in OpenTelemetry?

Show Answer
Answer

Library authors (Django OTel instrumentation) depend ONLY on the API — no implementation opinions imposed. Application owners (anihpj team) choose which SDK implementation (sampler, exporter, batching). This prevents library instrumentation from forcing specific implementation choices.

Explanation

If Django instrumentation depended on the SDK, every Django app would be forced to use whatever sampler/exporter the library author chose. By depending only on the API, the library works with ANY SDK configuration. This is a fundamental OTel design principle heavily tested on the OTCA exam.

Q3

What ports does OTLP use and for which protocols?

Show Answer
Answer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          OTLP PORTS — MEMORIZE FOR THE EXAM                   │
  │                                                              │
  │  ┌──────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 4317     │ gRPC         │ Binary protobuf, streaming   │ │
  │  │          │              │ Service-to-service (default)  │ │
  │  ├──────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤ │
  │  │ 4318     │ HTTP/1.1     │ Binary protobuf or JSON      │ │
  │  │          │              │ Browser/firewall-friendly     │ │
  │  └──────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                              │
  │  BOTH carry: 🔍 Traces + 📊 Metrics + 📝 Logs              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

OTLP uses one protocol for ALL signals — you don't need separate protocols for traces, metrics, and logs. The exam WILL ask about these ports.

Q4

What is the difference between the BatchSpanProcessor and SimpleSpanProcessor?

Show Answer
Answer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          BatchSpanProcessor vs SimpleSpanProcessor            │
  │                                                              │
  │  SimpleSpanProcessor (DEV ONLY):                             │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ span.end() → HTTP POST NOW → block until sent        │   │
  │  │ 1 span = 1 network call → KILLS performance          │   │
  │  │ Synchronous — your app WAITS for each export         │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                              │
  │  BatchSpanProcessor (PRODUCTION):                             │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ span.end() → queue → wait for batch → batch HTTP POST│   │
  │  │ 512 spans = 1 network call → 512x EFFICIENT          │   │
  │  │ Asynchronous — your app NEVER waits                  │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

SimpleSpanProcessor blocks on every span export. BatchSpanProcessor queues spans and sends them in batches. In production, always use BatchSpanProcessor — SimpleSpanProcessor will kill your application's performance.

Q5

What is the most critical Resource attribute that must always be set?

Show Answer
Answer

service.name. Without it, your telemetry is labeled "unknown_service" — making it impossible to identify which service generated the data.

Explanation

Every span, metric, and log record carries Resource attributes. service.name is the primary identifier. Set it via OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=anihpj-api environment variable or in code via Resource(attributes={SERVICE_NAME: "anihpj-api"}). The OTCA exam considers this a best practice.

Q6

What are the three pipeline stages in the OTel Collector?

Show Answer
Answer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          COLLECTOR PIPELINE: Receivers → Processors → Exporters│
  │                                                              │
  │  TELEMETRY IN                                                │
  │       │                                                      │
  │       ▼                                                      │
  │  RECEIVERS (Accept)         PROCESSORS (Transform)           │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │ OTLP (gRPC/HTTP) │     │ batch     → group spans  │     │
  │  │ Jaeger (Thrift)  │────▶│ memory    → prevent OOM  │     │
  │  │ Prometheus       │     │ filter    → drop health  │     │
  │  │ Kafka            │     │ attributes→ enrich       │     │
  │  └──────────────────┘     └───────────┬──────────────┘     │
  │                                       │                      │
  │                                       ▼                      │
  │                              EXPORTERS (Send)                │
  │                              ┌──────────────────────────┐   │
  │                              │ OTLP → Jaeger/Tempo       │   │
  │                              │ Prometheus → :9464        │   │
  │                              │ Logging → stdout (debug)   │   │
  │                              └──────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

The pipeline order is always: Receivers → Processors → Exporters. Data flows through processors in the order they're listed in the config. The OTCA exam may ask about the correct order or which stage performs a specific function (e.g., "Where would you filter out health-check spans?" → Processors).

Q7

What are Semantic Conventions and why do they matter?

Show Answer
Answer

Semantic Conventions are standardized attribute names (e.g., http.method, db.system) that are consistent across ALL OTel language SDKs. They enable cross-service, cross-language queries — and are the foundation of OTel's vendor neutrality.

Explanation

Without semantic conventions, Python might use http.method while Java uses HTTP_METHOD — making cross-service queries impossible. Conventions use lowercase, dot-separated names. The OTCA exam tests your knowledge of common convention categories: HTTP (http.method, http.status_code), Database (db.system, db.operation), and RPC/Messaging.

Q8

Is the OTel Collector required for using OpenTelemetry?

Show Answer
Answer

No. The Collector is OPTIONAL. You can export telemetry directly from the SDK to a backend. However, the Collector is RECOMMENDED for production — it provides centralized configuration, batching, filtering, enrichment, and multi-backend routing.

Explanation

Development: SDK → Jaeger (direct). Production: SDK → Collector → Jaeger + Prometheus + Loki. The Collector adds operational benefits without changing your application code. The OTCA exam expects you to know the Collector is optional but recommended for production.

Q9

What is the difference between Agent and Gateway deployment modes for the Collector?

Show Answer
Answer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          AGENT vs GATEWAY — COLLECTOR DEPLOYMENT MODES        │
  │                                                              │
  │  AGENT (DaemonSet):              GATEWAY (Deployment):       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ 1 per NODE            │       │ 1+ per CLUSTER        │    │
  │  │ Lightweight batching   │       │ Heavy processing       │    │
  │  │ Local attribute enrich │       │ Multi-backend routing  │    │
  │  │ Apps → localhost:4317  │       │ Apps → svc:4317        │    │
  │  └──────────┬───────────┘       └───────────┬──────────┘    │
  │             │                                │               │
  │             └──────── Agent → Gateway ───────┘               │
  │                                                              │
  │  PRODUCTION BEST PRACTICE: Agent (DaemonSet) → Gateway (Dep) │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Production best practice: Agent → Gateway → Backend. Agent handles local batching and attribute enrichment. Gateway handles advanced processing and multi-backend routing. The OTCA exam may ask about which deployment mode is appropriate for a given scenario.

Q10

Which component would you configure to sample only 10% of traces in production?

Show Answer
Answer

The SDK Sampler — specifically via OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=traceidratio and OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1 environment variables, or programmatically via TraceIdRatioBased(ratio=0.1) in the TracerProvider configuration.

Explanation

Sampling happens at the SDK level (before spans leave your application). The Collector can also do tail sampling, but head sampling is configured in the SDK. Environment variables are the recommended way to configure sampling — they work across all language SDKs without code changes. Exam tip: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER and OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG are the two most important OTel environment variables.

  • 1. "API = SDK" → WRONG. API = interfaces (no implementation). SDK = implementation. Library authors use API only.
  • 2. "Collector is required" → WRONG. It's optional (but recommended for production). SDK can export directly to backends.
  • 3. "OTLP only uses gRPC" → WRONG. OTLP supports both gRPC (4317) AND HTTP (4318). Know both.
  • 4. "SimpleSpanProcessor for production" → WRONG. Always use BatchSpanProcessor in production. SimpleSpanProcessor is for dev/debugging only.
  • 5. Forgetting to set service.name → Your telemetry will show "unknown_service" — useless for identifying which service is which.

Chapter 4: Context Propagation and Sampling 🟢 Beginner

Chapter 4: Context Propagation and Sampling — How Traces Stay Connected

When a request travels across multiple services, how does each service know it's part of the same trace? The answer is context propagation — the mechanism that passes trace IDs across service boundaries. And when you have millions of traces, how do you avoid storing all of them? That's sampling. These two concepts are foundational to distributed tracing and are tested heavily on the OTCA exam.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔗 Propagation 🎯 Core
🎓 OTCA Relevance
Domain 1: Fundamentals D2: SDK — Sampling

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What context propagation is and why it's essential for distributed tracing
  • ✅ The W3C Trace-Context standard — traceparent and tracestate headers
  • ✅ Baggage — passing custom data (user_id, tenant) across ALL downstream services
  • ✅ How context flows through HTTP headers: Extract → Process → Inject cycle
  • ✅ Head Sampling vs Tail Sampling — when to use each
  • ✅ Five sampling strategies: AlwaysOn, AlwaysOff, TraceIdRatioBased, ParentBased, RateLimiting

4.1 What is Context Propagation?

Context Propagation Across Microservices
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            CONTEXT PROPAGATION — How Services Share Trace Identity         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────┐   traceparent header    ┌──────────┐   traceparent    ┌──────────┐
  │  │ Service A│ ──── HTTP ──────────▶  │ Service B│ ──── HTTP ──────▶│ Service C│
  │  │          │                         │          │                  │          │
  │  │ Span A   │                         │ Span B   │                  │ Span C   │
  │  │trace_id=X│                         │trace_id=X│                  │trace_id=X│
  │  │span_id=A │                         │parent_id=│                  │parent_id=│
  │  │          │                         │    A     │                  │    B     │
  │  └──────────┘                         └──────────┘                  └──────────┘
  │                                                                          │
  │  🔑 ALL THREE SPANS share the SAME trace_id = X                          │
  │  → In Jaeger/Grafana: ONE unified trace showing the complete journey!    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WITHOUT propagation: 3 disconnected traces, no correlation.             │
  │  WITH propagation:    1 trace with 3 nested spans, full visibility.      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

In a monolithic application, everything runs in one process — there's no need to pass trace context around. But in microservices, a single user request bounces across multiple services (anihpj-api → auth-service → PostgreSQL → Redis). Without context propagation, each service would create its own independent trace — making it impossible to see the complete request journey.

Context propagation solves this by passing trace identity in HTTP headers. When Service A calls Service B, it injects a traceparent header into the HTTP request. Service B extracts this header and creates its span as a CHILD of Service A's span — sharing the same trace_id. This is how all spans in a trace stay connected, even across dozens of services.

4.2 Trace Context — The W3C Trace-Context Standard

Anatomy of the traceparent Header
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01   │
  │               │  │                              │                │       │
  │               │  └── trace_id (32 hex chars)────┘                │       │
  │               │         span_id (16 hex chars) ──────────────────┘       │
  │               └── version (always "00")                                   │
  │                      trace_flags (01 = sampled, 00 = not sampled) ────────┘
  │                                                                          │
  │  TRACE ID:  4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736  (16 bytes, 32 hex)       │
  │  SPAN ID:   00f067aa0ba902b7                    (8 bytes, 16 hex)        │
  │  FLAGS:     01 = this trace IS sampled (will be recorded)                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The W3C Trace-Context standard defines two HTTP headers:

HeaderFormatPurpose
traceparent00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-{flags}Carries the trace identity (REQUIRED)
tracestatevendor1=value1,vendor2=value2Vendor-specific data (OPTIONAL)

This is NOT an OpenTelemetry-specific standard — it's a W3C standard used by ALL distributed tracing systems. This means an OTel-instrumented service and a non-OTel service (using Zipkin, for example) can still participate in the same trace, as long as both respect the traceparent header.

4.3 Baggage — Passing Custom Data Across Services

Baggage is a set of key-value pairs that automatically propagates alongside trace context to ALL downstream services. It's like putting a sticky note on a request that every service can read.

🎒
Baggage Use Cases

user_id=42 → all services see which user. tenant_id=acme → multi-tenant tracing. environment=staging → filter by environment. cart_id=abc123 → trace e-commerce flow.

⚠️
Baggage Warnings

❌ NEVER put secrets in baggage (visible in headers!). ❌ Keep baggage small (headers have size limits). ❌ Baggage values propagate to ALL services — be careful with sensitive data.

Python — Setting and Getting Baggage
from opentelemetry import baggage

# SET baggage (in the originating service)
ctx = baggage.set_baggage("user.id", "42")
ctx = baggage.set_baggage("tenant.id", "acme-corp")

# GET baggage (in ANY downstream service)
user_id = baggage.get_baggage("user.id")  # → "42"

# The HTTP header automatically sent:
# baggage: user.id=42,tenant.id=acme-corp
🔥 OTCA EXAM TRAP: Baggage vs Span Attributes
AspectBaggageSpan Attributes
Propagation✅ AUTO to ALL downstream services❌ Stays on current span only
Headerbaggage: key1=val1No HTTP header — in span data only
APIbaggage.set_baggage("user.id", "42")span.set_attribute("user.id", "42")
Use WhenData needed by ALL downstream servicesMetadata about THIS specific operation
Exampleuser_id, tenant_id, plan_typehttp.method, db.operation, cache.hit

Classic exam trap: "I set span.set_attribute("user.id", 42) in Service A — will Service B see it?" → NO! Span attributes do NOT propagate. Use baggage.set_baggage("user.id", "42") instead.

4.4 How Context Flows — The Extract → Process → Inject Cycle

1
EXTRACT

Read traceparent from incoming request headers

2
BUILD

Create SpanContext from extracted IDs

3
CREATE

Start a new span with parent = extracted span_id

4
PROCESS

Execute business logic within the span

5
INJECT

Add traceparent to outgoing HTTP request headers

This cycle happens automatically with auto-instrumentation. When you use opentelemetry-instrumentation-django, every incoming HTTP request is extracted, every outgoing HTTP request has traceparent injected. For custom protocols (gRPC, Kafka, raw sockets), you may need to implement extract/inject manually using the Propagators API.

🔬 Under the Hood: What Actually Happens During Extraction

When the OTel SDK processes an incoming HTTP request, here is exactly what happens at the code level — this is HOW context propagation actually works:

Context Extraction — Step by Step Inside the SDK
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          HOW traceparent EXTRACTION WORKS — INSIDE THE SDK                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  INCOMING HTTP REQUEST:                                                   │
  │  GET /api/jobs/ HTTP/1.1                                                  │
  │  Host: anihpj-api                                                         │
  │  traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1: Django middleware receives request                               │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ OTel Django instrumentation middleware intercepts BEFORE your view │  │
  │  │ calls: W3CTraceContextPropagator().extract(request.headers)        │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STEP 2: Parse traceparent string into its components                     │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ "00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01"       │  │
  │  │   │  │                                │                   │        │  │
  │  │   │  └─ trace_id (32 hex chars)       │                   │        │  │
  │  │   │     = 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736              │        │  │
  │  │   │                                   └─ span_id (16 hex)│        │  │
  │  │   │                                      = 00f067aa0ba902b7       │  │
  │  │   │                                                      │        │  │
  │  │   └─ version (00 = W3C)                                  │        │  │
  │  │                                    trace_flags = 01 (sampled!)      │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STEP 3: Build SpanContext from extracted values                          │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ span_context = SpanContext(                                        │  │
  │  │     trace_id=0x4bf92f...,    ← NEVER changes across services      │  │
  │  │     span_id=0x00f067...,     ← THIS becomes parent_span_id!       │  │
  │  │     trace_flags=SAMPLED,     ← carry forward sampling decision     │  │
  │  │     is_remote=True           ← came from ANOTHER service            │  │
  │  │ )                                                                  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STEP 4: Your app creates a span — linked to the extracted context        │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ with tracer.start_as_current_span("POST /api/jobs/") as span:      │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ New span gets:                                                     │  │
  │  │   trace_id = 4bf92f...  ← SAME as parent (this is the KEY!)       │  │
  │  │   span_id = NEW random (generated fresh for this span)             │  │
  │  │   parent_span_id = 00f067aa0ba902b7  ← FROM traceparent!           │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🔑 THE KEY INSIGHT: trace_id NEVER changes. Every span in every service  │
  │     shares the SAME trace_id. This is HOW Jaeger shows one unified trace. │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

OTCA Exam Test: "What travels in traceparent across services?" → trace_id, parent's span_id, and trace flags. "What does NOT travel?" → span attributes, span events, span status, span duration. "What creates the parent-child tree in Jaeger?" → parent_span_id links each span to its parent.

4.5 Sampling Fundamentals — Head Sampling vs Tail Sampling

🧠 HEAD SAMPLING (SDK)

Decision at span START. Simple, low overhead. Examples: "Keep 10% of traces," "Keep 100 traces/second." ❌ Can't know if a trace contains an error before seeing it — you might drop the interesting ones.

🔍 TAIL SAMPLING (Collector)

Decision at trace END. After seeing the complete trace. "Keep ALL error traces," "Keep traces with latency > 2s." ✅ Never drops interesting data. ❌ Must buffer all spans temporarily — higher overhead.

4.6 Sampling Strategies

✅
AlwaysOn

Record every span. Dev/staging only — never production (100% of data = $$$).

🎲
TraceIdRatioBased

Keep % based on trace_id hash. 0.1 = 10%. Deterministic: same trace_id = same decision. Production standard.

👪
ParentBased

Child follows parent's decision. If parent was sampled → child IS sampled. Maintains trace integrity.

⏱️
RateLimiting

Max N spans/second. Not recommended — breaks traces (can sample parent but not child).

🔬 Under the Hood: How Hash-Based Sampling Decides (Keep or Drop)

The most important production sampler is parentbased_traceidratio. Here is EXACTLY how it works internally — this is tested on the OTCA exam:

TraceIdRatioBased Sampler — Internal Algorithm Explained
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          HOW HASH-BASED SAMPLING DECIDES KEEP vs DROP                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CONFIG: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.25  (keep 25% of all traces)          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1: Generate trace_id (random 128-bit = 16 bytes)                    │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ trace_id = 0x4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736                     │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Take the FIRST 8 bytes (64 bits) as an unsigned integer:           │  │
  │  │   first_8_bytes = 0x4bf92f3577b34da6                              │  │
  │  │   as_integer     = 5,472,938,472,938,182                          │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STEP 2: Calculate threshold from ratio                                    │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ threshold = ratio × 2^64                                           │  │
  │  │           = 0.25 × 18,446,744,073,709,551,616                     │  │
  │  │           = 4,611,686,018,427,387,904                              │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STEP 3: Compare — the DECISION                                           │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ IF as_integer (5.47T) <= threshold (4.61T) → DROP (NOT sampled)   │  │
  │  │ IF as_integer was < 4.61T              → KEEP (SAMPLED)           │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ In our example: 5.47T > 4.61T → DROP this trace                   │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Set trace_flags:                                                   │  │
  │  │   SAMPLED → 01  (bit 0 = 1)                                        │  │
  │  │   DROPPED → 00  (bit 0 = 0)                                        │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🔑 WHY THIS ALGORITHM IS BRILLIANT:                                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ ✅ DETERMINISTIC: Same trace_id → ALWAYS same decision             │  │
  │  │    This is WHY ParentBased works: child sees trace_flags=01        │  │
  │  │    in the parent and makes the SAME decision (no re-calculation)   │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ ✅ STATELESS: No counter to maintain, no memory needed             │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ ✅ UNIFORM: Statistically, exactly 25% of traces sampled           │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ ⚠️ RateLimiting is DIFFERENT: uses a COUNTER, not hash.           │  │
  │  │    This is why RateLimiting can BREAK traces: parent sampled       │  │
  │  │    but the counter runs out → child dropped → broken trace!        │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

OTCA Exam: "Why does ParentBased never break traces?" → Because it reads the parent's trace_flags bit (01=sampled) and copies that decision — no re-hashing. "Why can RateLimiting break traces?" → Because it uses an independent counter that may allow the parent but deny the child.

Configuring Sampling for anihpj
# Environment variables (recommended):
export OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio
export OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1  # Keep 10%

# Or programmatically:
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.sampling import TraceIdRatioBased, ParentBased
sampler = ParentBased(root_sampler=TraceIdRatioBased(ratio=0.1))

4.7 Hands-On: Trace Context Propagation Across anihpj Microservices

1
Set Up

Two Django services: anihpj-api + anihpj-auth

2
Instrument

Both with OTel Python auto-instrumentation

3
Call

anihpj-api calls anihpj-auth for token validation

4
Observe

HTTP call carries traceparent automatically!

5
Verify

Jaeger shows ONE trace with spans from BOTH services

6
Add Baggage

user_id in baggage → appears in ALL downstream spans

💡 The Magic Moment

When you first see a trace in Jaeger that spans TWO different services — anihpj-api AND anihpj-auth — with parent-child relationships intact, you've witnessed context propagation in action. The traceparent header automatically injected by OTel instrumentation made it possible, and you wrote ZERO code to make it happen. This is the power of standards-based observability.

4.8 Context Propagation Troubleshooting — Why Your Trace is Broken

One of the most common real-world OTel issues is broken traces — where spans that should be connected appear as separate, disconnected traces. The OTCA exam tests your ability to diagnose context propagation failures.

Broken vs Connected Traces — Diagnosing Context Propagation Issues
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              DIAGNOSING BROKEN TRACES                                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  HEALTHY TRACE (Context Propagating):                                     │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ TRACE: 4bf92f... (ONE trace_id, 4 spans)                          │  │
  │  │ ├─ SPAN A: anihpj-api POST /api/jobs/ [parent: null]              │  │
  │  │ │  ├─ SPAN B: auth.validate_token [parent: A]                     │  │
  │  │ │  ├─ SPAN C: INSERT jobpost [parent: A]                          │  │
  │  │ │  └─ SPAN D: SET cache:job:99 [parent: A]                        │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BROKEN TRACE (Context NOT Propagating):                                  │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ TRACE: abc111... (ONE)         TRACE: def222... (ANOTHER!)         │  │
  │  │ └─ SPAN: anihpj-api            └─ SPAN: auth.validate_token        │  │
  │  │                                └─ SPAN: INSERT jobpost             │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ PROBLEM: Two separate traces instead of one!                       │  │
  │  │ ROOT CAUSES:                                                       │  │
  │  │ 1. traceparent header NOT forwarded (manual HTTP client)           │  │
  │  │ 2. Custom middleware stripping headers                             │  │
  │  │ 3. Service uses non-OTel tracing library (no W3C support)         │  │
  │  │ 4. Sampling mismatch: parent sampled but child not (RateLimiting)  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
SymptomLikely CauseFix
Services A→B: separate tracestraceparent not forwardedEnable auto-instrumentation for HTTP client; check for header-stripping middleware
Sampled parent, unsampled childUsing RateLimiting sampler (not ParentBased)Switch to ParentBased(root_sampler=...)
Missing attributes on child spansBaggage not set / header too largeSet baggage in parent; check if HTTP headers exceed size limits
All traces show as "unknown_service"OTEL_SERVICE_NAME not setExport OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=anihpj-api

4.9 Baggage Deep Dive — Beyond Span Attributes

Baggage is the most misunderstood OTel signal. The OTCA exam frequently tests the distinction between span attributes (local) and baggage (propagates).

✅ USE BAGGAGE FOR:
  • user_id — needed by auth, billing, analytics
  • tenant_id — multi-tenant routing decisions
  • experiment_group — A/B test tracking
  • request_id — correlation across services
  • session_id — user session tracking
❌ DON'T USE BAGGAGE FOR:
  • Large data (>8KB total baggage header)
  • Sensitive data (visible in headers!)
  • Span-specific metadata (use attributes)
  • Values that change per-span (baggage persists)
  • Database connection strings, tokens, passwords
⚠️ Exam Trap: Baggage vs Span Attributes

span.set_attribute("user_id", "42") → Only visible on THIS span. Not available to downstream services.
baggage.set_baggage("user_id", "42") → Propagates to ALL downstream services. Available everywhere in the request chain.
OTCA will ask: "How do you make user_id available to all services in a request chain?" → Baggage, NOT span attributes.

📝 OTCA Practice Questions — Chapter 4

Q1

What is context propagation and why is it essential for distributed tracing?

Show Answer
Answer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          CONTEXT PROPAGATION — THE GLUE OF DISTRIBUTED TRACES │
  │                                                              │
  │  WITHOUT Propagation:              WITH Propagation:         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ TRACE AAA (api)      │         │ TRACE AAA (SHARED!)  │  │
  │  │ └── POST /api/jobs/  │         │  ├── POST /api/jobs/ │  │
  │  │                      │         │  │   (api, trace=AAA) │  │
  │  │ TRACE BBB (auth)     │         │  └── validate_token  │  │
  │  │ └── validate_token   │         │       (auth,trace=AAA)│  │
  │  │ 2 SEPARATE traces!   │         │ 1 UNIFIED trace!      │  │
  │  └──────────────────────┘         └──────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                              │
  │  traceparent header: 00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-{flags}       │
  │  carries the trace identity across HTTP calls                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

In anihpj: When api calls auth-service, the traceparent header tells auth-service "you're part of trace X, and your parent span is Y." Auth-service creates a child span with the same trace_id. Without propagation, you'd have 2 separate traces with no way to correlate them.

Q2

What is the format of the W3C traceparent header?

Show Answer
Answer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          traceparent HEADER FORMAT                            │
  │                                                              │
  │  00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01   │
  │  │  └──────── 32 hex trace_id ─────────┘└─ 16 hex span ─┘│  │
  │  │                                     (PARENT'S span_id!)│  │
  │  └─ version (always 00)                       trace_flags  │  │
  │                                                 01 = sampled│  │
  │                                                 00 = dropped│  │
  │                                                              │
  │  trace_id: 16 bytes (32 hex chars) — NEVER changes          │
  │  span_id:   8 bytes (16 hex chars) — parent's ID            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Example: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01. The span_id in traceparent is the CALLER'S span_id — it becomes the parent_span_id of the span created by the receiving service.

Q3

What is the difference between Baggage and Span Attributes?

Show Answer
Answer

Baggage propagates automatically to ALL downstream services via HTTP headers. Span Attributes stay on the current span — they do NOT automatically propagate to child spans. Baggage is for cross-service context; attributes are for single-span metadata.

Explanation

If you set span.set_attribute("user.id", 42) in Service A, Service B won't see it. But if you set baggage.set_baggage("user.id", "42"), Service B, C, D... ALL see it. OTCA exam trap: confusing baggage with span attributes. Use baggage when you need data to travel across services; use span attributes for metadata about one specific operation.

Q4

What is the difference between Head Sampling and Tail Sampling?

Show Answer
Answer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          HEAD SAMPLING vs TAIL SAMPLING                       │
  │                                                              │
  │  HEAD (SDK — at span START):       TAIL (Collector — at END):│
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Decide IMMEDIATELY    │         │ Buffer ALL spans      │  │
  │  │ "Keep 10% of traces" │         │ Wait for trace END    │  │
  │  │ Pros: Fast, low cost  │         │ "Keep ALL errors +    │  │
  │  │ Cons: Might drop      │         │  traces > 2s"         │  │
  │  │  error traces!        │         │ Pros: Keeps important │  │
  │  │                       │         │ Cons: Must see 100%   │  │
  │  │ Config: OTEL_TRACES_  │         │  first (higher mem)   │  │
  │  │ SAMPLER=traceidratio │         │ Config: tail_sampling │  │
  │  └──────────────────────┘         └──────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Head: "Keep 10% of traces" — you might drop the 0.1% that have errors. Tail: "Keep 100% of traces with status=ERROR OR duration > 5s" — keep everything interesting. Production pattern: Head sample at 10% in SDK, tail sample in Collector to keep error traces. Exam tip: Head = SDK, Tail = Collector.

Q5

Which sampling strategy should you use in production to keep 25% of traces while maintaining trace integrity?

Show Answer
Answer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          ParentBased(TraceIdRatioBased(0.25))                 │
  │                                                              │
  │  TraceIdRatioBased (root):          ParentBased (child):     │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Root span arrives         │      │ Child reads parent's │ │
  │  │ Hash trace_id → if <25%  │      │ trace_flags bit:     │ │
  │  │   → SAMPLED ✅            │      │   01 = sampled ✅     │ │
  │  │   → NOT sampled ❌        │      │   00 = dropped ❌     │ │
  │  │ Set trace_flags=01       │      │ No re-calculation!   │ │
  │  └──────────────────────────┘      └──────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                              │
  │  WHY: ParentBased prevents BROKEN traces (parent sampled    │
  │  but child dropped). Trace integrity is maintained.          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Without ParentBased: you could sample a parent span but NOT its child — resulting in broken traces with missing spans. ParentBased guarantees: if a trace is sampled at the root, ALL spans in that trace are sampled.

Q6

What should you NEVER put in Baggage?

Show Answer
Answer

Secrets, passwords, API keys, PII (personally identifiable information), or any sensitive data. Baggage values are transmitted in plain text in HTTP headers and are visible to ALL downstream services.

Explanation

Baggage appears as an HTTP header: baggage: user.id=42,tenant=acme. Anyone who can see HTTP headers (proxies, load balancers, logging systems) can see baggage values. Use baggage for non-sensitive context (user_id, tenant_id, environment) — never for secrets. OTCA exam may ask about baggage security considerations.

Q7

How does auto-instrumentation handle context propagation for HTTP requests?

Show Answer
Answer

Automatically. Auto-instrumentation libraries (like opentelemetry-instrumentation-requests) automatically: (1) EXTRACT traceparent from incoming requests, (2) CREATE child spans, and (3) INJECT traceparent into outgoing requests. No manual code needed.

Explanation

For anihpj: When Django receives a request, the Django instrumentation extracts traceparent. When your code calls requests.get("http://auth-service/validate"), the requests instrumentation automatically injects traceparent. You don't write any propagation code — it "just works." Manual propagation is only needed for custom protocols (raw sockets, proprietary RPC).

Q8

What environment variables configure sampling in OpenTelemetry?

Show Answer
Answer

OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER (strategy: always_on, always_off, traceidratio, parentbased_always_on, parentbased_traceidratio) and OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG (ratio value: 0.0 to 1.0).

Explanation

Example: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio + OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1 = keep 10% of traces with parent-based consistency. These env vars work across ALL language SDKs without code changes. Memorize these for the OTCA exam — they're the most commonly tested OTel env vars.

Q9

Is the W3C Trace-Context standard specific to OpenTelemetry?

Show Answer
Answer

No. W3C Trace-Context is an INDUSTRY STANDARD, not OTel-specific. It's used by all distributed tracing systems (Jaeger, Zipkin, Datadog, etc.). OTel implements the W3C standard — it didn't create it.

Explanation

This is important: an OTel-instrumented service and a Zipkin-instrumented service can participate in the SAME trace because both respect the W3C traceparent header. This interoperability is by design — the W3C created a standard that ALL tracing systems can use. OTel is the most popular implementation, not the creator.

Q10

In the Extract-Process-Inject cycle, what does the "Inject" step do?

Show Answer
Answer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          EXTRACT → PROCESS → INJECT CYCLE                     │
  │                                                              │
  │  Service A (api)                   Service B (auth)          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────┐  │
  │  │                      │  HTTP   │ 1. EXTRACT            │  │
  │  │ 5. INJECT            │────────▶│    Read traceparent   │  │
  │  │ Write traceparent:    │         │    → SpanContext      │  │
  │  │ 00-AAA...-BBB...-01  │         │                       │  │
  │  │                      │         │ 2. PROCESS             │  │
  │  │                      │         │    Create child span  │  │
  │  │                      │         │    Do business logic  │  │
  │  │                      │         │                       │  │
  │  │                      │         │ 3. INJECT (if calling │  │
  │  │                      │         │    another service)   │  │
  │  └──────────────────────┘         └──────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                              │
  │  Cycle repeats at every service hop — all share trace_id!   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Cycle: Extract (read traceparent from incoming request) → Process (create child span, do work) → Inject (write traceparent to outgoing request). This cycle repeats at every service hop, creating a chain of spans that all share the same trace_id.

  • 1. "Baggage = Span Attributes" → WRONG. Baggage propagates automatically; span attributes don't. Different use cases.
  • 2. "AlwaysOn sampling in production" → WRONG. 100% sampling at scale = massive costs. Use TraceIdRatioBased with 10% or less.
  • 3. "RateLimiting is the best sampler" → WRONG. RateLimiting breaks trace integrity (can sample parent but not child). Use ParentBased.
  • 4. Putting PII in baggage → NEVER. Baggage is plain text in HTTP headers visible to proxies and logging systems.
  • 5. "traceparent is OTel-specific" → WRONG. It's a W3C standard used by ALL tracing systems.

📋 Part 2 Summary — The OTel API & SDK (OTCA Domain 2 — 46%)

🎯 This is the HEAVIEST Domain — Nearly Half the Exam!

Domain 2 tests your ability to use OpenTelemetry: writing instrumentation code, configuring SDKs, understanding how auto-instrumentation works, reading traces, and choosing the right backend. Here's your exam readiness checklist:

  • Ch 5: Manual Instrumentation — Write spans, create metrics, bridge logs. Know the span lifecycle COLD.
  • Ch 6: Auto-Instrumentation — Zero-code observability. Know the 3 commands + 6 environment variables.
  • Ch 7: Instrumentation Ecosystem — OTel Registry, language support, best practices.
  • Ch 8: Distributed Traces — Trace/span anatomy, span kinds, events vs attributes, span links.
  • Ch 9: Traces in Practice — Tracing HTTP, DB, cache, Celery. Error recording. Business context.
  • Ch 10: Trace Analysis — 4 bottleneck patterns, RCA workflow, exemplars, comparing traces.
  • Ch 11: Jaeger & Backends — Architecture, deployment, UI, alternatives (Tempo, Honeycomb).

🧠 Must-Memorize for the OTCA Exam

Span Lifecycle

Start → set_attribute → add_event → set_status → end. Context manager (with...as span:) auto-ends.

5 Span Kinds

SERVER (in), CLIENT (out), INTERNAL (default), PRODUCER (send msg), CONSUMER (recv msg).

5 Metric Types

Counter (↑ only), UpDownCounter (↑↓), Histogram (buckets), ObservableGauge, ObsUpDownCounter.

3 Auto-Instr Commands

pip install opentelemetry-distro → opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install → opentelemetry-instrument python app.py

6 Critical Env Vars

OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER, OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG, OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, OTEL_PROPAGATORS

4 Bottleneck Patterns

Wide span (single slow op), N+1 queries, deep nesting (>5 hops), gaps (waiting time).

BatchSpanProcessor

ALWAYS use in production. SimpleSpanProcessor = dev only. Queues spans, exports async in batches.

OTLP Ports

gRPC: 4317 (binary, streaming). HTTP: 4318 (JSON, firewall-friendly). Jaeger UI: 16686.

☸️ Practical: anihpj with Auto-Instrumentation on K8s

K8s Pod spec — anihpj with OTel auto-instrumentation
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
spec:
  containers:
  - name: django
    image: anihpj/api:v2.4.1
    command: ["opentelemetry-instrument", "python", "manage.py", "runserver", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
    env:
    - name: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME
      value: "anihpj-api"
    - name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
      value: "http://otel-collector:4317"
    - name: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER
      value: "parentbased_traceidratio"
    - name: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG
      value: "0.25"
    - name: OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES
      value: "k8s.namespace.name=production,deployment.environment=prod"
# That's it! Every request, DB query, and cache op in this Pod is auto-traced.

Chapter 5: Manual Instrumentation with OpenTelemetry SDKs 🟡 Intermediate

Chapter 5: Manual Instrumentation — Creating Spans and Metrics by Hand

Now we get our hands dirty. Manual instrumentation means YOU write the code that creates spans, records metrics, and emits logs. While auto-instrumentation (Chapter 6) gives you 80% coverage with zero code, manual instrumentation gives you 100% control — you decide exactly what to name your spans, which attributes matter, and how to capture your business logic. We'll instrument anihpj/jobpost step by step.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~3 hours 💻 Hands-On 🎯 Core D2
🎓 OTCA Relevance
Domain 2: API & SDK ~46%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What manual instrumentation is and when you need it (vs auto-instrumentation)
  • ✅ Complete OTel Python SDK setup — TracerProvider, SpanProcessor, Exporter, Resource
  • ✅ Creating spans: start/end, attributes, events, status codes, exception recording
  • ✅ Creating all 5 metric types: Counter, UpDownCounter, Histogram, ObservableGauge, ObservableUpDownCounter
  • ✅ Connecting Python's logging module to OTel via the Logs Bridge API with trace_id injection
  • ✅ Configuring Resource attributes to properly identify your service
Manual Instrumentation is on the OTCA Exam — Know These Patterns

The OTCA exam tests your ability to read and understand manual instrumentation code. Key patterns to memorize:

  • Span lifecycle: tracer.start_as_current_span() → set_attribute() → add_event() → set_status() → auto-end on context exit
  • Metric creation: meter.create_counter("name") then counter.add(1, {"status": "ok"})
  • Resource: ALWAYS set service.name — otherwise your telemetry is labeled "unknown_service"

5.1 What is Manual Instrumentation?

Manual instrumentation means you write code to create spans, record metrics, and emit logs — rather than relying on auto-instrumentation libraries to do it for you. It gives you full control over span names, attributes, events, and status codes.

✅ When to Use Manual Instrumentation
  • Custom business logic not covered by auto-instrumentation
  • Domain-specific attributes (user.plan, job.category)
  • Fine-grained spans within a function (validate, calculate, save)
  • Custom protocols (raw sockets, proprietary RPC)
❌ When NOT to Use It
  • Standard HTTP/gRPC/database calls (auto-instrumentation handles these)
  • Simple CRUD endpoints with standard attributes
  • When you need consistency across 50+ services (auto-instrumentation is more uniform)

Best practice: Start with auto-instrumentation (Chapter 6) for 80% coverage, then add manual instrumentation for the 20% that matters — your business logic, custom attributes, and domain-specific spans.

5.2 The OTel Python SDK — Setup and Configuration

Python — Complete OTel SDK Initialization for anihpj
# ─── 1. IMPORTS ───
from opentelemetry import trace, metrics
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics import MeterProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.export import PeriodicExportingMetricReader
from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource, SERVICE_NAME
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.grpc.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.grpc.metric_exporter import OTLPMetricExporter

# ─── 2. RESOURCE — Who am I? (REQUIRED!) ───
resource = Resource(attributes={
    SERVICE_NAME: "anihpj-api",
    "service.version": "2.4.1",
    "deployment.environment": "production"
})

# ─── 3. TRACING SETUP ───
# Create a TracerProvider
tracer_provider = TracerProvider(resource=resource)

# Create an OTLP exporter (sends to Collector on port 4317)
span_exporter = OTLPSpanExporter(
    endpoint="http://localhost:4317",
    insecure=True  # No TLS for local dev
)

# Add BatchSpanProcessor (production — async batching)
tracer_provider.add_span_processor(
    BatchSpanProcessor(span_exporter)
)

# Set as the global TracerProvider
trace.set_tracer_provider(tracer_provider)

# ─── 4. METRICS SETUP ───
metric_reader = PeriodicExportingMetricReader(
    OTLPMetricExporter(endpoint="http://localhost:4317", insecure=True),
    export_interval_millis=60_000  # Export every 60 seconds
)
meter_provider = MeterProvider(
    resource=resource,
    metric_readers=[metric_reader]
)
metrics.set_meter_provider(meter_provider)

# ─── 5. NOW YOU'RE READY! ───
tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)
meter = metrics.get_meter(__name__)
print(f"✅ OTel initialized for {resource.attributes[SERVICE_NAME]}")
📖 Key Point: Global Providers

trace.set_tracer_provider() and metrics.set_meter_provider() set the GLOBAL default. Any code anywhere in your application that calls trace.get_tracer() or metrics.get_meter() will use these providers. This is how instrumentation libraries (like Django OTel) automatically "light up" with your configuration.

5.3 Creating Spans Manually

Span Lifecycle — Start → Attributes → Events → Status → End

Span Lifecycle Timeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                        SPAN LIFECYCLE                                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  t=0ms                    t=150ms                   t=235ms              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐                    │
  │  │ ① START                  │ ② DURING              │ ③ END              │
  │  │                          │                       │                    │
  │  │ with tracer.start_as_    │ .set_attribute(       │ span.end()         │
  │  │   current_span(          │   "user.id", 42)      │ (auto-called by    │
  │  │   "jobpost.create")      │ .add_event(           │  context manager)  │
  │  │   as span:               │   "validated",        │                    │
  │  │                          │   attrs={...})        │ → passed to        │
  │  │ Clock starts ticking     │ .set_status(OK)       │   SpanProcessor    │
  │  │ SpanContext created      │                       │ → exported         │
  │  │ (trace_id + span_id)     │                       │                    │
  │  └──────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Events timeline:                                                        │
  │  ──●──────────────────●──────────────────────●──────────────────▶        │
  │    │                  │                      │                           │
  │  "started"      "validated"            "saved_to_db"                     │
  │  t=0ms           t=80ms                 t=200ms                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Python — Complete Span Example for anihpj create_job view
tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

def create_job(request):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("jobpost.create") as span:
        # 1. Set attributes (metadata about the operation)
        span.set_attribute("user.id", request.user.id)
        span.set_attribute("job.title", request.data["title"])
        
        # 2. Add an event (timestamped annotation)
        span.add_event("validation.started", {"fields": len(request.data)})
        
        # 3. Do the actual work
        try:
            job = JobPost.objects.create(**request.data)
            span.set_attribute("job.id", job.id)
            span.add_event("saved_to_db", {"job.id": job.id})
        except Exception as ex:
            # 4. Record exceptions!
            span.record_exception(ex)
            span.set_status(StatusCode.ERROR, str(ex))
            raise
        
        # 5. Set status to OK
        span.set_status(StatusCode.OK)
        return Response({"id": job.id})

Span Kinds — Choosing the Right Type

📥
SERVER

Incoming request. Django receiving HTTP, gRPC server. SpanKind.SERVER

📤
CLIENT

Outgoing request. Calling an API, DB query. SpanKind.CLIENT

⚙️
INTERNAL

Internal operation. Computation, validation. SpanKind.INTERNAL (default)

📨
PRODUCER / CONSUMER

Message queue. Sending (PRODUCER) or receiving (CONSUMER) a message.

5.4 Creating Metrics Manually

The 5 Metric Instruments

📈
Counter — Only Increases

jobs_counter = meter.create_counter("jobs.created.total")
jobs_counter.add(1, {"status": "published"})
Use for: request count, error count, jobs created

📊
UpDownCounter — Goes Both Ways

connections = meter.create_up_down_counter("ws.connections")
connections.add(1) on connect, connections.add(-1) on disconnect
Use for: active connections, queue depth

📉
Histogram — Distribution

latency = meter.create_histogram("http.request.duration", unit="s")
latency.record(0.235, {"method": "POST"})
Use for: request latency, payload size

🔭
ObservableGauge — Callback-Based

meter.create_observable_gauge("db.pool.size", callback=get_pool_size)
OTel calls YOUR function every 60s to get the current value
Use for: memory usage, pool size, CPU temp

Manual Instrumentation Data Flow

Python — All 5 Metric Types for anihpj
meter = metrics.get_meter(__name__)

# 1. COUNTER — jobs created (only goes up)
jobs_counter = meter.create_counter(
    "jobs.created.total",
    description="Total number of jobs created"
)
jobs_counter.add(1, {"plan": "premium", "status": "published"})

# 2. UPDOWNCOUNTER — active WebSocket connections
ws_connections = meter.create_up_down_counter(
    "ws.connections.active",
    description="Active WebSocket connections"
)
ws_connections.add(1)   # Connection opened
ws_connections.add(-1)  # Connection closed

# 3. HISTOGRAM — request latency
request_latency = meter.create_histogram(
    "http.request.duration",
    unit="s",
    description="HTTP request duration in seconds"
)
request_latency.record(0.235, {"method": "POST", "route": "/api/jobs/"})

# 4. OBSERVABLE GAUGE — DB connection pool size (callback-based)
def get_db_pool_size(options):
    from django.db import connections
    yield metrics.Observation(
        len(connections.all()), {"db.name": "anihpj"}
    )
meter.create_observable_gauge(
    "db.connection_pool.size",
    callbacks=[get_db_pool_size],
    description="Database connection pool size"
)

# 5. OBSERVABLE UPDOWNCOUNTER — Celery queue depth
def get_queue_depth(options):
    from celery import current_app
    depth = current_app.control.inspect().active() or {}
    yield metrics.Observation(len(depth), {})
meter.create_observable_up_down_counter(
    "celery.queue.depth",
    callbacks=[get_queue_depth]
)

5.5 Creating Logs via the Logs Bridge API

OTel does NOT replace Python's logging — it bridges your existing logs into the OTel pipeline, automatically injecting trace_id and span_id for correlation.

Python — Bridging Standard Logging to OTel
import logging
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.logging import LoggingInstrumentor

# Bridge Python's standard logging to OTel
LoggingInstrumentor().instrument(set_logging_format=True)

# Now use normal Python logging — trace_id is auto-injected!
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.info("Job created", extra={"job_id": 99, "user_id": 42})
# Output includes: trace_id, span_id, service.name automatically!

5.9 Manual Instrumentation Best Practices & Patterns

Manual instrumentation gives you full control — but with great power comes great responsibility. Here are battle-tested patterns that the OTCA exam tests.

🎯 Span Naming Conventions

✅ GOOD Span Names
  • "POST /api/jobs/" — HTTP method + route
  • "INSERT jobpost" — DB operation + table
  • "process_payment" — business operation
  • "cache.get" — low-cardinality operation
❌ BAD Span Names
  • "cache.get:user:42" — HIGH card. (unique per user!)
  • "span-1" — meaningless
  • "handle_request" — too generic

⚡ Performance Considerations

OperationCostRecommendation
span.start() / span.end()~1-5μsSafe — OTel is designed to be fast
span.set_attribute()~0.1μs eachSafe for dozens of attributes per span
Exporter sending1-10ms (network)Async via BatchSpanProcessor — non-blocking
span.add_event()~0.5μs eachUse sparingly — events are always emitted
⚠️ DO NOT create spans in tight loops

A span per iteration of a 100K-item loop = 100K spans → memory explosion + backend overload. Pattern: create ONE span for the batch operation, use span.add_event() for notable iterations, or use metrics for per-item counts. The OTCA exam tests instrumentation performance implications.
