📝 OTCA Practice Questions — Chapter 11

Q1

Who created Jaeger and what is its CNCF status?

Show Answer
Answer
  Jaeger Timeline:
  2015: Uber creates Jaeger for 1,000+ microservices
  2017: Donated to CNCF
  2019: CNCF GRADUATED (highest maturity — alongside K8s & Prometheus)
  
  CNCF Maturity Levels:
  Sandbox → Incubating → Graduated ✅ (Jaeger, Prometheus, K8s, Loki)
Explanation

Jaeger is one of the few CNCF Graduated projects — the highest maturity level. It was created at Uber to trace their massive microservices architecture. OTCA: Know Jaeger's origin (Uber, 2015) and CNCF status (Graduated, 2019).

Q2

What signals does Jaeger handle?

Show Answer
Answer
  Jaeger = TRACES ONLY
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ TRACES:  ✅ Jaeger (OTLP on :4317)                  │
  │ METRICS: ❌ Use Prometheus or Mimir                  │
  │ LOGS:    ❌ Use Loki or Elasticsearch                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Jaeger stores, searches, and visualizes traces.
  It does NOT handle metrics or logs.
Explanation

Each CNCF observability tool handles ONE signal: Jaeger = traces, Prometheus = metrics, Loki = logs. OTel is unique in handling ALL three. OTCA: "Can Jaeger store metrics?" → NO. Traces only.

Q3

What are the 4 core Jaeger components?

Show Answer
Answer
  Jaeger Architecture:
  ┌──────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Agent    │ UDP listener on each host, batches spans  │
  │ Collector│ Validates, indexes, stores spans to DB    │
  │ Query    │ REST API + Web UI (port :16686)           │
  │ Storage  │ Elasticsearch / Cassandra / Badger        │
  └──────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Agent→Collector→Storage; Query reads from Storage
Explanation

Agent receives spans via UDP (low overhead), Collector processes and stores them, Storage persists them, Query serves the UI/API. In modern setups with OTel Collector, the Agent is often replaced by the OTel Collector. OTCA: Know the 4 components and their roles.

Q4

Does Jaeger accept OTLP natively?

Show Answer
Answer
  YES — Jaeger accepts OTLP on port 4317 (gRPC).
  
  OTel SDK/Collector          Jaeger
  ┌──────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
  │ OTLPSpanExporter │──OTLP─▶│ OTLP Receiver    │
  │ endpoint:        │ gRPC  │ :4317            │
  │ jaeger:4317      │       │                  │
  └──────────────────┘       └──────────────────┘
  
  No Jaeger-specific protocol needed. No Thrift. Just OTLP.
Explanation

Since 2022, Jaeger accepts OTLP natively. You no longer need the legacy Jaeger Thrift protocol. Just point your OTLP exporter to jaeger:4317 and traces flow directly. OTCA: Jaeger OTLP = port 4317. Jaeger UI = port 16686.

Q5

What is the difference between Jaeger All-in-One and Production deployment?

Show Answer
Answer
  ALL-IN-ONE (dev):                 PRODUCTION:
  ┌──────────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ 1 binary, 1 container    │     │ Separate components       │
  │ In-memory storage (lost  │     │ Persistent storage (ES/   │
  │   on restart)            │     │   Cassandra)              │
  │ No Kafka buffer          │     │ Kafka for buffering       │
  │ docker run jaeger:latest │     │ HA: multiple replicas     │
  │ Good for: local dev      │     │ Good for: production      │
  └──────────────────────────┘     └──────────────────────────┘
Explanation

All-in-One is for development ONLY — spans are lost on restart (in-memory storage). Production requires: persistent storage (ES/Cassandra), Kafka buffer between Collector and Storage, and multiple replicas for HA. OTCA: Never use All-in-One in production.

Q6

What is Grafana Tempo's main advantage over Jaeger?

Show Answer
Answer
  COST COMPARISON (1TB, 30 days):
  ┌──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │ Jaeger + ES  │ ~$1,000/mo   │ SSD storage + indexing   │
  │ Tempo + S3   │ ~$230/mo     │ Object storage, no index │
  └──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
  
  Tempo advantages:
  • S3/GCS object storage = ~10x cheaper than ES
  • No span indexing → scales to massive volumes
  • TraceQL: powerful query language for traces
  • Native Grafana integration (same UI)
Explanation

Tempo's killer feature is cost: object storage is ~10x cheaper than Elasticsearch. It doesn't index span attributes — uses label-based lookup instead. This makes it viable for long retention (months/years) at any scale. OTCA: Tempo = S3 + TraceQL + Grafana native.

Q7

What port does the Jaeger UI run on?

Show Answer
Answer
  Jaeger Ports (memorize for OTCA!):
  ┌──────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 16686    │ Jaeger UI (http://localhost:16686)        │
  │ 4317     │ OTLP gRPC (traces from OTel SDK/Collector)│
  │ 4318     │ OTLP HTTP (alternative)                   │
  │ 14250    │ Jaeger Thrift (LEGACY — don't use)        │
  └──────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Port 16686 is the Jaeger Web UI. Port 4317 is where OTel sends traces via OTLP. Port 14250 is the legacy Jaeger-native protocol — with OTel, you should use OTLP (4317) instead. OTCA: Know 16686=UI, 4317=OTLP.

Q8

How do you see service dependencies in Jaeger?

Show Answer
Answer
  Jaeger UI → Dependencies Tab:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Service Dependency Graph (auto-generated):          │
  │                                                      │
  │  anihpj-api ────1500 req──▶ auth-service            │
  │     │                                                    │
  │     ├────2300 req──▶ PostgreSQL                      │
  │     │                                                    │
  │     └────800 req───▶ Redis                           │
  │                                                      │
  │ Nodes = services. Edges = calls. Thickness = volume. │
  │ Built from span parent-child relationships.          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

The Dependencies tab shows a real-time service map built from trace data. Nodes = services, edges = calls between them, edge thickness = call volume. This is auto-generated — you don't configure it. OTCA: Dependencies tab shows the service topology from trace data.

Q9

Can you use OTel without Jaeger?

Show Answer
Answer
  YES — OTel is backend-agnostic:
  
  OTel generates traces → send to ANY OTLP backend:
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Jaeger           │ Open source, self-hosted         │
  │ Grafana Tempo    │ Open source, S3 storage          │
  │ Datadog APM      │ SaaS, all-in-one platform        │
  │ Honeycomb        │ SaaS, high-cardinality queries   │
  │ Grafana Cloud    │ SaaS, free tier available        │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘
  Switch by changing ONE YAML line: endpoint:
Explanation

OTel is NOT tied to Jaeger. You instrument once with OTel and can switch backends by changing configuration. Jaeger is just one of many OTLP-compatible backends. OTCA: OTel ≠ Jaeger. OTel generates; Jaeger (or Tempo/Datadog/etc.) stores.

Q10

What storage backends does Jaeger production support?

Show Answer
Answer
  Jaeger Storage Backends:
  ┌────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Elasticsearch  │ Most common. Full-text search.      │
  │ Cassandra      │ High write throughput. Scalable.    │
  │ Badger         │ Embedded (testing only).            │
  │ Kafka          │ Buffer between Collector→Storage.   │
  └────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘
  ES recommended for most deployments.
  Cassandra for extreme write volumes (Uber-scale).
Explanation

Elasticsearch is the most common production storage for Jaeger (full-text search, mature). Cassandra is for write-heavy workloads. Kafka acts as a buffer — Collector writes to Kafka, Storage reads from Kafka (decouples ingestion from storage). OTCA: ES=most common, Cassandra=high volume, Kafka=buffer.

Chapter 12: Understanding OTel Metrics 🟡 Intermediate

Metrics are the second telemetry signal in OpenTelemetry — alongside traces and logs. While traces show you the journey of one request, metrics give you the aggregated picture: how many requests per second? How fast? How many errors? In this chapter, you'll learn the five OTel metric instruments, the data model pipeline, and how to choose the right instrument for every scenario in the anihpj platform.

🎯 OTCA Exam Domain D3 (26%): Metrics are heavily tested. You MUST know all 5 instrument types, synchronous vs asynchronous, and the data model pipeline (MeterProvider → Meter → Instrument → MetricReader → Exporter).
📈 Counter

Only goes UP. Total requests, errors, jobs created.

📊 UpDownCounter

Goes UP & DOWN. Active connections, queue depth.

📉 Histogram

Distribution of values. Latency, payload size, query rows.

🔍 ObservableGauge

Point-in-time value via callback. CPU%, memory, cache size.

🔄 ObservableUpDownCounter

Async up/down. Queue depth where individual increments aren't possible.

⚡ ObservableCounter

Async monotonic counter. Items processed from external source.

12.1 What are OTel Metrics?

Metrics vs Traces — The Fundamental Difference
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              METRICS vs TRACES — WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE?                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  TRACES (Chapter 5-11):                  METRICS (Chapter 12-14):          │
  │  ┌────────────────────────┐            ┌────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ One request journey    │            │ Aggregated view over time  │    │
  │  │ Trace: a1b2c3...       │            │ rate(http_requests[5m])    │    │
  │  │ ├── POST /api/jobs/    │            │   = 42 req/s               │    │
  │  │ │   ├── auth (25ms)    │            │                            │    │
  │  │ │   ├── DB INSERT      │            │ All 10,000 requests in     │    │
  │  │ │   │   (180ms)        │            │ 5 minutes → one number     │    │
  │  │ │   └── SET cache (5ms)│            │                            │    │
  │  │ Total: 210ms           │            │ Answer: "HOW MANY?"        │    │
  │  │                        │            │ Answer: "HOW FAST?"        │    │
  │  │ Answer: "WHY slow?"    │            │ Answer: "HOW MANY ERRORS?" │    │
  │  └────────────────────────┘            └────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Together: Traces tell you WHY a request was slow.                       │
  │           Metrics tell you IF there's a problem across ALL requests.      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Metrics are numeric measurements collected over time intervals. Unlike traces (which capture individual request journeys), metrics are aggregated at collection time — they summarize thousands of individual events into a single data point.

✅ Key Properties of Metrics

• Aggregated (not individual)
• Low cost (1 data point per time window)
• Time-series based
• Good for alerting & dashboards
• Prometheus-compatible by design

📊 Example: anihpj Job Creation

• Trace: "User 42 created JobPost #99 in 210ms"
• Metric: "jobs_created_total{plan='premium'} = 847 in last hour"

Metrics Data Model — 4 Essential Terms You MUST Know
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              METRICS DATA MODEL — 4 KEY TERMS                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  TERM 1: INSTRUMENT (The Definition)     TERM 2: MEASUREMENT (One Reading)│
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ counter = meter.create_    │        │ counter.add(1, {           │   │
  │  │   counter("jobs.created",  │        │   "plan": "premium"})      │   │
  │  │   unit="1")                │        │                            │   │
  │  │                            │        │ → One measurement:         │   │
  │  │ Defined ONCE at startup.   │        │   value=1, plan=premium    │   │
  │  │ Like a "sensor type."      │        │                            │   │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘        │ Happens IN your code at    │   │
  │                                        │ request time.              │   │
  │  TERM 3: METRIC STREAM (Grouped)       └────────────────────────────┘   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐        TERM 4: METRIC POINT (Exported)   │
  │  │ All measurements with      │        ┌────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ plan="premium" grouped     │        │ {timestamp: 1717718400,    │   │
  │  │ together into one stream.  │        │  value: 847,               │   │
  │  │ One stream per unique      │        │  attributes: {             │   │
  │  │ attribute combination.     │        │    plan: "premium"}}       │   │
  │  │                            │        │                            │   │
  │  │ Aggregation: sum=847       │        │ One timestamped data point │   │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘        │ sent to backend every 60s. │   │
  │                                        └────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  PIPELINE: Instrument → Measurement → Metric Stream → Metric Point       │
  │            (define once)  (add in code)   (grouped by attrs) (exported)  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

12.2 The Metrics Data Model

OTel Metrics Pipeline — From Instrument to Backend
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              METRICS DATA MODEL — COMPLETE PIPELINE                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌───────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐          │
  │  │ APP CODE │───▶│  METER   │───▶│  METER   │───▶│  METRIC  │          │
  │  │          │    │ PROVIDER  │    │          │    │  READER  │          │
  │  │ counter  │    │           │    │ Creates  │    │          │          │
  │  │ .add(1)  │    │ Global    │    │ Instru-  │    │ Collects │          │
  │  │          │    │ config    │    │ ments    │    │ on timer │          │
  │  └──────────┘    └───────────┘    └──────────┘    └────┬─────┘          │
  │                                                       │                │
  │                    ┌──────────────────────────────────┘                │
  │                    ▼                                                    │
  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌───────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐        │
  │  │ BACKEND  │◀───│  METRIC   │◀───│ AGGREGA- │◀───│  VIEW    │        │
  │  │          │    │ EXPORTER  │    │  TION    │    │          │        │
  │  │ Prometh. │    │           │    │          │    │ Filters &│        │
  │  │ Grafana  │    │ Push/Pull │    │ Sum/Dist │    │ renames  │        │
  │  │ Jaeger   │    │           │    │ LastValue│    │          │        │
  │  └──────────┘    └───────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Key components:                                                         │
  │  • MeterProvider: Global config (resource, exporters)                    │
  │  • Meter: Namespace for instruments ("anihpj-api")                       │
  │  • Instrument: Counter, Histogram, etc. — captures measurements          │
  │  • MetricReader: PeriodicExportingMetricReader (60s default, push-based) or PullMetricReader (waits for Prometheus scrape)     │
  │  • View: Filters, renames, changes aggregation for specific instruments  │
  │  • Aggregation: Sum (Counter), Explicit Buckets (Histogram), LastValue   │
  │  • MetricExporter: OTLP gRPC, Prometheus, Console                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔧 MeterProvider Setup (Python)
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics import MeterProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.export import (
    PeriodicExportingMetricReader,
    ConsoleMetricExporter
)
reader = PeriodicExportingMetricReader(
    ConsoleMetricExporter(), 
    export_interval_millis=60000
)
provider = MeterProvider(metric_readers=[reader])
meter = provider.get_meter("anihpj-api", "1.0.0")
📐 Aggregation Types

• Sum: For Counters — total across all measurements
• LastValue: For Gauges — most recent value
• Explicit Buckets: For Histograms — count per predefined bucket
• Choice is AUTOMATIC based on instrument type

12.3 Metric Instruments Deep Dive

OpenTelemetry defines 6 instrument types. Each has a specific use case, aggregation behavior, and Prometheus mapping. You MUST know these for the OTCA exam.

InstrumentDirectionSync/AsyncPrometheusUse Case (anihpj)
CounterOnly UP ↑Synccounter (_total)jobs_created_total, errors_total
UpDownCounterUP ↑ & DOWN ↓Syncgaugeactive_connections, in_flight_requests
HistogramDistributionSynchistogramhttp_request_duration_seconds
ObservableGaugePoint valueAsyncgaugecpu_utilization, cache_size_bytes
ObservableUpDownCounterUP ↑ & DOWN ↓Asyncgaugecelery_queue_depth
ObservableCounterOnly UP ↑Asynccounterkafka_messages_consumed

12.3a Counter & UpDownCounter

Counter vs UpDownCounter — Direction Matters
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              COUNTER (Monotonic) vs UPDOWNCOUNTER (Non-Monotonic)          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  COUNTER — Only goes UP:                UPDOWNCOUNTER — Goes UP & DOWN:   │
  │  Value: 0 → 1 → 5 → 47 → 847           Value: 0 → 3 → 7 → 5 → 2 → 12   │
  │  ████                                   ██                                 │
  │  ████                                   ██      ██                        │
  │  ████                                   ██  ██  ██  ██                    │
  │  ████                                   ██  ██  ██  ██  ██                │
  │  ████████████████████████████████        ██  ██  ██  ██  ██  ██            │
  │  ───────────────────────────────        ██  ██  ██  ██  ██  ██  ██        │
  │  Use: requests.total, errors.total      Use: active_connections, queue    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CODE (anihpj):                                                          │
  │  counter = meter.create_counter(          updown = meter.create_up_down_  │
  │      "jobs.created.total",                counter("ws.connections.active",│
  │      description="Total jobs created")    description="Active WebSocket") │
  │  counter.add(1, {"plan": "premium"})     updown.add(1)   # user connects │
  │                                           updown.add(-1)  # disconnects   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ OTCA Exam Trap: You CANNOT call counter.add(-1) — Counters are monotonic! Use UpDownCounter instead. Also, Counter values restart at 0 on process restart, but Prometheus handles this via the rate() function.

12.3b Histogram & ObservableGauge

Histogram — How Buckets Work
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              HISTOGRAM — BUCKET DISTRIBUTION                               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RECORDED VALUES: 12ms, 45ms, 120ms, 230ms, 510ms, 1200ms               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BUCKETS: [0, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2500, ∞]                         │
  │  ┌────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┬─────┐ │
  │  │ 0-50ms │51-100ms│101-250 │251-500 │501-1000│1001-250│ 2500+  │Total││
  │  │   ██   │   █    │   ██   │   █    │   █    │   ██   │   0    │  7  ││
  │  │   2    │   1    │   2    │   1    │   1    │    1   │   0    │     ││
  │  └────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┴─────┘ │
  │                                                                          │
  │  From buckets, PromQL can ESTIMATE:                                      │
  │  • histogram_quantile(0.50, ...) → p50 ≈ 100ms (50% of values ≤ 100ms)  │
  │  • histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) → p95 ≈ 1200ms                          │
  │  • histogram_quantile(0.99, ...) → p99 ≈ 1200ms (approximate!)          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  OBSERVABLE GAUGE — Callback-Based:                                      │
  │  def get_cache_size(options):                                            │
  │      return [Observation(len(cache._cache), {})]                         │
  │  gauge = meter.create_observable_gauge(                                  │
  │      "cache.size_bytes", callbacks=[get_cache_size])                     │
  │  # OTel SDK calls get_cache_size() every 60s automatically              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📏 Bucket Strategy Tips

• 10-15 buckets, exponentially spaced
• Put buckets around your SLO
• Include long tail (2.5s, 5s, 10s)
• Too few buckets = imprecise percentiles
• Too many = high memory usage

🔍 When to use ObservableGauge

• Value exists independently (CPU, memory)
• You can't increment/decrement
• OTel polls you, you don't push
• Good for: DB pool size, cache size, thread count

12.4 Synchronous vs Asynchronous Instruments

Sync (You Call) vs Async (OTel Calls You)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              SYNCHRONOUS vs ASYNCHRONOUS INSTRUMENTS                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SYNCHRONOUS (Your code calls OTel):       ASYNCHRONOUS (OTel calls you): │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐           ┌────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ def create_job(request):   │           │ def get_pool_size():       │ │
  │  │     job = JobPost(...)     │           │     conns = db.pool.size   │ │
  │  │     counter.add(1)  ◀──────│           │     return [Observation(   │ │
  │  │     hist.record(0.21) ◀────│           │       conns, {})]          │ │
  │  │     ...                    │           │                            │ │
  │  │                            │           │ gauge = meter.create_      │ │
  │  │  Instruments:              │           │   observable_gauge(        │ │
  │  │  • Counter                 │           │   "pg.pool.size",          │ │
  │  │  • UpDownCounter           │           │   callbacks=[get_pool_size]│ │
  │  │  • Histogram               │           │ )                          │ │
  │  │                            │           │ # get_pool_size() runs     │ │
  │  │  WHEN: Event-driven code   │           │ # every 60s automatically  │ │
  │  │  (requests, errors, etc.)  │           │                            │ │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘           │  Instruments:              │ │
  │                                           │  • ObservableCounter       │ │
  │                                           │  • ObservableUpDownCounter │ │
  │                                           │  • ObservableGauge         │ │
  │                                           │                            │ │
  │                                           │  WHEN: Values that exist   │ │
  │                                           │  independently (CPU, pool) │ │
  │                                           └────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 OTCA Tip: The exam WILL ask you to choose between sync and async. Rule: If the value exists independently of your code (CPU%, memory, pool size, queue depth), use async (Observable*). If your code triggers the event (request received, job created, error occurred), use sync.

12.5 Metric Attributes — Adding Dimensions

Attributes = Dimensions — Low Cardinality is Critical
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              METRIC ATTRIBUTES & CARDINALITY                               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WITHOUT attributes:                   WITH attributes:                   │
  │  jobs_created_total = 1000             jobs_created_total{                │
  │                                          plan="premium"} = 300            │
  │  One number, no slicing                jobs_created_total{                │
  │                                          plan="free"} = 700               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ✅ GOOD Attributes (LOW cardinality):   ❌ BAD Attributes (HIGH card.):   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ plan: free/premium/enterp │        │ user.id: 1,2,3,...1,000,000│    │
  │  │ (3 unique values)         │        │ (1,000,000 unique values!)  │    │
  │  │                           │        │                            │    │
  │  │ method: GET/POST/PUT/DEL  │        │ session.id: new UUID every  │    │
  │  │ (4 unique values)         │        │ session → INFINITE!         │    │
  │  │                           │        │                            │    │
  │  │ status: 2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx  │        │ trace_id: 16 bytes random   │    │
  │  │ (4 unique values)         │        │ → 2^128 possible values!    │    │
  │  │                           │        │                            │    │
  │  │ Total combos: 3×4×4 = 48 │        │ Memory: 1M×2KB = 2GB!       │    │
  │  │ Memory: 48×2KB = 96KB ✅ │        │                            │    │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘        └────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CARDINALITY RULE: < 10 unique values per attribute, < 100 combinations │
  │  High cardinality = 💥 Prometheus OOM, slow queries, expensive storage   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ CRITICAL for OTCA: Know the cardinality rule. Never use user.id, email, session.id, request.id, or trace_id as metric attributes. These have unbounded cardinality and will destroy your metrics backend.

12.6 Hands-On: Create All 5 Metric Types for anihpj

Complete Metrics Setup — anihpj API
metrics_setup.py — All OTel Metric Instruments for anihpj
# metrics_setup.py — Complete OTel Metrics for anihpj
from opentelemetry import metrics
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics import MeterProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.export import (
    PeriodicExportingMetricReader,
    ConsoleMetricExporter
)
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.view import ExplicitBucketHistogramAggregation
from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource

# 1. MeterProvider setup
resource = Resource.create({"service.name": "anihpj-api", "service.version": "2.0.0"})
reader = PeriodicExportingMetricReader(
    ConsoleMetricExporter(),
    export_interval_millis=60000  # Every 60 seconds
)
provider = MeterProvider(resource=resource, metric_readers=[reader])
metrics.set_meter_provider(provider)
meter = provider.get_meter("anihpj-api", "2.0.0")

# 2. COUNTER: Total jobs created (monotonic, only goes up)
jobs_counter = meter.create_counter(
    "jobs.created.total",
    description="Total number of job posts created",
    unit="1"
)
# Usage: jobs_counter.add(1, {"plan": "premium", "category": "tech"})

# 3. UPDOWNCOUNTER: Active WebSocket connections
ws_connections = meter.create_up_down_counter(
    "ws.connections.active",
    description="Number of active WebSocket connections",
    unit="1"
)
# Usage: ws_connections.add(1) on connect, add(-1) on disconnect

# 4. HISTOGRAM: HTTP request duration
request_duration = meter.create_histogram(
    "http.server.request.duration",
    description="Duration of HTTP server requests in seconds",
    unit="s"
)
# Usage: request_duration.record(0.235, {"http.method": "POST", "http.route": "/api/jobs/"})

# 5. OBSERVABLE GAUGE: PostgreSQL connection pool size (async callback)
def get_db_pool_size(options):
    from django.db import connections
    pool_size = len(connections.all())  # Simplified
    return [metrics.Observation(pool_size, {"pool": "default"})]

meter.create_observable_gauge(
    "db.pool.size",
    callbacks=[get_db_pool_size],
    description="Database connection pool size",
    unit="1"
)

# 6. OBSERVABLE UPDOWN COUNTER: Celery queue depth
def get_celery_queue_depth(options):
    from celery import current_app
    # Get pending tasks for each queue
    observations = []
    for queue in ["default", "high_priority", "emails"]:
        depth = current_app.control.inspect().reserved().get(queue, 0)
        observations.append(metrics.Observation(depth, {"queue": queue}))
    return observations

meter.create_observable_up_down_counter(
    "celery.queue.depth",
    callbacks=[get_celery_queue_depth],
    description="Number of tasks pending in Celery queues",
    unit="1"
)
Step 1

Create MeterProvider with PeriodicExportingMetricReader (60s interval)

Step 2

Create Counter for jobs created (with plan & category attributes)

Step 3

Create UpDownCounter for active WebSocket connections

Step 4

Create Histogram for HTTP request duration (method + route)

Step 5

Create ObservableGauge for PostgreSQL connection pool

Step 6

Create ObservableUpDownCounter for Celery queue depth

  │    }]                                                                     │
  │  }                                                                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

12.X PromQL Common Patterns & Traps for the OTCA Exam

PromQL is the query language for Prometheus — and the OTCA exam tests your ability to write correct PromQL queries. Here are the patterns and traps you MUST know:

PromQL Functions — When to Use Each
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    PromQL FUNCTION DECISION TREE                           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  START: What are you trying to calculate?                                 │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         ├── Per-second rate of change ──▶ rate(metric[time])             │
  │         │   Example: rate(http_requests_total[5m])                       │
  │         │   ⚠️ ONLY for Counters! Never rate() a Gauge!                  │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         ├── Total increase over period ──▶ increase(metric[time])        │
  │         │   Example: increase(jobs_created_total[1h])                    │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         ├── Percentile from Histogram ──▶ histogram_quantile(p, rate())  │
  │         │   Example: histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(duration_bucket[5m])) │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         ├── Current value (Gauge) ──▶ just metric_name                   │
  │         │   Example: db_connections_active                               │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         └── Aggregation across labels ──▶ sum/count/avg by(label)        │
  │             Example: sum(rate(requests[5m])) by (endpoint)               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
PromQL FunctionWorks OnReturnsCommon Trap
rate()Counter ONLYPer-second rateNever use on Gauge — returns garbage!
increase()Counter ONLYTotal increaseExtrapolates at boundaries — not exact
histogram_quantile()HistogramPercentile (p95)Must use rate() on buckets first
sum by()AnyAggregated sumWithout "by", aggregates ALL labels
avg_over_time()GaugeAverage over windowDifferent from rate() — for Gauges only
⚠️ #1 PromQL Trap on the OTCA Exam

rate(cpu_usage[5m]) → WRONG! cpu_usage is a Gauge, not a Counter. Using rate() on a Gauge returns mathematically nonsensical results. For Gauges, use avg_over_time(cpu_usage[5m]) or just cpu_usage. The exam WILL test: "Which PromQL function should you use on a Gauge?" → avg_over_time(), NOT rate().

📝 OTCA Practice Questions — Chapter 12

Q1
Which OTel instrument type is monotonic and can only increase?
Show Answer
Answer

Counter. Counters only go up. If you need an instrument that goes up AND down, use UpDownCounter or ObservableUpDownCounter.

Explanation
  Counter ──────────────────────────────────────────────▶
  0 → 1 → 5 → 47 → 847 → 1200
  Monotonic: value NEVER decreases
  Use: TOTAL requests, TOTAL errors, TOTAL jobs created
  
  ❌ counter.add(-1)  ← ERROR! Counter cannot go down
  ✅ counter.add(1)   ← Correct

A Counter is designed for cumulative totals. On the OTCA exam, if a question asks about tracking "total jobs created since app start," the answer is always Counter.

Q2
What is the default export interval for PeriodicExportingMetricReader?
Show Answer
Answer
reader = PeriodicExportingMetricReader(
    OTLPMetricExporter(endpoint="http://collector:4317"),
    export_interval_millis=60000  # ← DEFAULT: 60,000ms = 60 seconds
)

60 seconds (60,000 milliseconds). Configurable via export_interval_millis.

Explanation
  INSTRUMENT ──measure──▶ METRIC READER ──every 60s──▶ EXPORTER ──▶ BACKEND
                            │
                            └── Default: 60000ms
                                Dev:    10000ms (10s)
                                Prod:   60000ms (60s) ← standard

The MetricReader collects measurements from instruments and passes them to the exporter. The default 60-second interval means your dashboard updates once per minute. Know this number for the OTCA exam.

Q3
What Prometheus type does an OTel Histogram map to?
Show Answer
Answer
OTel Instrument→ Prometheus Type
Countercounter (_total suffix)
UpDownCountergauge
Histogramhistogram (_bucket, _sum, _count)
ObservableGaugegauge
Explanation

This mapping is automatic — you don't write Prometheus-specific code. The OTel SDK handles the conversion. The OTCA exam tests this mapping frequently — expect at least one question asking which Prometheus type a specific OTel instrument maps to.

Q4
When would you use an ObservableGauge instead of a synchronous instrument?
Show Answer
Answer
# ObservableGauge — OTel POLLS your callback
def get_cpu_temp(options):
    return [Observation(psutil.sensors_temperatures()["cpu"], {})]

meter.create_observable_gauge(
    "system.cpu.temperature",
    callbacks=[get_cpu_temp]  # ← Called every 60s automatically
)

# vs. Histogram (sync) — YOUR code pushes values
histogram.record(0.235, {"method": "POST"})  # ← Called at request time
Explanation
  SYNC (you call OTel):              ASYNC (OTel calls you):
  ┌──────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Counter.add(1)       │          │ callback() returns   │
  │ Histogram.record(x)  │          │ current value        │
  │ UpDownCounter.add(1) │          │ OTel polls on timer  │
  │                      │          │                      │
  │ When: event happens   │          │ When: value exists    │
  │ (request received,    │          │ independently         │
  │  job created, error)  │          │ (CPU%, pool size)    │
  └──────────────────────┘          └──────────────────────┘

OTCA exam trap: "CPU utilization" → ObservableGauge (async), not Gauge (which doesn't exist in OTel). The value exists independently — you can't increment/decrement CPU%.

Q5
What is the cardinality rule for metric attributes?
Show Answer
Answer

Keep attribute values bounded and under 100 unique combinations. Never use user.id, session.id, trace_id, or email as metric attributes.

Explanation
  ✅ LOW CARDINALITY (safe):          ❌ HIGH CARDINALITY (danger!):
  ┌──────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ plan: free|premium|enter │       │ user.id: 1,2,3...1,000,000│
  │ (3 values)               │       │ (1,000,000 values!)        │
  │                          │       │                            │
  │ method: GET|POST|PUT|DEL│       │ session.id: UUID × every   │
  │ (4 values)               │       │ session = INFINITE!        │
  │                          │       │                            │
  │ Total combos: 3×4 = 12  │       │ Memory: 1M×2KB = 2GB!     │
  │ Memory: 12×2KB = 24KB ✅│       │ Prometheus OOM 💥          │
  └──────────────────────────┘       └──────────────────────────┘

Each unique attribute combination = one time series. 1M users = 1M time series × 2KB = 2GB RAM. This is one of the most-tested OTCA topics.

Q6
What happens if you call counter.add(-1)?
Show Answer
Answer

It will result in an error. Counters are monotonic — they only accept positive values. Use UpDownCounter for instruments that need to go both up and down.

Explanation
  COUNTER (monotonic ↑):              UPDOWNCOUNTER (non-monotonic ↕):
  ┌──────────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ counter.add(1)    │           │ ✅ updown.add(1)     │
  │ ✅ counter.add(5)    │           │ ✅ updown.add(-1)    │
  │ ❌ counter.add(-1)   │           │ ✅ updown.add(3)     │
  │    ↑ ERROR!          │           │ ✅ updown.add(-2)    │
  └──────────────────────┘           └──────────────────────┘
  
  Classic OTCA trap: "Track active WebSocket connections"
  → UpDownCounter (not Counter!) — connections open AND close
Q7
What does the MeterProvider do in the OTel metrics pipeline?
Show Answer
Answer
  MeterProvider (global config hub)
  ├── Creates Meters ("anihpj-api", "auth-service")
  │   └── Creates Instruments (Counter, Histogram, etc.)
  ├── Holds MetricReaders (collection schedule)
  │   └── PeriodicExportingMetricReader (every 60s)
  └── Holds Views (filter/rename/change aggregation)
Explanation

MeterProvider : Metrics :: TracerProvider : Traces. Create once at startup. The hierarchy is: MeterProvider → Meter → Instrument. The OTCA exam expects you to know that MeterProvider holds the export configuration while Meter creates the instruments your code uses.

Q8
How do histogram buckets affect percentile accuracy?
Show Answer
Answer
  BAD BUCKETS [0.1, 0.5, 1, 5]:       GOOD BUCKETS:
  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ All latencies fall in    │        │ [0.01,0.025,0.05,0.1,0.25,  │
  │ 0-100ms bucket.          │        │  0.5,0.75,1,2.5,5,10]       │
  │ p99 = "0-100ms"          │        │ SLO at 500ms → buckets on    │
  │ → USELESS estimate!      │        │ BOTH sides → precise p99!    │
  └──────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Percentiles are ESTIMATED from bucket boundaries. If your SLO is "p99 < 500ms" but all buckets are below 100ms, you can only say "p99 > 100ms" — useless. Place buckets around your SLO threshold on both sides for accurate estimation.

Q9
Name the 6 OTel metric instrument types.
Show Answer
Answer
#InstrumentSync/AsyncDirectionUse Case
1CounterSync↑ onlyTotal requests, errors
2UpDownCounterSync↕ up/downActive connections
3HistogramSyncDistributionRequest latency
4ObservableCounterAsync↑ onlyKafka msgs consumed
5ObservableUpDownCounterAsync↕ up/downQueue depth
6ObservableGaugeAsyncPoint valueCPU%, pool size
Explanation

Memorize all 6. First 3 = sync (you call OTel at event time). Last 3 = async (OTel polls your callback on a timer). The exam will ask "which instrument for X scenario?" — practice matching.

Q10
In the anihpj metrics setup, which instrument would you use for "number of active Celery workers"?
Show Answer
Answer
# ObservableUpDownCounter — OTel polls Celery for worker count
def get_celery_worker_count(options):
    inspector = current_app.control.inspect()
    stats = inspector.stats() or {}
    return [Observation(len(stats), {"queue": "default"})]

meter.create_observable_up_down_counter(
    "celery.workers.active",
    callbacks=[get_celery_worker_count]  # ← Polled every 60s
)

# NOT Counter.add() — workers start/stop OUTSIDE your code!
Explanation

The key insight: you can't call .add(1) every time a worker starts because workers start/stop OUTSIDE your request-handling code. You need OTel to POLL the current count. This is exactly what Observable* instruments do. The OTCA exam will test your ability to choose sync vs async based on whether the value is event-driven or independently existing.

⚠️ Common Mistakes in Metrics

  • Counter.add(-1): Not allowed — counters are monotonic only
  • High cardinality labels: Using user.id as a label will blow up Prometheus
  • Wrong bucket sizes: Buckets [1, 5, 10] for sub-second HTTP latency gives useless percentiles
  • Histogram for everything: Don't use histograms for values that don't need distribution (use Counter or Gauge instead)
  • Forgetting to set MeterProvider: Must call metrics.set_meter_provider() globally

Chapter 13: Implementing Metrics for the anihpj Platform 🟡 Intermediate

Now that you understand the 6 metric instruments, let's apply them to the anihpj job board platform. This chapter covers the three metric frameworks — RED (services), USE (infrastructure), and Business (user outcomes) — plus custom metrics, histogram configuration, cardinality management, and a complete Grafana dashboard build.

🎯 OTCA Context: The exam tests your ability to CHOOSE the right metric for a scenario. "You need to track job creation rate by plan type — which instrument?" = Counter with plan attribute.

13.1 RED Metrics: Rate, Errors, Duration (The Golden Signals)

The RED method (coined by Tom Wilkie) is the minimum viable metric set for EVERY service. If you only instrument three things, make it these:

RED Metrics — The Three Golden Signals for Every Service
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              🔴 RED METRICS FOR anihpj-api                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌───────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────┐    │
  │  │    R — RATE       │  │    E — ERRORS     │  │  D — DURATION     │    │
  │  │    "How many?"    │  │  "How many fail?" │  │  "How fast/slow?" │    │
  │  │                   │  │                   │  │                   │    │
  │  │  Counter          │  │  Counter          │  │  Histogram        │    │
  │  │  http_requests    │  │  http_errors      │  │  http_request     │    │
  │  │  _total           │  │  _total           │  │  _duration_seconds│    │
  │  │                   │  │                   │  │                   │    │
  │  │  Labels:          │  │  Labels:          │  │  Labels:          │    │
  │  │  method, route,   │  │  method, route,   │  │  method, route,   │    │
  │  │  status_code      │  │  error_type       │  │  status_code      │    │
  │  │                   │  │                   │  │                   │    │
  │  │  PromQL:          │  │  PromQL:          │  │  PromQL:          │    │
  │  │  rate(http_req-   │  │  rate(http_errors │  │  histogram_quant- │    │
  │  │  uests_total      │  │  _total[5m])      │  │  ile(0.95, rate(  │    │
  │  │  [5m])            │  │                   │  │  http_request_    │    │
  │  │                   │  │  Error Budget:    │  │  duration_seconds │    │
  │  │  = 42 req/s       │  │  errors / total   │  │  _bucket[5m]))    │    │
  │  │                   │  │  = 0.1%           │  │  = 235ms          │    │
  │  └───────────────────┘  └───────────────────┘  └───────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📈 Rate — Counter

http_requests_total{method="POST", route="/api/jobs/", status="201"}
Split by method + route + status. Answers: "Is traffic normal? Spiking? Dropping?"

❌ Errors — Counter

http_errors_total{method="POST", error_type="timeout"}
Error ratio = error rate / total rate. SLO: error ratio < 1%.

RED Metrics — Complete Exam Reference
SignalInstrumentKey AttributesPromQLDashboard Widget
RateCountermethod, route, status_coderate(http_requests_total[5m])Time Series (line chart)
ErrorsCountermethod, route, error_typerate(http_errors_total[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m])Stat Panel (big number)
DurationHistogrammethod, route, status_codehistogram_quantile(0.95, rate(http_request_duration_bucket[5m]))Heatmap or Time Series

13.1a Rate — Requests per Second

RED — Rate Implementation
# RED: Rate — Count every HTTP request
http_requests = meter.create_counter(
    "http.server.requests.total",
    description="Total HTTP requests received",
    unit="1"
)

# In Django middleware:
class REDMetricsMiddleware:
    def __call__(self, request):
        response = self.get_response(request)
        http_requests.add(1, {
            "http.method": request.method,
            "http.route": request.path,
            "http.status_code": str(response.status_code)
        })
        return response

13.1b Errors — Failed Requests

RED — Error Counter
# RED: Errors — Count failed requests
http_errors = meter.create_counter(
    "http.server.errors.total",
    description="Total HTTP request errors",
    unit="1"
)

# In Django middleware (extend previous):
if response.status_code >= 500:
    http_errors.add(1, {
        "http.method": request.method,
        "http.route": request.path,
        "error_type": "server_error"
    })
elif response.status_code >= 400:
    http_errors.add(1, {
        "http.method": request.method,
        "http.route": request.path,
        "error_type": "client_error"
    })

13.1c Duration — Latency Distribution

RED — Duration Histogram
# RED: Duration — Record latency as histogram
request_duration = meter.create_histogram(
    "http.server.request.duration",
    description="HTTP request duration in seconds",
    unit="s"
)

# In Django middleware (track duration):
import time

class REDMetricsMiddleware:
    def __call__(self, request):
        start = time.time()
        response = self.get_response(request)
        duration = time.time() - start
        
        request_duration.record(duration, {
            "http.method": request.method,
            "http.route": request.path,
            "http.status_code": str(response.status_code)
        })
        
        http_requests.add(1, { ... })
        return response
💡 PromQL for SLO Dashboard:
• Rate: rate(http_server_requests_total[5m])
• Error Ratio: rate(http_server_errors_total[5m]) / rate(http_server_requests_total[5m])
• P95 Latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(http_server_request_duration_bucket[5m]))

Custom Metrics: Cache, Upload, Auth & Notifications
# === CACHE EFFICIENCY (ObservableGauge) ===
cache_hits = meter.create_counter("cache.hits.total")
cache_misses = meter.create_counter("cache.misses.total")
def get_cache_hit_ratio(options):
    total = hits + misses
    return [Observation(hits / total if total > 0 else 0, {})]
meter.create_observable_gauge("cache.hit_ratio", callbacks=[get_cache_hit_ratio])

# === FILE UPLOAD METRICS ===
upload_size = meter.create_histogram("upload.size_bytes", unit="By")
upload_errors = meter.create_counter("upload.errors.total")

# === AUTH METRICS ===
login_attempts = meter.create_counter("auth.login.attempts")
login_failures = meter.create_counter("auth.login.failures")
token_refreshes = meter.create_counter("auth.token.refresh")

# === NOTIFICATION METRICS ===
emails_sent = meter.create_counter("notifications.emails.sent")
emails_failed = meter.create_counter("notifications.emails.failed")
push_notifications = meter.create_counter("notifications.push.sent")
💡 Auto-instrumentation gives you RED metrics for FREE. Custom metrics are for what auto-instrumentation CAN'T capture: business logic, cache hit rates, upload sizes, search results count, etc.

13.5 Histogram Bucket Configuration

Good Buckets vs Bad Buckets — The Difference is Accuracy
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              HISTOGRAM BUCKET CONFIGURATION                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BAD BUCKETS [0.1, 0.5, 1, 5]:          GOOD BUCKETS (for 500ms SLO):   │
  │  All values fall in 0-100ms bucket.       [0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1,      │
  │  p99 = "between 0 and 100ms"             0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 2.5,       │
  │  → USELESS!                              5, 10]                           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  0      100    500   1000   5000         0  50 100 250 500  1000  2500   │
  │  ├───────┼──────┼──────┼──────┤         ├──┼───┼───┼───┼────┼─────┼───┤  │
  │  │███████│      │      │      │         │██│███│███│███│ ██ │  █  │   │  │
  │  │ ALL   │      │      │      │         └──┴───┴───┴───┴────┴─────┴───┘  │
  │  │ here! │      │      │      │                                          │
  │  └───────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘         SLO at 500ms: buckets on BOTH    │
  │                                         sides → accurate p99 estimate!     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  In OTel Python SDK (View):                                              │
  │  from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.view import View, ExplicitBucketHistogram│
  │  provider.add_view(                                                      │
  │      View(                                                               │
  │          instrument_name="http.server.request.duration",                 │
  │          aggregation=ExplicitBucketHistogramAggregation(                 │
  │              boundaries=[0.005,0.01,0.025,0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5,1,2.5,5,10] │
  │          )                                                               │
  │      )                                                                   │
  │  )                                                                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ OTCA Exam: Know that bucket configuration affects percentile accuracy. Too few buckets = inaccurate p99. Default OTel buckets may not match your SLO — always configure them.

13.6 Cardinality Management

Cardinality Explosion — The Silent Killer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              CARDINALITY MANAGEMENT — DOS AND DON'TS                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ✅ DO use bounded labels:               ❌ NEVER use:                    │
  │  • http.method (4 values)               • user.id (millions)             │
  │  • http.status_code class (4 values)    • email (millions)               │
  │  • plan.type (3 values)                 • session.id (UUIDs)             │
  │  • endpoint (bounded list)              • trace.id (16-byte random)      │
  │                                          • request.id (UUID)             │
  │  Cost: 4×4×3 = 48 series                • ip_address (millions)          │
  │  Memory: ~96 KB ✅                                              │
  │                                          Cost: INFINITE series            │
  │  OTel View to DROP high-card labels:    Memory: OOM 💥                    │
  │  provider.add_view(                                                     │
  │      View(                                                               │
  │          instrument_name="*",                                            │
  │          attribute_keys={                                                │
  │              "http.method", "http.route",                                │
  │              "http.status_code"                                          │
  │          }  # ← ONLY these survive                                       │
  │      )                                                                   │
  │  )                                                                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

PromQL Queries for Dashboard Panels
# ROW 1 — RED Metrics
# Request Rate per route
rate(http_server_requests_total{service="anihpj-api"}[5m])

# Error Ratio
rate(http_server_errors_total{service="anihpj-api"}[5m]) 
/ rate(http_server_requests_total{service="anihpj-api"}[5m])

# P95 Latency
histogram_quantile(0.95, 
  rate(http_server_request_duration_bucket{service="anihpj-api"}[5m]))

# ROW 2 — Business Metrics
# Jobs created per hour by plan
sum(rate(jobs_created_total[1h])) by (plan)

# Applications submitted today
sum(increase(applications_total[24h]))

# ROW 3 — USE Metrics
# DB connection pool utilization
(pg_pool_size - pg_pool_available) / pg_pool_size * 100

# Cache hit ratio
rate(cache_hits_total[5m]) / rate(cache_requests_total[5m])

# ROW 4 — SLO Tracking
# Error budget remaining (30-day, 99% SLO)
1 - (sum(increase(http_server_errors_total[30d])) / 86400 / 0.01)

🎯 Dashboard Design Principles
  • RED at TOP — first thing you see when something is wrong

📊 OTCA Exam: Dashboard Structure

The exam may ask about dashboard layout. Remember: RED first (what is broken?), USE second (is infrastructure the cause?), Business third (what is the impact?), SLO fourth (can we still ship features?). Exemplar links connect dashboards to traces for instant root cause analysis.

📝 OTCA Practice Questions — Chapter 13

Q1
What does the RED acronym stand for?
Show Answer
Answer
  R = RATE      → Counter   → "How many requests/sec?"
  E = ERRORS    → Counter   → "How many failures/sec?"
  D = DURATION  → Histogram → "How fast/slow (p50/p95/p99)?"
Explanation

RED is the minimum viable metric set for ANY service. Tom Wilkie coined this at Google. If you only instrument three things, make it Rate (Counter split by method+route), Errors (Counter split by error_type), and Duration (Histogram). Auto-instrumentation gives you these for FREE.

Q2
When should you use USE metrics vs RED metrics?
Show Answer
Answer
  RED = SERVICES (user-facing)        USE = RESOURCES (infrastructure)
  ┌──────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ Rate:    req/s           │       │ Utilization: CPU%, Mem%  │
  │ Errors:  failures/s      │       │ Saturation: run queue    │
  │ Duration: latency dist   │       │ Errors:     disk fails   │
  │                          │       │                          │
  │ For: anihpj API          │       │ For: PostgreSQL, Redis   │
  └──────────────────────────┘       └──────────────────────────┘
  Complementary — use BOTH for complete coverage
Explanation

RED tells you "is my API healthy?" USE tells you "is my database healthy?" The OTCA exam will ask you to choose: API latency trend → RED. Database connection pool saturation → USE. They are complementary, not alternatives.

Q3
What instrument would you use for "active WebSocket connections" in anihpj?
Show Answer
Answer
ws_connections = meter.create_up_down_counter(
    "ws.connections.active",
    description="Active WebSocket connections"
)
ws_connections.add(1)   # User connects
ws_connections.add(-1)  # User disconnects
# NOT Counter — Counter.add(-1) = ERROR!
Explanation

Connections go UP (open) and DOWN (close). Counter is monotonic only — it can't decrease. UpDownCounter is the correct choice. Classic OTCA trap: "tracking active connections" → don't pick Counter!

Q4
How do you calculate error ratio in PromQL?
Show Answer
Answer
# Error ratio = errors / total requests
rate(http_server_errors_total{service="anihpj"}[5m])
/ 
rate(http_server_requests_total{service="anihpj"}[5m])

# SLO check: error ratio < 1%?
# If > 1% → alert fires, error budget burning
Explanation

Both counters must use the SAME time window [5m]. Divide errors by total to get the ratio. Multiply by 100 for percentage. This is the foundation of SLO-based alerting — fire when error ratio exceeds the SLO threshold.

Q5
What happens if your histogram buckets don't surround your SLO threshold?
Show Answer
Answer
  SLO: p99 < 500ms
  
  BAD [0.1, 0.5, 1, 5]:               GOOD [..., 0.5, 0.75, 1, ...]:
  ┌──────────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ p99 = "between 100ms     │         │ p99 = ~480ms (precise!) │
  │        and 500ms"         │         │ 500ms has buckets on    │
  │ → 400ms uncertainty!     │         │ BOTH sides              │
  └──────────────────────────┘         └──────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Histogram percentiles are ESTIMATES based on bucket boundaries. The accuracy depends on having buckets close to your SLO on both sides. Without this, you can't prove you're meeting your SLO — and the OTCA exam will test this.

Q6
Name three business metrics you'd track for anihpj.
Show Answer
Answer
  Metric                    Instrument      Labels        Business Q?
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  jobs.created.total        Counter         plan, category  Are we growing?
  applications.submitted    Counter         job_id, plan    Conversion rate?
  users.registered.total    Counter         source, plan    User growth?
  revenue.estimated         ObservableGauge plan            Revenue trend?
Explanation

Business metrics connect engineering to outcomes. "Deploy v2.3 → jobs created +15% per hour → revenue +12%." Without business metrics, you know IF the system works but not WHAT users are doing. OTCA exam: know the difference between technical (RED/USE) and business metrics.

Q7
How do you limit cardinality in OTel Python SDK?
Show Answer
Answer
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.view import View

provider.add_view(View(
    instrument_name="*",           # Apply to ALL instruments
    attribute_keys={               # ONLY these attributes survive
        "http.method",
        "http.route",
        "http.status_code"
    }
))
# All other attributes DROPPED — user.id, session.id, etc.
Explanation

Views are the OTel mechanism to filter, rename, or change aggregation for metrics. Use attribute_keys as a whitelist — only listed attributes survive. This is your defense against high-cardinality labels that could OOM your Prometheus instance.

Q8
What's the difference between a Counter and an UpDownCounter?
Show Answer
Answer
  Counter (monotonic ↑):              UpDownCounter (↕):
  ┌──────────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ counter.add(1)    │           │ ✅ updown.add(1)     │
  │ ✅ counter.add(5)    │           │ ✅ updown.add(-1)    │
  │ ❌ counter.add(-1)   │           │ ✅ updown.add(3)     │
  │ Prometheus: counter  │           │ Prometheus: gauge    │
  └──────────────────────┘           └──────────────────────┘
  
  Counter = "How many TOTAL?"    UpDownCounter = "How many RIGHT NOW?"
Explanation

Counter for cumulative totals (requests served, errors encountered). UpDownCounter for current state (active connections, in-flight requests). The Prometheus mapping differs: Counter → counter (with _total), UpDownCounter → gauge. OTCA exam tests this distinction frequently.

Q9
What does auto-instrumentation give you for metrics?
Show Answer
Answer
  AUTO-INSTRUMENTATION → FREE RED METRICS:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ http.server.requests.total    ← Counter (Rate)           │
  │ http.server.errors.total      ← Counter (Errors)         │
  │ http.server.request.duration  ← Histogram (Duration)     │
  │ db.client.operations.total    ← DB query metrics         │
  │ db.client.operation.duration  ← DB latency metrics       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ZERO code needed! Just pip install + env vars.
Explanation

Django auto-instrumentation creates RED metrics for every HTTP endpoint automatically — no code required. Database instrumentations add query metrics. Custom business metrics (jobs_created) still need manual instrumentation. Auto covers 80%; manual covers the business-specific 20%.

Q10
What is the recommended number of histogram buckets for HTTP latency?
Show Answer
Answer
# Good bucket config for HTTP latency (SLO: p99 < 500ms)
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.view import ExplicitBucketHistogramAggregation

buckets = [0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 
           0.5, 0.75, 1, 2.5, 5, 10]
# ↑ 12 buckets, exponentially spaced, SLO at 500ms
#   has buckets on both sides for accurate p99
Explanation

10-15 buckets, exponentially spaced (multiply by ~2-3 each step). Include buckets around your SLO threshold. Include long tail (5s, 10s) to catch outliers. Too few = inaccurate; too many = memory waste. OTCA exam expects you to know the tradeoff.

⚠️ Common Mistakes in Metrics Implementation

  • Using Counter for active connections: Can't decrement — use UpDownCounter
  • user.id as a label: Infinite cardinality = Prometheus OOM
  • Not configuring histogram buckets: Default buckets may not match your SLO
  • RED only, no business metrics: Tech team knows system is healthy, business team doesn't know what users are doing
  • Not setting error_type label: "How many errors?" without "what kind?" limits debugging

Chapter 14: Prometheus Integration and Metric Backends 🟡 Intermediate

You've created metrics — now where do they go? This chapter covers the journey from OTel metrics to Prometheus (the industry standard for metric storage), through Grafana (visualization), and explores alternative backends. You'll learn the Pull vs Push model, the Prometheus exporter, exemplars, and build a complete dashboard for the anihpj platform.

🎯 OTCA Exam: Know the Prometheus pull model vs OTel push model, how the Collector bridges them, and the role of exemplars in connecting metrics to traces.

14.1 Prometheus as a Metrics Backend (Pull Model)

Pull (Prometheus) vs Push (OTel) — Bridging the Gap
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              PULL vs PUSH — TWO DIFFERENT PARADIGMS                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  PROMETHEUS PULL MODEL:                   OTEL PUSH MODEL:                 │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐                  ┌────────────────────┐           │
  │  │     Prometheus     │                  │   anihpj-api       │           │
  │  │  (scrapes targets) │                  │   (OTel SDK)       │           │
  │  │         │          │                  │        │           │           │
  │  │    ┌────┴────┐     │                  │   PUSH ▼           │           │
  │  │    ▼         ▼     │                  │  ┌──────────┐      │           │
  │  │ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ │                  │  │  OTel    │      │           │
  │  │ │anihpj│ │ Post-│ │                  │  │Collector │      │           │
  │  │ │:8000 │ │greSQL│ │                  │  │ :4317    │      │           │
  │  │ │/metr │ │:9187 │ │                  │  └────┬─────┘      │           │
  │  │ └──────┘ └──────┘ │                  │       │ PUSH       │           │
  │  └────────────────────┘                  │       ▼            │           │
  │                                          │  ┌──────────┐      │           │
  │  Pros:                                   │  │Prometheus│      │           │
  │  • No push infrastructure needed         │  │/Jaeger   │      │           │
  │  • Service discovery built-in           │  └──────────┘      │           │
  │  • Targets can be ephemeral              │                    │           │
  │                                          │  Pros:             │           │
  │  Cons:                                   │  • Works behind    │           │
  │  • Firewalls block scrapes               │    firewalls       │           │
  │  • Need /metrics endpoint per target     │  • No /metrics     │           │
  │                                          │    endpoint needed │           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔌 How OTel Bridges Pull/Push

OTel Collector exposes a /metrics endpoint on port 9464. Prometheus scrapes it. Behind the scenes, OTel SDK PUSHES to the Collector, Collector buffers, Prometheus PULLS.

📊 Prometheus TSDB

Prometheus stores metrics in a custom Time Series Database (TSDB). 2-hour blocks, compressed (snappy), append-only. Each time series ~1-3KB in memory.

14.2 Configuring OTel Collector for Prometheus

OTel Collector → Prometheus — Two Configuration Patterns
Option A: Prometheus Scrapes Collector (Pull Bridge)
# otel-collector-config.yaml
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

exporters:
  prometheus:
    endpoint: 0.0.0.0:9464  # Prometheus scrapes THIS
    namespace: anihpj

service:
  pipelines:
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [prometheus]

---
# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'otel-collector'
    scrape_interval: 30s
    honor_labels: true
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['otel-collector:9464']
Option B: OTel Pushes to Prometheus (Remote Write)
exporters:
  prometheusremotewrite:
    endpoint: "http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/write"
    tls:
      insecure: true

service:
  pipelines:
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [prometheusremotewrite]
✅ Option A (Pull)

• Prometheus discovers & scrapes Collector
• Standard Prometheus setup
• Better for existing Prometheus shops
• Port 9464 is OTel convention

✅ Option B (Push/Remote Write)

• Collector actively pushes to Prometheus
• Use for firewalled environments
• Requires Prometheus remote write enabled
• Newer approach, gaining adoption

Kubernetes Deployment — OTel Collector + Prometheus on K8s

  │              KUBERNETES DEPLOYMENT ARCHITECTURE                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │                        KUBERNETES CLUSTER                         │   │
  │  │                                                                  │   │

K8s ServiceMonitor for Prometheus Operator
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: otel-collector
  namespace: observability
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: otel-collector
  endpoints:
  - port: metrics
    interval: 30s
    honorLabels: true

14.3 Prometheus Exporter vs OTLP Metric Export

AspectPrometheus Exporter (Pull)OTLP Export (Push)
ProtocolPrometheus exposition format (text)OTLP (Protobuf over gRPC/HTTP)
DirectionPrometheus pulls from CollectorCollector pushes to backend
Firewall Friendly❌ Needs open inbound port✅ Outbound only
Ephemeral Workloads❌ Short-lived targets may be missed✅ Push before termination
Setup Complexity✅ Simple (standard Prometheus)Medium (needs OTLP-native backend)
Exemplars✅ Supported✅ Supported (OTLP 1.0+)
Best ForExisting Prometheus shopsGreenfield OTel-native setups
💡 OTCA Recommendation: Use OTLP throughout your pipeline. Only use the Prometheus exporter at the FINAL hop if Prometheus doesn't support OTLP natively (newer versions do).

Key PromQL Queries for anihpj Grafana Panels
# Panel 1: Request Rate (Time Series)
sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{service="anihpj-api"}[5m])) by (http_route)

# Panel 2: Error Rate % (Stat)
sum(rate(http_server_errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(http_server_requests_total[5m])) * 100

# Panel 3: P95 Latency (Time Series with threshold)
histogram_quantile(0.95, 
  sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_bucket[5m])) by (le))

# Panel 4: Latency Heatmap
sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_bucket[5m])) by (le)

# Panel 5: Jobs Created by Plan (Stacked Bar)
sum(rate(jobs_created_total[5m])) by (plan)

# Panel 6: Error Budget Remaining (Gauge)
(1 - sum(increase(http_server_errors_total[30d])) / 
  (sum(increase(http_server_requests_total[30d])) * 0.01)) * 100

14.X SLO Implementation — From OTel Metrics to Business Decisions

Service Level Objectives (SLOs) turn raw OTel metrics into business guarantees. The OTCA exam tests your understanding of the SLI→SLO→Error Budget chain.

The SLI → SLO → Error Budget Chain
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              FROM RAW METRICS TO BUSINESS DECISIONS                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1: OTel generates SLIs (Service Level Indicators)                   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Counter: http_requests_total{status!="500"}   = 99,847            │  │
  │  │ Counter: http_requests_total                   = 100,000           │  │
  │  │ Histogram: http_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket               │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ SLI (Availability) = 99,847 / 100,000 = 99.847%                   │  │
  │  │ SLI (Latency p95)   = histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) = 234ms      │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STEP 2: SRE defines SLOs (Service Level Objectives)                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ SLO: "99.9% of requests succeed AND complete in < 250ms"         │  │
  │  │ Measured over: 30-day rolling window                               │  │
  │  │ Compliance: Must meet BOTH availability AND latency targets        │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  STEP 3: Error Budget determines release velocity                         │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Allowed errors: 100% - 99.9% = 0.1% of requests                    │  │
  │  │ Per month: 0.1% × 2,592,000 seconds = 2,592 seconds = 43 minutes  │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Error Budget Remaining:  ████████░░  78% (33 min remaining)       │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ RULE: Budget > 50%  → Ship features freely                        │  │
  │  │       Budget 20-50% → Slow down, focus on reliability              │  │
  │  │       Budget < 20%  → STOP all feature work, fix reliability      │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 OTCA Exam: OTel's Role in SLOs

OTel generates SLIs (the raw metrics). SRE defines SLOs (the targets). OTel does NOT define SLOs — that is a human/business decision. The exam trap: "Does OpenTelemetry define your SLOs?" → NO. OTel provides the telemetry data that SLO calculations are based on, but the SLO targets themselves are defined by your team based on business requirements.

📝 OTCA Practice Questions — Chapter 14

Q1
What is the fundamental difference between Prometheus pull model and OTel push model?
Show Answer
Answer
  PROMETHEUS (PULL):                    OTEL (PUSH):
  ┌──────────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Prometheus scrapes   │            │ App/Collector sends   │
  │ targets on schedule  │            │ data to backend       │
  │ GET :9464/metrics    │            │ gRPC → :4317         │
  │ Targets must be      │            │ Works behind NAT/     │
  │ reachable by Prom    │            │ firewalls             │
  └──────────────────────┘            └──────────────────────┘
  
  BRIDGE: Collector exposes :9464/metrics → Prometheus scrapes it
Explanation

The OTel Collector bridges these two worlds. Apps push OTLP to the Collector (port 4317), and the Collector exposes a /metrics endpoint (port 9464) that Prometheus scrapes. This is the standard production pattern. OTCA exam tests your understanding of how the Collector bridges push and pull.

Q2
What port does OTel Collector expose for Prometheus scraping?
Show Answer
Answer
  Port Map:
  ┌──────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 4317     │ OTLP gRPC (app → Collector)         │
  │ 4318     │ OTLP HTTP (app → Collector)         │
  │ 9464     │ Prometheus /metrics ← ANSWER        │
  │ 16686    │ Jaeger UI                           │
  │ 9090     │ Prometheus UI                       │
  │ 3000     │ Grafana UI                          │
  └──────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Memorize all 6 ports. The OTCA exam will ask about port numbers. 9464 is the OTel convention for Prometheus scraping — this is where the Collector's prometheus exporter listens.

Q3
What is an exemplar in OpenTelemetry metrics?
Show Answer
Answer
  GRAFANA DASHBOARD                     JAEGER TRACE VIEW
  ┌──────────────────────┐             ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Latency P95          │  CLICK      │ Trace: a1b2c3d4...   │
  │      ▄               │  EXEMPLAR   │ ├── POST /api/jobs/  │
  │    ▄██▄              │────────────▶│ │   ├── auth (25ms)  │
  │  ▄█████▄             │             │ │   ├── DB INSERT    │
  │ ▄████████▄ ← SPIKE!  │             │ │   │   (2100ms!)    │
  └──────────────────────┘             └──────────────────────┘
  
  Exemplar = trace_id attached to metric data point
  Enabled BY DEFAULT with OTLP export
Explanation

Exemplars bridge metrics and traces. When a histogram records a high value, the current span's trace_id is attached as an exemplar. In Grafana, outlier data points become clickable links to the exact trace. No extra configuration needed — it's automatic with OTLP export.

Q4
Name two alternatives to Prometheus for long-term metric storage.
Show Answer
Answer
  Prometheus → local TSDB (days-weeks retention)
  
  Long-term alternatives:
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │ Grafana Mimir    │ Thanos       │ Cortex (legacy)   │
  │ S3/GCS backed    │ S3/GCS backed│ S3/GCS backed     │
  │ 1B+ active series│ Global query │ Mimir successor   │
  │ Recommended ✅   │ Alternative  │ Migrate to Mimir  │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────┘
Explanation

Prometheus's local TSDB is great for short-term (days to weeks). For months/years, use Mimir or Thanos with S3-compatible object storage — it's ~10x cheaper than SSD. Mimir is the CNCF-recommended successor to Cortex.

Q5
What PromQL function converts a Counter to a per-second rate?
Show Answer
Answer
# rate() — per-second average over time window
rate(http_requests_total{job="anihpj"}[5m])
# → 42.5 (42.5 requests/second averaged over 5 minutes)

# increase() — total change in time window
increase(http_requests_total{job="anihpj"}[1h])
# → 153000 (153,000 requests in the last hour)

# NEVER rate() on a gauge! Gauges use avg_over_time()
Explanation

rate() is for counters (monotonic, always increasing). It calculates the per-second average rate, automatically handling counter resets. increase() gives the total change. For gauges, use avg_over_time(). OTCA exam trap: using rate() on a gauge.

Q6
How do you calculate p95 latency from a histogram in PromQL?
Show Answer
Answer
# p95 latency (95th percentile)
histogram_quantile(0.95, 
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

# p50 (median)
histogram_quantile(0.50, 
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

# p99 (near-worst case)
histogram_quantile(0.99, 
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
Explanation

histogram_quantile() estimates percentiles from histogram bucket counts. The accuracy depends on your bucket configuration. Use _bucket suffix (not _sum or _count). Must wrap in rate() to handle the counter nature of histogram buckets.

Q7
What is the advantage of OTLP push over Prometheus pull?
Show Answer
Answer
  OTLP PUSH advantages:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ Works behind firewalls (outbound connections only)    │
  │ ✅ Ephemeral workloads (push before termination)         │
  │ ✅ Single protocol (OTLP) for traces + metrics + logs    │
  │ ✅ No /metrics endpoint needed per target                │
  │ ✅ Serverless/batch friendly (Lambda, Fargate)           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Push works where pull can't: behind NAT/firewalls, short-lived containers, serverless functions. The OTCA exam will ask about scenarios where push is preferred — ephemeral workloads and firewalled environments are the key answers.

Q8
Which Grafana panel type is best for visualizing latency distribution over time?
Show Answer
Answer
  Grafana Panel Types:
  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Time Series  │ Line chart — request rate over time     │
  │ Stat         │ Big number — current error rate         │
  │ Heatmap      │ Latency distribution ← BEST FOR THIS    │
  │ Gauge        │ Error budget remaining %               │
  │ Table        │ Top 10 slowest endpoints               │
  └──────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Heatmap shows histogram buckets as color intensity over time. It's the best way to visualize latency distribution shifts. Each horizontal band is a bucket, color density = count. Requires histogram metric type with properly configured buckets.

Q9
What does the prometheusremotewrite exporter do?
Show Answer
Answer
exporters:
  prometheusremotewrite:
    endpoint: "http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/write"
    tls:
      insecure: true
    # PUSHES metrics to Prometheus (push model)
    # vs. prometheus exporter which exposes :9464 (pull model)
Explanation

Remote write flips the model — the Collector actively pushes to Prometheus instead of waiting for Prometheus to scrape. Use when: Prometheus can't reach the Collector (firewall), you want push-based architecture, or you're using Grafana Cloud/Mimir which accept remote write.

Q10
How do you enable exemplars in OTel Python SDK?
Show Answer
Answer
# Exemplars are ENABLED BY DEFAULT with OTLP export
# No extra code needed!

# What happens automatically:
histogram.record(2.5)  
# ↑ Current span's trace_id is attached as exemplar
# Prometheus stores: metric_point + exemplar{trace_id="4bf92f..."}

# Requirement: Use OTLP exporter (not Prometheus exporter)
# Exemplars don't work with Prometheus pull exporter
Explanation

Exemplars require OTLP export (gRPC or HTTP). They do NOT work with the Prometheus exporter (pull model) because the Prometheus exposition format doesn't carry exemplar data. OTCA exam: "How to enable exemplars?" → "They're on by default with OTLP."

⚠️ Common Mistakes — Prometheus + Grafana

  • Scraping the wrong port: Prometheus port is 9090, not 9464 (that's the Collector metrics endpoint)
  • Forgetting honor_labels: Without honor_labels: true, Prometheus may override OTel labels
  • Using increase() for gauges: increase() only works for counters; use avg_over_time() for gauges
  • Exemplars not showing: Must use OTLP export (not Prometheus exporter) for exemplars to flow through
  • Heatmap without histogram buckets: Heatmap panel requires histogram metric type with buckets
