🔑 Exam Must-Know: Metric Pipeline

MeterProvider → Meter → Instrument → MetricReader (60s default) → Aggregation (Sum/ExplicitBuckets/LastValue) → Exporter (OTLP/Prometheus) → Backend

🔑 Exam Must-Know: PromQL Basics

rate() for counters, histogram_quantile() for histograms, increase() for total change. Never rate() on a gauge!

⚠️ Top 5 Part 3 Exam Traps

  • Counter.add(-1): Not allowed — counters are monotonic
  • user.id as metric label: Infinite cardinality = OOM
  • Prometheus scrape interval vs export interval: Different things — scrape is Prometheus pulling, export is OTel pushing to Collector
  • Exemplars only work with OTLP: Not available with Prometheus exporter (pull model)
  • Histogram buckets affect accuracy: Too few buckets around SLO = useless p99 estimates

📝 Part 3 Consolidation Questions (10 Q&A)

Q1: Which metric instrument would you use for "total jobs created since application start"?

Answer: Counter. Monotonic, only increases. Never use UpDownCounter for totals.

Q2: What port does Prometheus scrape the OTel Collector on?

Answer: 9464 (by OTel convention). OTLP gRPC is 4317, OTLP HTTP is 4318.

Q3: How do exemplars connect metrics to traces?

Answer: Each histogram measurement attaches the current span's trace_id. Prometheus stores it. Grafana shows a clickable link on outlier data points.

Q4: What's the difference between RED and USE metrics?

Answer: RED = services (Rate, Errors, Duration). USE = resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors). Complementary — RED for APIs, USE for infrastructure.

Q5: Why should you NEVER use user.id as a metric attribute?

Answer: Unbounded cardinality. 1 million users = 1 million time series × 2KB = 2GB RAM for ONE metric. Prometheus will OOM.

Q6: What is the default MetricReader export interval?

Answer: 60 seconds (60,000ms) for PeriodicExportingMetricReader.

Q7: Name two alternatives to Prometheus for long-term metric storage.

Answer: Grafana Mimir (horizontally scalable, S3-backed) and Thanos (global query view, downsampling).

Q8: What PromQL function would you use to calculate per-second request rate?

Answer: rate(). rate(http_requests_total[5m]) gives the per-second average over 5 minutes.

Q9: What happens if your histogram buckets are all below your actual latency?

Answer: All values fall in the +Inf bucket. You can only say "p99 > largest bucket" — useless for SLO tracking. Must include buckets around your SLO threshold.

Q10: Which Grafana panel type is best for latency distribution?

Answer: Heatmap panel. Shows histogram buckets as color intensity over time, revealing latency distribution shifts.

Chapter 15: OpenTelemetry Logs and Events 🔴 Advanced

Logs are the third telemetry signal in OpenTelemetry — the newest (stable 2024) and the one that completes the observability triangle. OTel doesn't replace your existing logger (Python logging, Java log4j, Node.js winston). Instead, it bridges them — automatically injecting trace context into every log line and sending logs through the same OTLP pipeline as traces and metrics. This chapter covers the Logs Bridge API, data model, structured logging, and the game-changing power of log-trace correlation for the anihpj platform.

🎯 OTCA Exam D4 (10%): Know the Logs Bridge API concept (NOT a replacement), the LogRecord fields, severity mapping, and how trace_id injection enables correlation. The exam focuses on the WHY — "why bridge instead of replace?"
Three-Signal Correlation — One trace_id Rules Them All

  │  │ POST /api/jobs/      │  │ Filter: {trace_id=    │  │ Exemplar on  │  │
  │  │ ├── auth (25ms)      │  │   "4bf92..."}         │  │ latency spike│  │
  │  │ ├── DB INSERT (180ms)│  │                      │  │              │  │
  │  │ │   ERROR ❌         │  │ 14:30:00 INFO Job    │  │ Click → opens │  │
  │  │ └── SET cache (5ms)  │  │ created, user_id=42   │  │ the SAME     │  │
  │  │                      │  │ 14:30:00 WARN DB     │  │ trace!       │  │
  │  │ Click error span →   │  │ pool at 95%          │  │              │  │
  │  │ copy trace_id        │  │ 14:30:01 ERR         │  │ ▁▂▃▄▅█▅▄▃▂  │  │
  │  │                      │  │ IntegrityError!      │  │      ▲       │  │
  │  └──────────┬───────────┘  └──────────┬───────────┘  └──────┬───────┘  │
  │             │                         │                      │          │
  │             └─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┘          │
  │                         ALL share the SAME trace_id!                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

15.1 What are OTel Logs?

Logs are immutable, timestamped records of discrete events. Unlike traces (one request's journey) or metrics (aggregated numbers), logs capture individual moments: "User 42 created JobPost #99", "DB connection timeout after 30s", "Cache miss for key user:42".

✅ What OTel Logs ARE

• A bridge to your EXISTING logging
• Automatic trace_id + span_id injection
• Unified OTLP pipeline for all 3 signals
• Structured, machine-parseable records
• Correlated: click log → see trace → see metrics

❌ What OTel Logs are NOT

• NOT a replacement for Python logging/log4j
• NOT a log storage backend (that's Loki/ES)
• NOT a replacement for existing log aggregation
• NOT auto-instrumented (you still write log lines)
• NOT a replacement for structured logging tools

15.2 The Logs Bridge API — Bridging, Not Replacing

The core principle: DO NOT replace your logger. BRIDGE it. OTel provides a Logs Bridge API that connects your existing logging framework to the OTel ecosystem. Your code doesn't change — you still call logger.info() — but OTel automatically enriches every log with trace context and routes it through OTLP.

🐍 Python

LoggingInstrumentor().instrument()
Bridges logging.getLogger()
Auto-injects trace_id + span_id

☕ Java

log4j2 + logback appenders
opentelemetry-log4j-context-data
MDC auto-populated with trace context

🟨 JavaScript/Node.js

winston + pino transports
@opentelemetry/winston-transport
trace_id injected into log metadata

Python Logging Bridge — Complete Setup for anihpj
# settings.py or app.py — Bridge Python logging to OTel
import logging
from opentelemetry._logs import set_logger_provider
from opentelemetry.sdk._logs import LoggerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk._logs.export import BatchLogRecordProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.grpc._log_exporter import OTLPLogExporter
from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource

# 1. Create LoggerProvider (like TracerProvider/MeterProvider)
resource = Resource.create({"service.name": "anihpj-api"})
logger_provider = LoggerProvider(resource=resource)
set_logger_provider(logger_provider)

# 2. Configure OTLP log exporter (same Collector endpoint!)
log_exporter = OTLPLogExporter(
    endpoint="http://collector:4317",
    insecure=True
)
logger_provider.add_log_record_processor(
    BatchLogRecordProcessor(log_exporter)
)

# 3. Bridge Python's standard logging to OTel
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.logging import LoggingInstrumentor
LoggingInstrumentor().instrument(set_logging_format=True)

# 4. Now EVERY logging.getLogger() call is OTel-aware!
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.info("User created job", extra={
    "user_id": 42, "job_id": 99, "plan": "premium"
})
# ↑ This log now has trace_id + span_id automatically injected!

15.4 Structured vs Unstructured Logging

Unstructured vs Structured — The Queryability Difference
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              UNSTRUCTURED (BAD) vs STRUCTURED (GOOD)                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  UNSTRUCTURED:                           STRUCTURED (JSON):               │
  │  "User 42 created job 99 titled          {"timestamp":"2026-06-06T14:30", │
  │   Software Engineer at 14:30"             "severity":"INFO",              │
  │                                           "body":"Job created",           │
  │  ❌ Needs regex to parse                  "trace_id":"4bf92f35...",       │
  │  ❌ Breaks when message format changes    "span_id":"00f067aa...",        │
  │  ❌ Can't query: "user_id=42"              "attributes":{                 │
  │  ❌ Can't aggregate by plan                 "user_id":42,                 │
  │                                             "job_id":99,                 │
  │  grep "User 42" → maybe finds it           "plan":"premium",             │
  │  (if you guess the exact text)              "job_title":"Software Eng"}} │
  │                                                                          │
  │                                             ✅ Machine-parseable          │
  │                                             ✅ Query: {user_id=42}        │
  │                                             ✅ Aggregate: count by plan   │
  │                                             ✅ Format changes don't break │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ anihpj Production Rule: ALL logs MUST be structured JSON in production. The cost of unstructured logging isn't storage — it's the engineer's TIME spent regex-parsing log files at 3 AM.

15.5 Log Correlation — Connecting Logs to Traces

The killer feature: every log line automatically gets the current span's trace_id and span_id. This means you can jump from a trace in Jaeger to the exact log lines in Loki, or from a log error to the full trace that caused it.

Correlation Workflow — 30-Second Root Cause
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              LOG-TRACE CORRELATION WORKFLOW                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BEFORE OTel (30 minutes):               AFTER OTel (30 seconds):         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │ 1. See error in app      │           │ 1. See error span in     │     │
  │  │ 2. Open 10 log files     │           │    Jaeger (RED)          │     │
  │  │ 3. grep "User 42"        │           │ 2. Copy trace_id         │     │
  │  │ 4. grep "14:30"          │           │ 3. Paste in Loki:        │     │
  │  │ 5. Find log → maybe?     │           │    {trace_id="4bf9..."}  │     │
  │  │ 6. What caused it? 🤷    │           │ 4. See ALL logs for that │     │
  │  └──────────────────────────┘           │    request instantly     │     │
  │                                         │ 5. "DB pool exhausted"  │     │
  │  RESULT: Slow, error-prone              │    → root cause found!  │     │
  │                                         └──────────────────────────┘     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

15.6 Python Logging Integration — Production Setup

anihpj Production Logging — Complete Django Setup
# anihpj/settings.py — Production logging with OTel bridge

LOGGING = {
    "version": 1,
    "disable_existing_loggers": False,
    "formatters": {
        "json": {
            "()": "pythonjsonlogger.jsonlogger.JsonFormatter",
            "format": "%(timestamp)s %(level)s %(name)s %(message)s"
        }
    },
    "handlers": {
        "console": {
            "class": "logging.StreamHandler",
            "formatter": "json",
            "stream": "ext://sys.stdout"
        }
    },
    "root": {
        "handlers": ["console"],
        "level": "INFO"  # DEBUG logs NOT sent to production
    },
    "loggers": {
        "django": {"level": "WARNING"},  # Reduce Django noise
        "anihpj": {"level": "INFO"},      # Our app = INFO
        "celery": {"level": "INFO"}
    }
}

# In wsgi.py or AppConfig.ready():
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.logging import LoggingInstrumentor
LoggingInstrumentor().instrument(set_logging_format=True)

# Now use in views:
import logging
logger = logging.getLogger("anihpj.views")

def create_job(request):
    logger.info("Creating job", extra={
        "user_id": request.user.id,
        "plan": request.user.plan
    })
📝 Production Tips

• Set root logger to INFO (not DEBUG)
• Use JSON formatter always
• Add business context as attributes
• Batch export logs (BatchLogRecordProcessor)
• Same OTLP endpoint as traces

🔗 The OTel Advantage

• Zero code changes to existing logs
• trace_id auto-injected into every line
• Logs travel same OTLP pipeline as traces
• One Collector: traces + metrics + logs
• Query Loki with same trace_id from Jaeger

⚠️ Two Configuration Approaches:
Auto-instrument (recommended): LoggingInstrumentor().instrument() — all loggers bridged automatically.
Manual handler: logger.addHandler(OTelLoggingHandler()) — only specific loggers bridged. Use when you need fine-grained control.

⚠️ Caveat: Libraries that do their own formatting (uvicorn, gunicorn) need specific handlers. The auto-bridge only intercepts standard logging.getLogger() calls — not custom formatters. For uvicorn, configure --log-config with OTel handler; for gunicorn, use --logger-class.

15.X Logs-Traces-Metrics Correlation — The Holy Grail of Observability

The true power of OTel is not in each signal individually — it is in their correlation. When logs, traces, and metrics share the same trace_id, debugging transforms from guesswork into a deterministic path.

The Three-Signal Correlation — A Complete Debugging Story
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          THE CORRELATION FLOW — METRICS → TRACES → LOGS                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  📊 METRICS: "Error rate spiked to 8.2% at 14:30"                        │
  │       │                                                                  │
  │       │ Exemplar link (auto-generated by OTel)                           │
  │       ▼                                                                  │
  │  🔍 TRACES: "Trace 4bf92f... shows INSERT timeout at 30s"                │
  │       │                                                                  │
  │       │ Copy trace_id                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                  │
  │  📝 LOGS: {trace_id="4bf92f..."} → "Connection pool exhausted,           │
  │            all 20 connections held by SELECT FOR UPDATE since 14:28"     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🎯 ROOT CAUSE FOUND: Long-running transaction held table lock           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  HOW OTel ENABLES THIS:                                                  │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ 1. Metrics have EXEMPLARS → link to specific traces               │  │
  │  │ 2. Traces carry trace_id → unique identifier across services       │  │
  │  │ 3. Logs auto-injected with trace_id → filterable in Loki           │  │
  │  │ 4. Jaeger UI has "Logs" tab → queries Loki by trace_id            │  │
  │  │ 5. Grafana can show metrics + traces + logs in one dashboard       │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔗 How Correlation Works
  • OTel SDK auto-injects trace_id into every log line
  • Metrics carry exemplars — links to specific traces
  • Loki stores logs indexed by trace_id for instant lookup
  • Grafana can jump: dashboard → trace → logs in 3 clicks
⚠️ Without Correlation
  • Metrics show "error rate 8%" — but which requests?
  • Traces show slow requests — but what do the logs say?
  • Logs show errors — but which trace do they belong to?
  • Engineer jumps between 3 tools manually — 30+ minutes

📝 OTCA Practice Questions — Chapter 15

Q1
Does OpenTelemetry replace my existing logging library (Python logging, log4j)?
Show Answer
Answer
  ❌ OTel does NOT replace your logger
  ✅ OTel BRIDGES your existing logger
  
  Your code:                  OTel adds:
  logger.info("Job created")  → trace_id=4bf92f...
                              → span_id=00f067aa...
                              → routed through OTLP
Explanation

The Logs Bridge API connects your existing logger to OTel's context propagation. You keep using logger.info() — OTel automatically enriches every log with trace context and routes it through OTLP. This is a fundamental OTCA concept: bridge, don't replace.

Q2
What two fields are automatically injected into every log line by OTel?
Show Answer
Answer
  LogRecord auto-injected fields:
  ┌─────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ trace_id    │ 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736     │
  │ span_id     │ 00f067aa0ba902b7                     │
  └─────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Injected by LoggingInstrumentor automatically
  If no active span → fields are empty (all zeros)
Explanation

These come from the currently active span context. At log emission time, OTel checks if a span is active. If yes, its trace_id and span_id are added to the LogRecord. This is what enables log-trace correlation.

Q3
What is the difference between Timestamp and ObservedTimestamp in a LogRecord?
Show Answer
Answer
  LogRecord timeline:
  ┌────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Timestamp          │ When the event ACTUALLY occurred │
  │                    │ Set by your code (logger.info()) │
  │                    │ Nanosecond precision             │
  ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ ObservedTimestamp  │ When OTel COLLECTED the log     │
  │                    │ May differ due to batching      │
  │                    │ Set by OTel SDK                  │
  └────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

If you call logger.info() at 14:30:00.000 but BatchLogRecordProcessor exports the batch at 14:30:05.000, Timestamp = 14:30:00.000 and ObservedTimestamp = 14:30:05.000. The OTCA exam may test that these two timestamps serve different purposes.

Q4
Why is structured logging (JSON) preferred over unstructured (plain text)?
Show Answer
Answer
  UNSTRUCTURED (❌):                      STRUCTURED / JSON (✅):
  "User 42 created job 99"               {"timestamp":"...","severity":"INFO",
                                           "body":"Job created",
  • Needs regex: r'User (\d+) created     "trace_id":"4bf92f...",
    job (\d+)'                            "attributes":{"user_id":42,
  • Breaks when message changes                      "job_id":99,
  • Can't query: {user_id=42}                        "plan":"premium"}}
  • Can't aggregate by plan               
                                          • Machine-parseable ✅
                                          • Query in Loki: {user_id=42} ✅
                                          • Count by plan type ✅
Explanation

Structured logs are queryable and aggregatable. In Loki, you can filter {user_id=42} or count logs by plan type. Unstructured logs require regex that breaks when message formats change. OTCA exam: always prefer structured JSON logging in production.

Q5
What Python package bridges the standard logging module to OTel?
Show Answer
Answer
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.logging import LoggingInstrumentor

# Bridge ALL Python logging to OTel
LoggingInstrumentor().instrument(set_logging_format=True)

# Now every logging.getLogger() call is OTel-aware
import logging
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.info("User created job", extra={"user_id": 42})
# ↑ Automatically gets trace_id + span_id injected!
Explanation

opentelemetry-instrumentation-logging is the package. Call LoggingInstrumentor().instrument() once at startup. set_logging_format=True replaces Python's default format with OTel's structured format. All existing logging.getLogger() calls become OTel-aware automatically.

Q6
What is the OTel severity number for INFO level?
Show Answer
Answer
  OTel Severity Mapping:
  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────┬────────────────────┐
  │ 1-4  TRACE   │ Below DEBUG     │ Framework internals │
  │ 5-8  DEBUG   │ DEBUG           │ Diagnostic info    │
  │ 9-12 INFO    │ INFO     ← Q6   │ Normal operations  │
  │ 13-16 WARN   │ WARNING         │ Potential issues   │
  │ 17-20 ERROR  │ ERROR           │ Operation failed   │
  │ 21-24 FATAL  │ CRITICAL        │ App cannot continue│
  └──────────────┴─────────────────┴────────────────────┘
Explanation

OTel uses numeric severity (1-24) while Python uses string levels. The mapping is automatic via LoggingInstrumentor. INFO = 9. The OTCA exam may ask for the severity number of a specific level.

Q7
How does log-trace correlation help with debugging?
Show Answer
Answer
  DEBUGGING WORKFLOW:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. Grafana alert: "POST /api/jobs/ error rate > 5%"         │
  │ 2. Click exemplar → opens trace in Jaeger                   │
  │ 3. Error span shows: "IntegrityError: duplicate key"        │
  │ 4. Copy trace_id: 4bf92f3577b34da6...                       │
  │ 5. Paste in Loki: {trace_id="4bf92f..."}                    │
  │ 6. See ALL logs: "DB pool at 95%", "retry failed"          │
  │ 7. Root cause found: pool exhaustion                        │
  │                                                              │
  │ BEFORE OTel: grep 10 files, 30+ minutes                     │
  │ AFTER OTel:  copy trace_id → paste → found in 30 seconds    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Without OTel, you grep through log files hoping to find related entries. With OTel, every log line from a request shares the same trace_id — query once, see everything. This is the killer feature that makes OTel worth adopting.

Q8
What is the Logs Bridge API?
Show Answer
Answer
  LOGS BRIDGE API:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Existing Logger ──bridge──▶ OTel LoggerProvider           │
  │ (Python logging,          │ → trace_id injection          │
  │  log4j, winston)          │ → OTLP export                 │
  │                           │ → same pipeline as traces     │
  │                           └──▶ Collector ──▶ Loki/ES      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  It BRIDGES — it does NOT replace your logger
Explanation

The Logs Bridge API is the OTel interface that connects existing logging frameworks to OTel's ecosystem. Your code doesn't change — you still use your preferred logger. OTel enriches and routes the logs transparently.

Q9
Should DEBUG-level logs be sent to production through OTel?
Show Answer
Answer
  LOG LEVEL STRATEGY:
  ┌──────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ DEBUG    │ ❌ NEVER in production                      │
  │          │ 10x volume, 10x storage cost, 0x value     │
  │          │ Set root logger to INFO                     │
  ├──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ INFO     │ ✅ Production standard                      │
  │          │ Business events, normal operations          │
  ├──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ WARNING+ │ ✅ Always send                              │
  │          │ Important for debugging                     │
  └──────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Defense in depth:
  1. Python: logging.getLogger().setLevel(logging.INFO)
  2. Collector: filter logs where severity < INFO
Explanation

DEBUG logs can be 10x the volume of INFO. At scale, that's 10x the storage cost for logs no one reads. Set root logger to INFO in production, and use Collector filtering as a second line of defense.

Q10
What protocol do OTel logs use to reach the backend?
Show Answer
Answer
  ALL THREE SIGNALS → OTLP → Collector → Backend
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ TRACES  ──OTLP/gRPC──▶                              │
  │ METRICS ──OTLP/gRPC──▶  Collector  ──▶  Backend     │
  │ LOGS    ──OTLP/gRPC──▶                              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  One protocol (OTLP) for ALL three signals
  Ports: gRPC=4317, HTTP=4318
Explanation

Before OTel, you'd use Jaeger protocol for traces, Prometheus format for metrics, and Fluentd/Logstash for logs — three different protocols. OTLP unifies all three into one wire format. This simplicity is a key reason for OTel's rapid adoption.

⚠️ Common Mistakes — OTel Logs

  • Replacing logger instead of bridging: OTel bridges — keep using your existing logger
  • Unstructured logs in production: Always use JSON. grep is not a query language
  • Sending DEBUG to production: 10x volume, 10x cost, 0x value
  • Forgetting LoggingInstrumentor: Without it, trace_id won't be injected
  • Not adding business attributes: user_id, plan, job_id make logs actually useful

Chapter 16: The OpenTelemetry Collector 🔴 Advanced

The OpenTelemetry Collector is the central routing layer between your applications and observability backends. It's a standalone Go binary that receives telemetry, processes it (batch, filter, enrich, transform), and exports it to one or more destinations. This chapter covers the complete Collector architecture, deployment modes, every component type, and a production-ready configuration for the anihpj platform.

🎯 OTCA Exam D4 (10%): The Collector is heavily tested. Know: Agent vs Gateway deployment, processors (batch, memory_limiter, attributes, filter), the pipeline YAML structure, and that the Collector is OPTIONAL but RECOMMENDED.
📥 Receive

Accept telemetry from: OTLP (4317/4318), Jaeger, Prometheus scrape, Zipkin, Kafka, Filelog, Host Metrics, Kubeletstats

⚙️ Process

Transform in-flight: Batch + Memory Limiter (ALWAYS), Attributes (enrich), Filter (drop health checks), Transform (OTTL rules)

📤 Export

Send to backends: OTLP, Jaeger, Prometheus (:9464), Prometheus Remote Write, Kafka, File, Logging (debug), Load Balancing

16.1 What is the OTel Collector?

Collector as Central Telemetry Router
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              OTEL COLLECTOR — THE CENTRAL ROUTING LAYER                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WITHOUT Collector:                     WITH Collector:                    │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐               ┌────────────────────┐              │
  │  │   anihpj API        │               │   anihpj API        │              │
  │  │   ├── Jaeger export │               │   OTLP only →       │              │
  │  │   ├── Prom export   │               │   Collector ────────┤              │
  │  │   └── Log export    │               └────────────────────┘              │
  │  └────────────────────┘                         │                          │
  │  ❌ Config in EVERY app                       ▼                          │
  │  ❌ No batching              ┌────────────────────────────────────┐       │
  │  ❌ No central enrichment    │         OTel Collector             │       │
  │  ❌ No protocol conversion   │  Receive → Process → Export        │       │
  │                              │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────────┐│       │
  │  Key features:               │  │Batch │  │Filter│  │Multi-    ││       │
  │  • ~30MB Go binary           │  │& Mem │  │Health│  │Backend   ││       │
  │  • Vendor-agnostic           │  │Limit │  │Checks│  │Routing   ││       │
  │  • Pluggable components      │  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────────┘│       │
  │  • otelcol vs otelcol-contrib│                                    │       │
  │  • OTLP-native at all stages └────────────────┬───────────────────┘       │
  │                                               │                           │
  │                           ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐       │
  │                           ▼                   ▼                   ▼       │
  │                      ┌────────┐         ┌──────────┐         ┌──────┐    │
  │                      │ Jaeger │         │Prometheus│         │ Loki │    │
  │                      └────────┘         └──────────┘         └──────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
✅ Why Use the Collector?

• Centralized config (not in every app)
• Batching + retry (reduces network overhead)
• Enrichment (add cluster/region without code changes)
• Routing (traces→Jaeger, metrics→Prom, logs→Loki)
• Filtering (drop health-check spans)
• Protocol conversion (OTLP→Jaeger native)

📦 otelcol vs otelcol-contrib

otelcol: Core receivers, processors, exporters
otelcol-contrib: Community contributions (more options). Use contrib for production — it has everything you need.

16.2 Deployment Modes: Agent (Sidecar) vs Gateway (Centralized)

Agent → Gateway Architecture (Recommended)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              AGENT (DaemonSet) → GATEWAY (Centralized)                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │                     KUBERNETES CLUSTER                            │   │
  │  │                                                                  │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐           │   │
  │  │  │   Node 1     │  │   Node 2     │  │   Node 3     │           │   │
  │  │  │ ┌──────────┐ │  │ ┌──────────┐ │  │ ┌──────────┐ │           │   │
  │  │  │ │App Pod   │ │  │ │App Pod   │ │  │ │App Pod   │ │           │   │
  │  │  │ │OTLP→Agent│ │  │ │OTLP→Agent│ │  │ │OTLP→Agent│ │           │   │
  │  │  │ └──────────┘ │  │ └──────────┘ │  │ └──────────┘ │           │   │
  │  │  │ Agent: batch  │  │ Agent: batch  │  │ Agent: batch  │           │   │
  │  │  │ + enrich      │  │ + enrich      │  │ + enrich      │           │   │
  │  │  └──────┬───────┘  └──────┬───────┘  └──────┬───────┘           │   │
  │  │         └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘                    │   │
  │  │                           │ OTLP                                  │   │
  │  │                           ▼                                       │   │
  │  │              ┌────────────────────────┐                            │   │
  │  │              │   GATEWAY COLLECTOR    │                            │   │
  │  │              │   (2-3 replicas)       │                            │   │
  │  │              │   Advanced processing: │                            │   │
  │  │              │   Multi-backend routing│                            │   │
  │  │              │   Tail sampling        │                            │   │
  │  │              └────────────────────────┘                            │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
AspectAgent (Sidecar/DaemonSet)Gateway (Centralized)
DeploymentOne per node (DaemonSet)Few replicas per cluster
ProsLocal batching, no SPOF, reduced networkCentralized config, fewer instances
ConsMore instances to manageNetwork dependency, potential SPOF
ProcessingLight: batch + enrichHeavy: routing, tail sampling, transform
Best ForProduction K8s (recommended with Gateway)Multi-tenant, multi-backend routing

16.3 Receivers: Accepting Telemetry

ReceiverProtocolDefault PortUse Case
OTLPgRPC/HTTP+Proto4317 / 4318Primary — all signals from OTel SDKs
JaegerThrift (legacy)14250Legacy Jaeger clients (pre-OTel)
PrometheusHTTP scrape(configurable)Collector scrapes Prometheus targets
ZipkinHTTP/JSON9411Legacy Zipkin clients
KafkaKafka protocol(configurable)Consume telemetry from Kafka topics
FilelogFile tail—Tail container/app log files
Host MetricsOS-level—CPU, memory, disk from host OS
KubeletstatsKubelet API—Pod/container metrics from Kubelet

16.4 Processors: Transforming Telemetry In-Flight

5 Essential Processors — What They Do
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              COLLECTOR PROCESSORS — THE PROCESSING PIPELINE                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  TELEMETRY IN → ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ →  │
  │                 │  Batch   │ │  Memory  │ │Attributes│ │  Filter  │     │
  │                 │ 200ms/   │ │  Limiter │ │ Add/Del  │ │ Drop     │     │
  │                 │ 8192 sp. │ │ 512 MiB  │ │ Upsert   │ │ health   │     │
  │                 └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  1. BATCH: Groups spans/metrics/logs for efficient export                │
  │     timeout: 200ms | send_batch_size: 8192 | send_batch_max_size: 0     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  2. MEMORY LIMITER: Prevents OOM by limiting memory use                  │
  │     limit_mib: 512 | spike_limit_mib: 256 | check_interval: 1s          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  3. ATTRIBUTES: Add/update/delete attributes                             │
  │     actions: [{key: "cluster", value: "prod-us-east", action: upsert}]   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  4. FILTER: Drop unwanted telemetry                                      │
  │     spans: [name == "GET /health"]  ← drop health checks!               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  5. TRANSFORM: OTTL (OpenTelemetry Transformation Language)              │
  │     set(span.name, attributes["http.route"]) where attributes["http."]   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

16.4a Batch & Memory Limiter — Always Use These

Production-Ready Batch + Memory Limiter
processors:
  batch:
    timeout: 5s
    send_batch_size: 512
    send_batch_max_size: 0  # no max, use timeout instead
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 512          # Hard limit: force GC
    spike_limit_mib: 256    # Soft limit: start rejecting
⚠️ CRITICAL: NEVER run a Collector in production without batch and memory_limiter processors. Without them: OOM kills, network saturation, and dropped telemetry.

16.4b Attributes, Filter & Transform

Production Filter + Attributes + Transform
processors:
  attributes:
    actions:
      - key: deployment.environment
        value: production
        action: upsert
      - key: k8s.cluster.name
        value: prod-us-east
        action: upsert
  filter:
    traces:
      span:
        - 'name == "GET /health"'
        - 'name == "GET /metrics"'
        - 'attributes["http.target"] == "/ready"'
  transform:
    trace_statements:
      - context: span
        statements:
          - set(name, attributes["http.route"]) where attributes["http.route"] != nil

16.4c Under the Hood — How the Collector Pipeline Actually Works

Understanding the Collector's internal processing model is essential for debugging pipeline issues and for the OTCA exam. Here is exactly what happens when a span enters the Collector:

Collector Internal Processing — A Span's Journey
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          HOW A SPAN FLOWS THROUGH THE COLLECTOR — INTERNAL VIEW            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  TIME: 0ms — RECEIVE                                                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ OTLPReceiver listens on :4317 (gRPC)                               │  │
  │  │ Receives: ExportTraceServiceRequest (protobuf)                      │  │
  │  │ Deserializes protobuf → internal pdata.Traces (Go struct)          │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ At this point: Raw spans in memory, no processing applied yet      │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  TIME: ~0.01ms — PROCESS (in order listed in config)                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Processor 1: memory_limiter                                         │  │
  │  │   → Checks: Is memory usage > limit_mib?                            │  │
  │  │   → If YES: returns "data refused" → SDK retries                   │  │
  │  │   → If NO: passes data through                                      │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Processor 2: attributes                                             │  │
  │  │   → Adds k8s.cluster.name="prod-us-east" to every span             │  │
  │  │   → Adds deployment.environment from resource detector              │  │
  │  │   → Each span now has MORE attributes than when it arrived          │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Processor 3: filter                                                 │  │
  │  │   → Checks each span: name == "GET /health"?                        │  │
  │  │   → If YES: span is DROPPED (removed from batch)                    │  │
  │  │   → If NO: span passes through                                      │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ Processor 4: batch (LAST processor — accumulates before export)     │  │
  │  │   → Accumulates spans into batch of size send_batch_size           │  │
  │  │   → OR waits until timeout expires                                  │  │
  │  │   → When batch is full OR timeout fires → flush to Exporters       │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                    │                                     │
  │                                    ▼                                     │
  │  TIME: ~200ms (batch timeout) — EXPORT                                     │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ OTLPExporter:                                                       │  │
  │  │   → Serializes pdata.Traces → protobuf                             │  │
  │  │   → Opens gRPC connection to backend:4317                           │  │
  │  │   → Sends ExportTraceServiceRequest                                 │  │
  │  │   → Waits for ExportTraceServiceResponse (ACK)                      │  │
  │  │                                                                   │  │
  │  │ If backend returns error:                                           │  │
  │  │   → Retry with exponential backoff (1s → 2s → 4s → ...)           │  │
  │  │   → Eventually drop if queue is full (configurable)                 │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🔑 KEY INSIGHTS:                                                         │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ 1. Processors run IN ORDER — batch should be LAST                   │  │
  │  │ 2. memory_limiter should be FIRST (reject early if OOM)             │  │
  │  │ 3. filter BEFORE attributes (don't enrich spans you'll drop)        │  │
  │  │ 4. Batch is per-signal: traces batch separately from metrics        │  │
  │  │ 5. Connectors are special: exporter in pipeline A, receiver in B    │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔧 Processor Order Matters

ALWAYS: memory_limiter FIRST, batch LAST. Filter before attributes (don't enrich spans you will drop). Transform before export. Wrong order = wasted CPU or OOM crashes.

⚡ Connectors: Pipeline Bridging

Connectors appear as EXPORTERS in one pipeline and RECEIVERS in another. Example: spanmetrics connector reads traces → generates RED metrics → feeds into metrics pipeline. This is how you get service-level metrics from traces automatically.

16.5 Exporters: Sending to Backends

ExporterSignalsProtocolUse Case
OTLPTraces, Metrics, LogsgRPC/HTTPTo another Collector or OTLP-native backend
JaegerTracesThrift gRPCLegacy Jaeger (use OTLP if Jaeger supports it)
PrometheusMetricsHTTP /metricsExpose endpoint for Prometheus to scrape
PrometheusRWMetricsRemote WritePush metrics to Prometheus-compatible backend
LoggingAllstdoutDebugging/development only
KafkaAllKafkaBuffer telemetry in Kafka for replay
FileAllFile systemDebugging, audit trail

16.6 Connectors: Span Metrics & Service Graph

Span Metrics Connector — Traces → RED Metrics
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              SPAN METRICS CONNECTOR                                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  TRACES PIPELINE                                    METRICS PIPELINE      │
  │  ┌──────────────┐                                  ┌──────────────┐      │
  │  │Spans from    │                                  │Derived RED   │      │
  │  │anihpj API    │──▶ ┌──────────────────┐─────────▶│Metrics:      │      │
  │  │              │    │ SPANMETRICS      │          │calls_total,  │      │
  │  │ POST /jobs/  │    │ CONNECTOR        │          │latency_bucket│      │
  │  │ GET /users/  │    │                  │          │errors_total  │      │
  │  └──────────────┘    │ Counts requests  │          │per service!  │      │
  │                      │ per span name    │          └──────────────┘      │
  │                      │ Measures latency │                                │
  │                      │ Counts errors    │   No need to instrument        │
  │                      └──────────────────┘   metrics separately!          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

16.7 Collector Configuration — YAML Deep Dive

Production Collector Config for anihpj
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

processors:
  batch:
    timeout: 5s
    send_batch_size: 512
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 512
  attributes:
    actions:
      - key: deployment.environment
        value: production
        action: upsert
  filter:
    traces:
      span:
        - 'name == "GET /health"'

exporters:
  otlp/jaeger:
    endpoint: jaeger:4317
    tls:
      insecure: true
  prometheus:
    endpoint: 0.0.0.0:9464
  logging:
    loglevel: debug

connectors:
  spanmetrics:
    histogram:
      explicit:
        buckets: [1ms, 5ms, 10ms, 50ms, 100ms, 500ms, 1s, 5s, 10s]

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch, attributes, filter]
      exporters: [otlp/jaeger, spanmetrics]
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp, spanmetrics]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [prometheus]
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [logging]

16.8 Hands-On: Deploy OTel Collector + Route anihpj Telemetry

1
Create Config
Save the production config above as otelcol-config.yaml
2
Start Collector
docker run -d --name otel-collector -p 4317:4317 -p 9464:9464 -v ./otelcol-config.yaml:/etc/otelcol/config.yaml otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib
3
Start Backends
docker run -d --name jaeger -p 16686:16686 -p 4317:4317 jaegertracing/all-in-one
4
Point anihpj to Collector
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4317 opentelemetry-instrument python manage.py runserver
5
Generate Traffic
Make requests to anihpj endpoints (GET /jobs/, POST /jobs/)
6
Verify
Traces in Jaeger (:16686), metrics at :9464/metrics, Collector logs on stdout

16.X Collector Troubleshooting — Common Issues and Fixes

The Collector is the central routing layer — when it breaks, ALL telemetry stops flowing. The OTCA exam tests your ability to diagnose common Collector issues.

Collector Troubleshooting Decision Tree
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              COLLECTOR TROUBLESHOOTING — WHAT IS BROKEN?                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SYMPTOM: "No traces appearing in Jaeger"                                 │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         ├── Check Collector logs first:                                   │
  │         │   docker logs otel-collector                                   │
  │         │   Look for: "connection refused", "timeout", "unauthorized"    │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         ├── Is Collector RECEIVING data?                                  │
  │         │   Enable logging exporter at debug level                        │
  │         │   If NO spans in log → app not sending to Collector             │
  │         │   Fix: Check OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT in app                │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         ├── Is Collector PROCESSING data?                                 │
  │         │   Check memory_limiter: is it dropping spans (OOM)?            │
  │         │   Check batch processor: timeout too short?                    │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         └── Is Collector EXPORTING data?                                  │
  │             Check exporter config: correct endpoint? TLS settings?       │
  │             Test: curl http://jaeger:4317 (reachable from Collector?)    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  TOP 5 COLLECTOR ISSUES:                                                  │
  │  ┌─────┬───────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  1  │ "connection refused"      │ Backend not running or wrong port │  │
  │  │  2  │ "OOM killed"              │ memory_limiter not configured     │  │
  │  │  3  │ "no data in backend"     │ Pipeline misconfigured            │  │
  │  │  4  │ "high latency"            │ Batch timeout too long            │  │
  │  │  5  │ "missing k8s attributes"  │ k8sattributes processor not set  │  │
  │  └─────┴───────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ #1 Collector Mistake: No Memory Limiter

Running the Collector without memory_limiter processor is the most common production outage cause. Under load, the Collector consumes more and more memory until the OOM killer terminates it — all telemetry stops flowing. The fix is 4 lines of YAML: add memory_limiter with limit_mib set to 50% of the container's memory limit. The OTCA exam WILL ask: "Which two processors should ALWAYS be enabled?" → batch + memory_limiter.

📝 OTCA Practice Questions — Chapter 16

Q1
Is the OTel Collector required for using OpenTelemetry?
Show Answer
Answer
  Collector = OPTIONAL but RECOMMENDED
  
  WITHOUT Collector:              WITH Collector:
  App → SDK → Backend             App → SDK → Collector → Backend
  ✅ Simpler setup                ✅ Batching + retry
  ❌ No central config            ✅ Central enrichment
  ❌ No multi-backend routing     ✅ Filter + transform
  ❌ No protocol conversion       ✅ Multi-backend routing
Explanation

The Collector is optional — you can export directly from SDK to backend. But in production, the Collector provides essential capabilities: batching, filtering, enrichment, and multi-backend routing. OTCA exam: "Is Collector required?" → NO, but recommended.

Q2
What is the difference between Agent and Gateway deployment?
Show Answer
Answer
  AGENT (per-node):                GATEWAY (centralized):
  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ DaemonSet (1/node)   │        │ Deployment (2-3 reps)│
  │ Local batching       │        │ Advanced processing  │
  │ Light enrichment     │──OTLP─▶│ Multi-backend routing│
  │ No SPOF              │        │ Tail sampling        │
  └──────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘
  
  BEST PRACTICE: Agent → Gateway → Backend
Explanation

Agent handles local batching per node (reduces network). Gateway handles centralized processing (routing, tail sampling, advanced transforms). The recommended architecture uses both: apps → local Agent → centralized Gateway → backends.

Q3
Which two processors should ALWAYS be enabled in production?
Show Answer
Answer
  MANDATORY processors:
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ batch            │ Groups spans into batches            │
  │ timeout: 5s      │ Reduces network calls by 100-1000x  │
  │ send_batch: 512  │ Without it: 1 span = 1 network call │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ memory_limiter   │ Prevents OOM kills                   │
  │ limit_mib: 512   │ Soft limit (spike) → reject          │
  │ spike_limit: 256 │ Hard limit → force GC                │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

NEVER run Collector without these two. Batch reduces network overhead by 100-1000x. Memory limiter prevents the Go runtime from OOM-ing under load — it will start rejecting data at the soft limit rather than crashing.

Q4
What does the Span Metrics Connector do?
Show Answer
Answer
  SPANMETRICS CONNECTOR: Traces → RED Metrics
  
  TRACES PIPELINE              METRICS PIPELINE
  ┌──────────────┐            ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Spans from   │            │ calls_total      │
  │ anihpj API   │──CONNECTOR─▶│ latency_bucket   │
  │ POST /jobs/  │            │ errors_total     │
  └──────────────┘            └──────────────────┘
  
  Result: RED metrics AUTOMATICALLY from spans
  No metric instrumentation code needed!
Explanation

The Span Metrics Connector bridges the traces and metrics pipelines. It counts requests, measures latency, and counts errors from span data — generating RED metrics automatically. OTCA exam: "How to get RED metrics without writing metric code?" → Span Metrics Connector.

Q5
What are the default OTLP ports on the Collector?
Show Answer
Answer
  Collector Ports:
  ┌──────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 4317 │ OTLP gRPC — primary, high performance      │
  │ 4318 │ OTLP HTTP — browser/firewall friendly       │
  │ 9464 │ Prometheus /metrics — for scraping          │
  │ 8888 │ Collector health check endpoint             │
  └──────┴────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

4317 (gRPC) is the primary receiver port. 4318 (HTTP) is used when gRPC is blocked or for browser-based telemetry. Know both port numbers for the OTCA exam.

Q6
How do you drop health check spans in the Collector?
Show Answer
Answer
processors:
  filter:
    traces:
      span:
        - 'name == "GET /health"'
        - 'name == "GET /metrics"'
        - 'name == "GET /ready"'
# These can be 15-30% of all traffic!
# Dropping them saves significant storage cost
Explanation

Health checks, metrics scrapes, and readiness probes generate massive amounts of low-value telemetry. The Filter processor drops them before they reach storage. This alone can reduce trace volume by 15-30%. OTCA exam expects you to know how to use the Filter processor.

Q7
What is the difference between otelcol and otelcol-contrib?
Show Answer
Answer
  otelcol (core):                   otelcol-contrib:
  ┌──────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ OTLP receiver        │         │ Everything in core   │
  │ Batch processor      │         │ + Jaeger receiver    │
  │ Memory limiter       │         │ + Prometheus receiver│
  │ Logging exporter     │         │ + Kafka exporter     │
  │ OTLP exporter        │         │ + Filelog receiver   │
  │                      │         │ + Host metrics       │
  │ Use for: minimal     │         │ + Many more...       │
  └──────────────────────┘         │ Use for: PRODUCTION  │
                                   └──────────────────────┘
Explanation

Core has only the most essential components. Contrib includes community contributions — most production deployments need at least one contrib component (e.g., prometheus exporter, kafka receiver). Always use contrib for production. OTCA exam may ask about this distinction.

Q8
Can the Collector receive data from and export to multiple backends simultaneously?
Show Answer
Answer
  Multi-backend routing:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   OTel Collector                     │
  │                                                     │
  │  traces ──▶ [otlp/jaeger, otlp/tempo]               │
  │  metrics──▶ [prometheus, otlp/mimir]                │
  │  logs  ──▶ [otlp/loki, logging]                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  YES — list multiple exporters per pipeline
  Each exporter receives the SAME data
Explanation

Multi-backend routing is a key Collector feature. During migrations, you can dual-write to old and new backends simultaneously. List multiple exporters in the pipeline array — both receive identical data. OTCA exam: this enables zero-downtime backend migrations.

Q9
What is the purpose of the Attributes processor?
Show Answer
Answer
processors:
  attributes:
    actions:
      - key: deployment.environment    # ADD cluster info
        value: production              # without touching
        action: upsert                 # application code!
      - key: k8s.cluster.name
        value: prod-us-east
        action: upsert
      - key: user.email                # DELETE sensitive data
        action: delete                  # before it reaches storage
Explanation

The Attributes processor modifies telemetry in-flight. Use upsert to add cluster/region/environment metadata. Use delete to remove sensitive data (emails, PII) before storage. This is done at the Collector level — no application code changes needed.

Q10
How do pipelines work in the Collector YAML config?
Show Answer
Answer
  Pipeline structure:
  service:
    pipelines:
      traces:                          # One pipeline per signal
        receivers:  [otlp]             # ← Where data comes IN
        processors: [batch, filter]    # ← How data is TRANSFORMED
        exporters:  [otlp/jaeger]      # ← Where data goes OUT
      metrics:
        receivers:  [otlp, spanmetrics] # Can have MULTIPLE receivers!
        processors: [batch]
        exporters:  [prometheus]
      logs:
        receivers:  [otlp]
        processors: [batch]
        exporters:  [logging]
Explanation

Each signal (traces, metrics, logs) gets its own pipeline. The pipeline defines the flow: receivers → processors → exporters. Connectors (like spanmetrics) can bridge between pipelines — they appear as an exporter in one pipeline and a receiver in another.

⚠️ Common Mistakes — Collector

  • No batch processor: Every span = one network call = terrible performance
  • No memory_limiter: Traffic spike = OOM kill = lost telemetry
  • Using core instead of contrib: Core is minimal; contrib has what you need
  • Health checks filling storage: Use filter processor to drop /health, /ready, /metrics
  • One pipeline for all signals: Traces, metrics, logs need separate pipelines

Chapter 17: OpenTelemetry Exporters 🔴 Advanced

Exporters are the exit point of the OTel pipeline — they send telemetry OUT to backends. They exist in TWO places: the SDK (SimpleSpanProcessor → OTLPSpanExporter) and the Collector (YAML-configured exporters). This chapter covers every exporter type, their protocols, and a hands-on demonstration of routing anihpj telemetry to multiple backends with zero code changes.

🎯 OTCA Exam: Know the difference between SDK exporters (in-app, simple) and Collector exporters (centralized, multi-destination). OTLP is the STANDARD — always prefer it over legacy exporters like native Jaeger or Zipkin.

17.1 What are Exporters?

AspectSDK ExporterCollector Exporter
LocationInside your applicationInside the Collector
ConfigurationPython/Java/JS codeYAML config file
CapabilitySingle signal, single destinationMulti-signal, multi-destination routing
RetryLimited (in-process)Persistent queue + retry + DLQ
Use WhenDevelopment, simple setupsProduction (ALWAYS)

17.2 OTLP Exporter — The Standard

OTLP — SDK and Collector Configuration
# SDK: OTLP Exporter (Python)
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.grpc.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter
exporter = OTLPSpanExporter(
    endpoint="http://collector:4317",
    insecure=True,
    headers={"api-key": "xxx"},
    timeout=10
)

# Collector: OTLP Exporter
exporters:
  otlp:
    endpoint: backend:4317
    tls:
      cert_file: /certs/client.crt
      key_file: /certs/client.key
🔌 gRPC (4317)

Binary protobuf, streaming, high performance. Default for service-to-service. Best for: Collector-to-backend.

🌐 HTTP/Protobuf (4318)

Binary protobuf over HTTP, no streaming. Browser-friendly, works with restrictive firewalls. Best for: Browser RUM, serverless.

17.3 Console/Logging Exporter — For Debugging

Prints telemetry to stdout. Development ONLY — never in production. Useful for: "Am I generating spans? What attributes are on this span?"

from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import ConsoleSpanExporter
# SDK: Print spans to console
span_processor = SimpleSpanProcessor(ConsoleSpanExporter())

17.4 Jaeger Exporter (Traces)

💡 Recommendation: Use OTLP exporter → Jaeger (Jaeger accepts OTLP natively on 4317). The native Jaeger exporter (thrift, port 14250) is LEGACY. OTLP is the future.
exporters:
  otlp/jaeger:
    endpoint: jaeger-collector:4317
    tls:
      insecure: true

17.5 Prometheus Exporter (Metrics — Pull)

Prometheus Pull Model via Collector
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  anihpj SDK → OTLP → Collector → /metrics (:9464) → Prometheus  │
  │                          ▲                                       │
  │                          └── Prometheus scrapes this endpoint    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

# Collector config
exporters:
  prometheus:
    endpoint: 0.0.0.0:9464
    namespace: anihpj
    resource_to_telemetry_conversion:
      enabled: true  # resource attrs → metric labels

# Prometheus scrape config
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'otel-collector'
    scrape_interval: 30s
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['collector:9464']

17.6 OTLP HTTP Exporter (Metrics — Push)

Push metrics via OTLP/HTTP — alternative to Prometheus pull. Use when: backend supports OTLP native ingestion (Grafana Cloud, Datadog), ephemeral workloads (serverless, batch), or you want consistent OTLP protocol for all signals.

17.7 Zipkin, Kafka, and File Exporters

ExporterPurposeWhen to Use
ZipkinLegacy Zipkin backend supportExisting Zipkin installations (migrate to OTLP)
KafkaPublish to Kafka topics (decoupled, replayable)Buffer telemetry in Kafka before backend ingestion
FileWrite to files (JSON or protobuf)Debugging, audit trail, offline analysis
Load BalancingRoute to multiple backends (trace_id hash)Horizontal scaling of backends, A/B testing

17.8 Hands-On: Configure Multiple Exporters for anihpj

Multi-Exporter Collector Config
exporters:
  otlp/jaeger:
    endpoint: jaeger:4317
    tls:
      insecure: true
  prometheus:
    endpoint: 0.0.0.0:9464
  logging:
    loglevel: debug

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [batch]
      exporters: [otlp/jaeger, logging]
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [batch]
      exporters: [prometheus, logging]
🔑 The OTel Promise: Change backends by editing ONE YAML file. Zero code changes in anihpj. Switch from Jaeger to Tempo: just change endpoint: jaeger:4317 to endpoint: tempo:4317.

17.X Exporter Selection — Which Exporter for Which Use Case?

The OTCA exam tests your ability to choose the right exporter. Here is the definitive framework:

Exporter Decision Framework — Which One When?
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              WHICH EXPORTER TO USE? — DECISION TREE                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  START: What signal and destination?                                      │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         ├── Sending ALL signals to any backend ──▶ OTLP exporter         │
  │         │   endpoint: jaeger:4317 (or tempo, datadog, grafana cloud)     │
  │         │   ONE protocol for traces + metrics + logs                     │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         ├── Metrics scraped by Prometheus ──▶ Prometheus exporter        │
  │         │   endpoint: 0.0.0.0:9464  (Prometheus PULLS from here)        │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         ├── Debugging/development ──▶ Console/Logging exporter           │
  │         │   Prints to stdout — NEVER in production                      │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         ├── Async/buffered pipeline ──▶ Kafka exporter                   │
  │         │   Good for: decoupling, replay, multi-consumer                 │
  │         │                                                                │
  │         └── Static analysis/offline ──▶ File exporter                    │
  │             Saves to JSON files on disk                                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  GOLDEN RULE: ALWAYS use OTLP exporter as primary. Add Prometheus        │
  │  exporter if using Prometheus (pull model). Add logging exporter at       │
  │  DEBUG level for troubleshooting. NEVER Console exporter in production.   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 OTCA Practice Questions — Chapter 17

Q1
What is the recommended exporter for all signals?
Show Answer
Answer
  OTLP — One protocol for ALL signals:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ TRACES ──OTLP──▶                                    │
  │ METRICS──OTLP──▶  Collector ──▶  Backend            │
  │ LOGS  ──OTLP──▶                                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Always prefer OTLP over legacy exporters:
  ❌ Jaeger native (thrift)  →  ✅ OTLP to Jaeger
  ❌ Zipkin                   →  ✅ OTLP to Zipkin
  ❌ Prometheus pull only     →  ✅ OTLP + Prom exporter
Explanation

OTLP is the standard, vendor-neutral protocol defined by the OpenTelemetry specification. It supports gRPC (4317) and HTTP (4318). All major backends now accept OTLP natively. The OTCA exam expects you to know that OTLP is the preferred exporter for ALL signals.

Q2
Where can exporters exist in the OTel ecosystem?
Show Answer
Answer
  SDK EXPORTER:                      COLLECTOR EXPORTER:
  ┌──────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Inside your app      │          │ Inside Collector     │
  │ SimpleSpanProcessor  │          │ YAML-configured      │
  │ Single destination   │          │ Multi-destination    │
  │ Limited retry        │          │ Persistent queue     │
  │                      │          │ + retry + DLQ        │
  │ Use: Development     │          │ Use: PRODUCTION      │
  └──────────────────────┘          └──────────────────────┘
Explanation

Exporters can be in the SDK (SimpleSpanProcessor → OTLPSpanExporter) or in the Collector (YAML). Production always uses Collector exporters for batching, retry, and multi-backend routing. SDK exporters are mainly for development and simple setups.

Q3
What are the default OTLP ports?
Show Answer
Answer
  OTLP Ports:
  ┌──────┬──────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 4317 │ gRPC     │ Binary protobuf, high-perf      │
  │ 4318 │ HTTP     │ JSON or binary, browser-friendly │
  └──────┴──────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Other important ports:
  9464 = Prometheus /metrics    16686 = Jaeger UI
  9090 = Prometheus UI          3000  = Grafana UI
Explanation

4317 is the default for gRPC (streaming, high performance). 4318 is for HTTP/Protobuf (browser-friendly, works behind restrictive firewalls). Memorize both — the OTCA exam will test port numbers.

Q4
When should you use the Console/Logging exporter?
Show Answer
Answer
  Console/Logging exporter:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ Use: Development & Debugging                      │
  │    "Am I generating spans at all?"                   │
  │    "What attributes are on this span?"               │
  │                                                      │
  │ ❌ NEVER: Production                                 │
  │    Noisy stdout, synchronous I/O, adds latency       │
  │    No retry, no batching, data lost on restart       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

The Console/Logging exporter prints telemetry to stdout. It's invaluable during development to verify spans are being created, but it's synchronous and adds latency. In production, always use OTLP or other buffered exporters.

Q5
What is the Prometheus exporter in the Collector and how does it bridge push/pull?
Show Answer
Answer
  BRIDGE: OTel PUSH → Prometheus PULL
  
  ┌──────────┐   OTLP PUSH   ┌──────────┐   HTTP GET    ┌──────────┐
  │ anihpj   │──────────────▶│ Collector│◀──────────────│Prometheus│
  │ SDK      │   (:4317)     │ :9464    │   /metrics    │ (:9090)  │
  └──────────┘               └──────────┘               └──────────┘
  
  Collector exposes /metrics endpoint
  Prometheus scrapes it on schedule (every 30s)
Explanation

The Prometheus exporter exposes a /metrics endpoint (default :9464). This is how the Collector bridges OTel's push model with Prometheus's pull model. Apps push OTLP to the Collector; Prometheus scrapes the Collector's /metrics endpoint.

Q6
How does the Kafka exporter help with reliability?
Show Answer
Answer
  KAFKA as Telemetry Buffer:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ App → Collector → Kafka → Collector → Backend        │
  │                     │                                │
  │                     └── Buffer/Queue                 │
  │                         If backend is DOWN:          │
  │                         telemetry stays in Kafka     │
  │                         When backend UP:             │
  │                         replay from Kafka            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Decoupled ✅  Durable ✅  Replayable ✅
Explanation

Kafka acts as a durable buffer between the Collector and the backend. If the backend is down for hours, no telemetry is lost — it stays in Kafka. When the backend recovers, it replays from the Kafka offset. This is used by high-reliability systems that can't afford to lose telemetry.

Q7
What is the Load Balancing exporter used for?
Show Answer
Answer
  LOAD BALANCING EXPORTER:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               Collector                              │
  │                 │                                    │
  │    ┌────────────┼────────────┐                      │
  │    ▼            ▼            ▼                      │
  │ Backend-1   Backend-2   Backend-3                   │
  │                                                      │
  │ Consistent hashing on trace_id                      │
  │ Same trace_id → always same backend                 │
  │ Use: Scale backends horizontally                     │
  │ Use: A/B test new backend version                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

The Load Balancing exporter routes spans to multiple backend instances using consistent hashing on trace_id. This ensures all spans from the same trace go to the same backend instance (required for trace assembly). Use it to horizontally scale your tracing backend or canary-test new versions.

Q8
Can one Collector pipeline have multiple exporters?
Show Answer
Answer
  YES — Multiple exporters per pipeline:
  
  service:
    pipelines:
      traces:
        exporters: [otlp/jaeger, otlp/tempo, logging]
        #           ↑              ↑            ↑
        #      All three receive the SAME trace data!
  
  Use cases:
  • Dual-write during migration (Jaeger → Tempo)
  • Debugging: add logging exporter temporarily
  • Evaluate new backend alongside existing one
Explanation

Multiple exporters in a pipeline ALL receive identical data. This is used for dual-write migrations (evaluate a new backend while keeping the old one) and debugging (add a logging exporter to see what's being sent). OTCA exam: dual-write = list multiple exporters.

Q9
Why should you prefer OTLP over native Jaeger exporter?
Show Answer
Answer
  OTLP vs Native Jaeger:
  ┌──────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ OTLP (preferred) │ Native Jaeger (legacy)          │
  ├──────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Vendor-neutral   │ Jaeger-specific                 │
  │ All 3 signals    │ Traces only                     │
  │ gRPC:4317        │ Thrift:14250                    │
  │ Future-proof     │ Being phased out                │
  │ Jaeger accepts   │ Still works but...              │
  │ OTLP natively!   │ OTLP is the standard now        │
  └──────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘
Explanation

Jaeger now accepts OTLP natively on port 4317 — you don't need the native Jaeger exporter anymore. Use the OTLP exporter pointed at Jaeger. This future-proofs your setup and uses a single protocol for all signals. OTCA exam: always prefer OTLP.

Q10
How do you switch backends with zero code changes?
Show Answer
Answer
  SWITCHING BACKENDS — ZERO APP CHANGES:
  
  BEFORE (Jaeger):                AFTER (Tempo):
  exporters:                      exporters:
    otlp:                           otlp:
      endpoint: jaeger:4317          endpoint: tempo:4317
                                      ↑ ONLY THIS LINE CHANGES
  
  ┌────────────────────┐          ┌────────────────────┐
  │ anihpj: UNCHANGED  │          │ anihpj: UNCHANGED  │
  │ settings.py: same  │          │ settings.py: same  │
  │ views.py: same     │          │ views.py: same     │
  │ OTLP → Collector   │          │ OTLP → Collector   │
  └────────────────────┘          └────────────────────┘
  
  "Instrument once. Export anywhere. Forever."
Explanation

The OTel promise: your application code NEVER changes when switching backends. The app always sends OTLP to the Collector. Only the Collector's YAML config changes — one line. This eliminates vendor lock-in. OTCA exam will test this core OTel value proposition.

Chapter 18: Vendor Backends and Observability Platforms 🔴 Advanced

The ultimate value of OpenTelemetry is backend freedom — instrument once, export anywhere. This chapter covers the major backends: the open-source Grafana LGTM stack (Loki, Grafana, Tempo, Mimir) and commercial platforms (Datadog, Honeycomb, New Relic, Dynatrace, Splunk). You'll learn their unique features, pricing models, and how OTel enables switching between them with ZERO code changes in anihpj.

18.1 Open Source: The Grafana LGTM Stack

LGTM Stack — Open Source, OTLP-Native

  │                    GRAFANA LGTM STACK (All Open Source)                    │

  │  │ API      │  │ Worker   │  │ Tasks    │                               │
  │  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘                               │
  │       └──────────────┼─────────────┘                                     │
  │                      │ OTLP                                              │
  │                      ▼                                                   │

  │              └───┬───┬───┬────┘                                          │

  │  │ Traces     │ │ Metrics  │ │ Logs      │                               │
  │  │ S3 Storage │ │ S3 Store │ │ S3 Store  │                               │

  │        └──────────────┼────────────┘                                     │
  │                       ▼                                                  │
  │              ┌────────────────┐                                          │
  │              │ 📈 Grafana      │  ← Single UI for ALL data               │
  │              │ Dashboards     │                                          │
  │              │ Alerts + SLOs  │                                          │
  │              │ Explore view   │                                          │
  │              └────────────────┘                                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔍 Tempo (Traces)

• Object storage (S3/GCS) — cheap, infinite scale
• TraceQL: query language for traces
• No span attribute indexing (cost-efficient)
• OTLP-native ingestion

📝 Loki (Logs)

• "Prometheus for logs" — label-based indexing
• LogQL: {service="anihpj"} |= "ERROR"
• S3/GCS storage = cheap, long retention
• OTLP-native log ingestion

📊 Mimir (Metrics)

• Horizontally scalable Prometheus
• 1B+ active series, multi-tenant
• S3-backed, 100% Prometheus compatible
• OTLP-native metric ingestion

📈 Grafana (Visualization)

• Single UI for traces, metrics, logs
• Correlate: click log → "View trace"
• Dashboard as Code (JSON, GitOps)
• Unified alerting across all sources

🔥 Pyroscope — The 4th Signal (Continuous Profiling): Grafana Pyroscope adds continuous profiling to the LGTM stack. It captures CPU/memory flame graphs per service and integrates with Grafana: click a slow span → "View Profile" → see exactly which function is consuming CPU. Think of it as "traces, but for code execution." Emerging as the 4th observability signal alongside traces, metrics, and logs.

18.2a Datadog & Honeycomb

🐶 Datadog — All-in-One Platform

• Infrastructure + APM + Logs + RUM + Security
• Auto-correlates traces with logs and host metrics
• Watchdog AI: automated anomaly detection
• OTLP native ingestion (newer)
• Pricing: ~$15-40/host/month
• Best for: Teams wanting one platform for everything

🍯 Honeycomb — Observability-First

• Founded by Charity Majors (ex-Facebook)
• BubbleUp: statistical analysis of traces
• HIGH cardinality: query by user_id, trace_id
• SLO-based: real-time error budget tracking
• OTLP-native since 2019 (earliest adopter!)
• Pricing: ~$0.10/1M events
• Best for: Unknown unknowns discovery

18.2b New Relic, Dynatrace & Splunk

📊 New Relic

• Traditional APM, recently added OTLP
• Strengths: Service maps, deployment markers
• JVM/.NET deep instrumentation
• Free tier: 100GB/month
• Best for: Java/.NET shops

🤖 Dynatrace

• Enterprise AIOps with Davis® AI engine
• OneAgent: auto-instruments 12+ languages
• Automatic topology mapping + RUM
• Pricing: per-host (enterprise)
• Best for: Large enterprises

📈 Splunk Observability

• NoSample™: stores EVERY span (not sampled)
• Real-time streaming analytics
• Splunk Enterprise integration
• Pricing: complex (talk to sales)
• Best for: Splunk-heavy orgs
